Abstract.

These are live-TeXed (for all talks besides my own and those of Shuai Guo, some figures were inserted later using Codex or Claude Code) notes from the log GLSM summer school at Sichuan University in July 2026. Note that all talks (besides mine) were given in Chinese. I apologize for any translation errors as well as for any errors in my lectures. In addition, the notes for the two lectures by Shuai Guo are experimental AI-generated transcriptions of his slides. While I did give Claude access to all of my other notes to see what my writing style is, please let me know if there is a mismatch in writing style or if there are any errors. Finally, I would like to thank You-Cheng Chou, Tingting Fang, and Yaoxiong Wen for pointing out mistakes in the notes.

1 Theta-stratifications (Yaoxiong Wen and Bin Wang)

1.1 Our first moduli problems.

Our first moduli space will be ℙN−1, which parameterizes 1-dimensional linear subspaces in ℂN, or equivalently is the geometric quotient (ℂN∖{0})/ℂ×. In this case every ℂ×-orbit in ℂN∖{0} is closed. This construction is our first example of geometric invariant theory. In general, a set-valued moduli problem assigns to every scheme T a collection of isomorphism classes of families over T, and we can think of it as a functor

F:(𝖲𝖼𝗁/S)op→𝖲𝖾𝗍.
Example 1.1.

Let C be a smooth projective curve. Then consider the assignment

Fr,d:T⟼{E| E⁢ is a vector bundle on ⁢C×T,
rk(Et¯)=r,deg(Et¯)=d for every geometric point t¯→T}/∼,

where Et¯=E|C×{t¯} and ∼ denotes isomorphism of vector bundles on C×T. This parameterizes isomorphism classes of families of vector bundles on C, but it is still not the correct stack-valued moduli problem.

Example 1.2.

By the Yoneda Lemma, every scheme Y defines a moduli problem.

Unfortunately, not every groupoid-valued moduli problem can be represented, as a stack, by a scheme or algebraic space. A scheme or algebraic space has trivial inertia, whereas objects in a moduli problem may have nontrivial automorphisms. For example, if we consider the moduli of line bundles on ℙ1, each line bundle has an entire ℂ× of automorphisms. Therefore, when we consider moduli problems, we need to remember both the objects and the isomorphisms between them, and the target of the functor should be the category of groupoids.

Definition 1.3 (informal).

A stack 𝔛 over S is a pseudofunctor

(𝖲𝖼𝗁/S)op→𝖦𝗋𝗉𝖽

which satisfies descent for objects and morphisms with respect to the fppf topology.

Example 1.4.

Consider the stack 𝖡𝗎𝗇r,d⁢(C) which sends a scheme T to the groupoid whose objects are vector bundles E on T×C such that every geometric fiber Et¯ has rank r and degree d, and whose morphisms are isomorphisms of vector bundles on T×C.

Unfortunately, there are far too many stacks to consider, so we will need to consider a subclass of stacks which is amenable to the methods of algebraic geometry.

Definition 1.5.

An algebraic stack is a stack with representable (by algebraic spaces) diagonal and with a smooth surjective morphism from a scheme U (which is called an atlas).

Note that the first condition means that for any morphism T→𝔛×𝔛 from an algebraic space, then T×𝔛×𝔛𝔛 is an algebraic space. This is equivalent to all Isom sheaves being algebraic spaces and implies that any morphism from a scheme to 𝔛 is representable.

Remark 1.6.

For sets, if we have morphisms f:A→C and g:B→C, then the fiber product is

A×CB={(a,b)|f⁡(a)=g⁡(b)}.

For schemes or algebraic spaces, the same formula describes the T-points of the scheme-theoretic fiber product. For stacks, a T-point of the 2-fiber product 𝔄×ℭ𝔅 is a triple (a,b,ϕ), where a∈𝔄⁡(T), b∈𝔅⁡(T), and

ϕ:f⁡(a)→∼g⁡(b)

is an isomorphism in ℭ⁡(T). Thus equality must be replaced by an isomorphism, and the isomorphism must be recorded as part of the data.

1.2 Quotient stacks.

Let G be an algebraic group and let X be a scheme with a left action of G.

Definition 1.7.

The quotient stack [X/G] sends a scheme T to the groupoid whose objects are diagrams

where P→T is a right principal G-bundle for the fppf topology and φ satisfies φ⁡(p⁢g)=g−1⁢φ⁢(p). A morphism from (P,φ) to (P′,φ′) is an isomorphism of principal G-bundles P→∼P′ compatible with the maps to X.

Example 1.8.

Let 𝔛 be a smooth separated DM stack of finite type over ℂ. If either the generic stabilizer of 𝔛 is trivial or the coarse moduli space of 𝔛 is quasi-projective, then 𝔛 is a global quotient [EHKV01]. Here, a DM stack is an algebraic stack with unramified diagonal, and a global quotient means a stack of the form [U/GLn] for some algebraic space U with an action of GLn.

Exercise 1.9.

Show that the groupoid [X/G]⁢(ℂ) is equivalent to the action groupoid of G⁡(ℂ) acting on X⁡(ℂ).

After choosing one representative xi∈X⁡(ℂ) of each G⁡(ℂ)-orbit, the above exercise implies that, as an abstract groupoid and not as an algebraic stack, we have

[X/G]⁢(ℂ)≃⨆[xi]∈X⁡(ℂ)/G⁡(ℂ)B⁢Gxi,

where Gxi is the stabilizer of xi.

1.3 Fine vs coarse vs good moduli spaces.

Definition 1.10.

A fine moduli space for a moduli problem is a scheme or algebraic space M which represents the functor.

Unfortunately, it is very hard to find a fine moduli space, so we want to weaken this condition.

Definition 1.11.

A coarse moduli space for an algebraic stack 𝔛 is a morphism π:𝔛→M to an algebraic space such that

  1. (1)

    For every algebraic space Y, composition with π induces a bijection

    Hom⁡(M,Y)→∼Hom⁡(𝔛,Y);
  2. (2)

    For every algebraically closed field K, the induced map

    π0⁢(𝔛⁡(K))={isomorphism classes in ⁢𝔛⁢(K)}⟶M⁡(K)

    is a bijection.

Even these do not always exist. A good moduli space is a different weakening: it replaces the requirement of a bijection on geometric points by a cohomological affineness condition [Alp13].

Definition 1.12.

A quasi-compact morphism q:𝔛→X from an algebraic stack to an algebraic space is a good moduli space if

  1. (1)

    The pushforward functor q∗:𝖰𝖢𝗈𝗁⁡(𝔛)→𝖰𝖢𝗈𝗁⁡(X) is exact;

  2. (2)

    The natural map 𝒪X→q∗⁢𝒪𝔛 is an isomorphism.

The existence of these moduli spaces is not determined only by whether stabilizers are finite or infinite. For example, B⁢𝔾m→Spec⁡ℂ is both a coarse moduli space and a good moduli space, even though its stabilizer is 𝔾m.

Theorem 1.13 (Keel-Mori [KM97]).

Let 𝔛 be an algebraic stack of finite type over ℂ. If its inertia morphism

I𝔛≔𝔛×𝔛×𝔛𝔛⟶𝔛

is finite, then 𝔛 admits a coarse moduli space. The fiber of I𝔛→𝔛 over a geometric point x is the automorphism group Aut⁡(x).

Theorem 1.14 (Alper–Hall–Rydh [AHR20]).

Let

q:𝔛⟶X

be a good moduli space, where 𝔛 is a Noetherian algebraic stack over ℂ with affine diagonal. Let x∈𝔛⁡(ℂ) be a closed point, and denote its stabilizer group by Gx.

Then there exists an affine scheme Spec⁡A equipped with an action of Gx, together with a Cartesian diagram

where

Spec⁡(AGx)⟶X

is an étale neighborhood of q⁡(x).

For r≥2, the stack 𝖡𝗎𝗇r,d⁢(C) is locally of finite type, but it is neither quasi-compact nor separated. To see that it is not quasi-compact, choose line bundles Ln and Md−n of degrees n and d−n, respectively, and consider

En=Ln⊕Md−n⊕𝒪C⊕r−2.

The bundle En contains a line subbundle of degree n. In any quasi-compact family of vector bundles of fixed rank and degree, the degrees of line subbundles are bounded above, so the bundles En cannot all lie in a quasi-compact substack as n→∞. To see that the stack is not separated, note that every vector bundle E has scalar automorphisms 𝔾m⊂Aut⁡(E). Stabilizer groups of a separated algebraic stack are proper, whereas 𝔾m is not proper. Passing to semistable bundles does not make the stack separated; rather, it cuts out a bounded open substack of finite type which admits a good moduli space whose closed points are S-equivalence classes.

Definition 1.15 (Slope stability).

For a nonzero vector bundle E, define its slope by

μ⁡(E)=deg⁡Erk⁡E.

The vector bundle E is semistable if

μ⁡(F)≤μ⁡(E)

for every nonzero proper saturated subsheaf F⊂E, and it is stable if the inequality is strict. Since C is a smooth curve, a saturated subsheaf of a vector bundle is a subbundle, so it is equivalent to test nonzero proper subbundles.

Armed with this definition, we may now consider the open substack 𝖡𝗎𝗇r,dss⁢(C). Semistable bundles of fixed rank and degree form a bounded family, so this stack is of finite type, and in particular quasi-compact. It is still not separated because every object has the nonproper scalar stabilizer 𝔾m.

Definition 1.16 (S-equivalence).

Let E be a semistable vector bundle. A Jordan–Hölder filtration of E is a filtration

0=J0⊂J1⊂⋯⊂JN=E

such that every quotient Ji/Ji−1 is stable of slope μ⁡(E). The filtration is not necessarily unique, but the associated graded vector bundle

gr⁡(E)=⨁i=1NJi/Ji−1

is unique up to noncanonical isomorphism. Two semistable vector bundles E and E′ of the same slope are S-equivalent if gr⁡(E)≃gr⁡(E′).

Now we consider the moduli space Mr,dss⁢(C) of S-equivalence classes of semistable vector bundles on C. There is a good moduli space morphism

𝖡𝗎𝗇r,dss⁢(C)⟶Mr,dss⁢(C),

and the closed points of Mr,dss⁢(C) are in bijection with S-equivalence classes of semistable vector bundles.

Remark 1.17.

The original method of proof for this theorem was to construct the moduli space using geometric invariant theory. The goal of this series of lectures will be to discuss an intrinsic approach using Θ-stratifications together with existence criteria for good moduli spaces, without first choosing a GIT presentation.

1.4 Theta-stratifications.

The framework of Θ-stratifications and numerical invariants used here is developed in [Hal14].

Let 𝔛 be an algebraic stack and consider Θ≔[𝔸1/𝔾m], where the action on points is λ⋅z=λ⁢z; equivalently, the coordinate function t has weight −1. Assume that the mapping stacks below are algebraic. Then define the stack 𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛)≔𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(Θ,𝔛) of filtered objects and the stack 𝖦𝗋𝖺𝖽⁡(𝔛)≔𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(B⁢𝔾m,𝔛) of graded objects. There are canonical morphisms

ev1:𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛)→𝔛,gr:𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛)→𝖦𝗋𝖺𝖽⁡(𝔛),σ:𝖦𝗋𝖺𝖽⁡(𝔛)→𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛).

Here ev1 is restriction to 1∈𝔸1, gr is induced by the inclusion B⁢𝔾m={0}/𝔾m↪Θ, and σ is induced by the projection Θ→B⁢𝔾m. In particular, gr∘σ=id. We also write tot=ev1∘σ:𝖦𝗋𝖺𝖽⁡(𝔛)→𝔛.

Definition 1.18.

A Θ-stratum in an algebraic stack 𝔜 is a union of connected components S⊂𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔜) such that the restriction

ev1|S:S⟶𝔜

is a closed immersion.

A Θ-stratification of 𝔛 consists of

  1. (1)

    A totally ordered set I with a least element 0;

  2. (2)

    An increasing collection of open substacks 𝔛≤α⊂𝔛, indexed by α∈I, such that

    𝔛≤α⊂𝔛≤βfor ⁢α≤β,⋃α∈I𝔛≤α=𝔛,

    and such that for every x∈|𝔛|, the set {α∈I|x∈|𝔛≤α|} has a least element;

  3. (3)

    For every α>0, a Θ-stratum Sα⊂𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛≤α) such that

    𝔛<α≔⋃β<α𝔛≤β=𝔛≤α∖ev1⁡(Sα).

The semistable locus is 𝔛ss≔𝔛≤0, and the stratification gives a disjoint decomposition

𝔛=𝔛ss⊔⨆α>0ev1⁡(Sα).

Consider the stack 𝖡𝗎𝗇G⁢(C)=𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(C,B⁢G). We will consider the stack

𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(Θ,𝖡𝗎𝗇G⁢(C))=𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(Θ×C,B⁢G).

Any such map f is equivalent to a 𝔾m-equivariant principal G-bundle ℰ over 𝔸1×C. When G=GLn, this is equivalent to a 𝔾m-equivariant vector bundle on 𝔸1×C, or equivalently to a finitely generated graded locally free 𝒪C⁢[t]-module

ℰ=⨁w∈ℤℰw.

With the convention above, the coordinate function t has weight −1, so multiplication by t gives maps

t:ℰw⟶ℰw−1.

Since ℰ is locally free over 𝒪C⁢[t], multiplication by t is injective.

Remark 1.19.

Consider the vector bundle E=ℰ|{1}×C. Since 𝔾m acts freely on 𝔾m×C, equivariant descent gives

ℰ|𝔾m×C≃PC∗⁢E,

where PC:𝔾m×C→C is the projection. Equivalently,

E≃(ℰ⁡[t−1])0.

Define

Fw⁢E≔tw⁢ℰw⊂(ℰ⁡[t−1])0=E.

Since t⁢ℰw+1⊂ℰw, we have Fw+1⁢E⊂Fw⁢E. The finite generation and local freeness of ℰ imply that this is a finite, exhaustive, and separated decreasing filtration by subbundles, which may be written as

0=Fb+1⁢E⊂Fb⁢E⊂⋯⊂Fa⁢E=E.

In the other direction, let E be a vector bundle with a finite decreasing filtration F∙⁢E by subbundles such that the quotients Fw⁢E/Fw+1⁢E are locally free. The Rees construction is the graded 𝒪C⁢[t]-module

𝖱𝖾𝖾𝗌⁡(E,F∙)≔⨁w∈ℤt−w⁢Fw⁢E⊂E⊗ℂℂ⁡[t,t−1].

It is locally free over 𝒪C⁢[t], and its fibers at t=1 and t=0 satisfy

𝖱𝖾𝖾𝗌⁡(E,F∙)|t=1≃E,𝖱𝖾𝖾𝗌⁡(E,F∙)|t=0≃⨁wFw⁢E/Fw+1⁢E.

Therefore, a map from Θ to the stack of vector bundles is equivalent to a finite ℤ-weighted filtration of a vector bundle by subbundles with locally free associated graded pieces.

1.5 Non-abelian localization.

We will begin with the classical setting. Let X be a smooth projective variety with an action of 𝔾m, let F be a 𝔾m-equivariant perfect complex, and write

X𝔾m=⨆αZα

for the decomposition of the fixed locus into connected components. After localizing the representation ring R⁡(𝔾m) so that the equivariant Euler classes below become invertible, we have

χ𝔾m⁢(X,F)=∑αχ𝔾m⁢(Zα,F|Zα⊗e⁢(NZα/X)−1),

where

e⁡(NZα/X)=λ−1⁢(NZα/X∨)=∑i≥0(−1)i⁢[Λi⁢NZα/X∨].

We will now consider the stacky version. Let

𝔛=𝔛ss⊔⨆αev1⁡(Sα)

be a Θ-stratification. Since ev1|Sα is a closed immersion, we may identify Sα with its image in 𝔛. The center of the stratum is

Zα≔σ−1⁢(Sα)⊂𝖦𝗋𝖺𝖽⁡(𝔛),

where σ:𝖦𝗋𝖺𝖽⁡(𝔛)→𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛) is induced by the projection Θ→B⁢𝔾m.

Theorem 1.20 (Virtual non-abelian localization [Hal15, Theorem 5.1]).

Let 𝔛 be a quasi-smooth derived stack with a Θ-stratification

𝔛=𝔛ss⊔⨆αSα,

where we identify every stratum with its image under ev1, and let Zα be its center. Decompose the restriction of the cotangent complex according to the 𝔾m-weights as

𝕃𝔛|Zα≃𝕃α−⊕𝕃α0⊕𝕃α+,

where the homology of 𝕃α−, 𝕃α0, and 𝕃α+ is concentrated in negative, zero, and positive weights, respectively. Define

𝔼α≔Sym⁡(𝕃α−⊕(𝕃α+)∨)⊗det(𝕃α+)∨⁢[−rk⁡(𝕃α+)]∈𝖰𝖢𝗈𝗁⁡(Zα).

Here det(𝕃α+) and rk⁡(𝕃α+) denote the determinant and virtual rank of the perfect complex 𝕃α+. We say that a complex of vector spaces is finite-dimensional if the direct sum of all of its cohomology groups is finite-dimensional. Let F∈𝖯𝖾𝗋𝖿⁡(𝔛). Assume that

R⁢Γ⁢(Zα,F|Zα⊗𝔼α)

is finite-dimensional for every α and is acyclic for all but finitely many α. Then R⁢Γ⁢(𝔛,F) is finite-dimensional if and only if R⁢Γ⁢(𝔛ss,F) is finite-dimensional, and

χ⁡(𝔛,F)=χ⁡(𝔛ss,F)+∑αχ⁡(Zα,F|Zα⊗𝔼α).

Here quasi-smooth means that 𝕃𝔛 is perfect of Tor-amplitude contained in [−1,1].

1.6 Geometric invariant theory.

For geometric invariant theory, see [MFK94]. The vector-bundle example below uses the Harder–Narasimhan filtration [HN74].

Let G be a reductive group and X be a projective scheme equipped with a G-equivariant line bundle ℒ. The semistable locus can be defined using the Hilbert-Mumford criterion, where it consists of all points where for all cocharacters λ:𝔾m→G, we can define the point

x0=limt→0λ⁡(t)⁢x

and define the quantity

μL⁢(x,λ)≔−wtx0⁡(ℒ)‖λ‖.

A point is semistable if μL⁢(x,λ)≤0 for all cocharacters of G. The stable locus consists of all points where the inequality is strict and the stabilizer is finite.

Theorem 1.21 ([MFK94]).

The stable and semistable loci are open in X. Moreover, Xss/G is a good quotient and Xs/G is a geometric quotient.

Example 1.22.

Consider the moduli stack 𝖡𝗎𝗇r,d of vector bundles of rank r and degree d on a curve of genus at least 2. Then recall that the semistable locus was defined to consist of slope semistable vector bundles. In fact, this can be obtained via GIT.

Fix an ample line bundle 𝒪⁡(1) on C. Then there exists some n0 such that for all n≥n0 and E∈𝖡𝗎𝗇r,d, E⁡(n) is globally generated. Therefore, we can consider

H0⁢(C,E⁡(n))↠E⁡(n).

If we set V=ℂN, where N=h0⁢(E⁡(n)), then there is a surjection

V⊗𝒪C⁢(−n)↠E.

Therefore, we can think of E as a member of a Quot scheme. On the Quot scheme, we can consider the universal family

Now define the line bundle

ℒ≔detR0⁢p∗⁢(ℰ⁡(m))

for some m≫0. We can also consider the action of SL⁡(V) on the Quot scheme. For some cocharacter λ, we can split

V=V1⊕V2

with weights s and N−s. Then consider

V1⊗𝒪C⁢(−n)⊂V⊗𝒪C⁢(−n)↠E

and consider the filtration

0→F1⁢E→E→E/F1⁢E→0

induced by this. Then we see that

limt→0λ⁡(t)⁢E=F1⁢E⊕E/F1⁢E.

Then we compute the restriction ℒ|grFE and obtain the spaces H0⁢(C,F1⁢E⁢(m)) and H0⁢(C,E⁡(m)/F1⁢E⁢(m)), and therefore the weight of ℒ is given by

(N−s)⁢pF1⁢E⁢(m)−s⁢pE/F1⁢E⁢(m),

which recovers GIT.

We will now consider the unstable locus. Let E be a vector bundle on C. Then there exists a unique filtration

0⊂Fℓ⁢E⊆⋯⊆F0⁢E=E

such that

  1. (1)

    All grFi⁡E are semistable;

  2. (2)

    We have μ⁡(grFi⁡E)>μ⁡(grFi−1⁡E) for all i.

Remark 1.23.

From the GIT perspective, we should really take μ to be the reduced Hilbert polynomial.

1.7 Construction of Theta-stratifications.

Let 𝔛 be a reasonable algebraic stack.1 Now consider some family ℰ over 𝔸1×C. If we restrict to the central fiber, we see that 𝔾m acts on grF⁡E, which means we have a map 𝔾m→Aut⁡grF⁡E, and from this we can compute the weight.

Note that the morphism σ:𝖦𝗋𝖺𝖽⁡(𝔛)→𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛) is a Θ-contraction, and therefore

π0⁢(𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛))=π0⁢(𝖦𝗋𝖺𝖽⁡(𝔛)).
Example 1.24.

Let 𝔛=B⁢G. Then we have

𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛)=⨆[λ]B⁢Pλ,

where Pλ is the parabolic subgroup corresponding to the cocharacter λ, and we can always choose representatives in a single Weyl chamber. Moreover, we have

𝖦𝗋𝖺𝖽⁡(𝔛)=⨆λ∈𝕏∗⁢(T)/WB⁢Lλ,

where Lλ is the Levi subgroup corresponding to λ.

Definition 1.25.

A Θ-stratum in 𝔛 is a union of connected components S⊆𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛) such that

ev1:S→𝔛

is a closed immersion.

Roughly speaking, closed immersions are injective, so an object in S consists of an object in 𝔛 and a “canonical filtration.”

Definition 1.26.

A Θ-stratification is an increasing family of open substacks

𝔛≤c⊆𝔛,c∈Γ,

where Γ is some totally ordered set, together with Θ-strata

Sc⊆𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛≤c),

which are required to satisfy

𝔛≤c=ev1⁡(Sc)⊔⋃c′<c𝔛≤c′.

In particular, this implies that

𝔛=𝔛ss⊔⨆c>0ev1⁡(Sc).

Analogously to the Hilbert-Mumford criterion, we will construct Θ-stratifications using numerical invariants.

Definition 1.27.

A numerical invariant μ with values in a totally ordered set Γ consists of an assignment of a scaling invariant function

μ:ℝq∖{0}→Γ

for any p∈𝔛⁡(ℂ) and any nondegenerate homomorphism γ:𝔾mq→Aut⁡(p). These are required to satisfy

  1. (1)

    The assignment is invariant under field extensions. This point will not be elaborated on because we are working over ℂ;

  2. (2)

    If we have 𝔾mq↪𝔾mn↪Aut⁡(p), then we have a factorization ℝq∖{0}→ℝn∖{0}→Γ;

  3. (3)

    If we have some ξ:S→𝔛 and γ:𝔾m,Sq→Aut⁡(ξ) with finite kernel, the function μκ⁡(s) is locally constant on S, where s ranges over points of S.

We will give a naive version of a construction starting with a numerical invariant μ. Define x∈𝔛 to be semistable if μ⁡(f)≤0 for any nondegenerate f∈𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛) satisfying f⁡(1)=x. If x is unstable, then we define its instability level

Mμ⁢(x)≔sup{μ⁡(f)|f∈𝖥𝗂𝗅𝗍⁡(𝔛),ev1⁡(f)=x}.

If a filtration f attains this supremum, we call it a “Harder-Narasimhan filtration.”

Definition 1.28.

A numerical invariant μ is standard if

  1. (1)

    μ⁡(x) and μ⁡(−x) are not both positive for x∈ℝq∖{0};

  2. (2)

    Each function μγ is strictly quasi-concave, namely for all δ∈[0,1] and linearly independent x0,x1∈ℝq such that μ⁡(x0),μ⁡(x1)≥0, then

    μγ⁢(δ⁢x0+(1−δ)⁢x1)≥max⁡{μγ⁢(x0),μγ⁢(x1)}.

    If either value is strictly positive, the inequality is required to be strict.

The next condition is that we need some kind of rationality. We consider 𝕏∗⁢(T)ℝ, and our goal is to find the rational points. This leads us to condition (R): if μγ attains a positive value for some γ, then it attains a maximal value at a rational point.

Theorem 1.29 ([Hal14]).

Let 𝔛 be a stack and μ be a standard numerical invariant satisfying condition (R). Then μ defines a Θ-stratification if and only if it satisfies the following:

  • •

    For any DVR R with fraction field K and residue field k, then μ⁡(fKHN)≤Mμ⁢(fk) (HN-specialization);

  • •

    For any map B:T→𝔛 from a finite type scheme, there exists a quasi-compact open 𝔛′⊆𝔛 such that for any point of finite type p∈T⁡(k) and a filtration f of B⁡(p) for which μ⁡(f)>0, there exists another filtration f′ of B⁡(p) with μ⁡(f′)≥μ⁡(f) satisfying f′⁢(0)∈𝔛′ (HN-boundedness).

The point here is that the conditions of being standard and (R) combined with HN-boundedness imply existence and HN-specialization implies uniqueness.

2 Intro to log geometry (Tingting Fang and Zijian Han)

2.1 Motivation.

In enumerative geometry, we will consider intersection numbers on compactified moduli spaces. This is going to require our objects to degenerate in some way, for example for domain curves to be nodal, maps to land in boundary divisors, or we degenerate the target. In ordinary geometry, we view these as singular, but in log geometry, there is a way to think of these situations as being log smooth. In log geometry, we are going to replace functions with the data of functions and how they vanish on the boundary (or namely the morphism α:MX→𝒪X).

Example 2.1.

Consider a family of curves (x⁢y=t) over 𝔸1, where the central fiber is nodal. In log geometry, if we place the divisorial log structure on 𝔸1, then this family is log smooth.

2.2 Monoids.

Definition 2.2.

A monoid is a commutative semigroup with a unit.

For a monoid P, we may associate a group Pgp via the standard Grothendieck construction

Pgp={(a,b)|(a,b)∼(c,d)⁢ if there exists ⁢s∈P⁢ such that ⁢a+d+s=b+c+s}.
Definition 2.3.

If the natural morphism P↪Pgp is injective, we say that P is integral.

Example 2.4.

If P has generators a,b,c with relation a+c=b+c, then in Pgp we have a=b, so P is not integral.

Definition 2.5.

A monoid P is

  • •

    fine if P is finitely generated and integral;

  • •

    saturated if for all p∈Pgp and all natural numbers n, if n⁢p∈P then p∈P;

  • •

    torsion-free if Pgp is;

  • •

    sharp if the identity is the only invertible element.

2.3 Log structures.

Let X be a scheme.

Definition 2.6.

A pre-log structure on X is a sheaf of monoids MX on the small étale site of X and a morphism α:MX→𝒪X. It is a log structure if α−1⁢(𝒪X×)≃𝒪X×, where the isomorphism is given by α.

We now consider the exact sequence

0→α−1⁢(𝒪X×)→MX→M¯X→0,

and the quotient here is called the characteristic sheaf or the ghost sheaf.

Example 2.7.

Let MX=𝒪X× and α be the identity. Then there is no additional information provided by the log structure.

Example 2.8.

Let X be a regular variety and D be a closed subscheme. Set U=X∖D. Then define

MX=𝒪X∩j∗⁢𝒪U×,

where j:U→X is the open immersion. If D is a divisor, then this is called the divisorial log structure.

For example, if X=𝔸1 and D={0}, then the characteristic sheaf vanishes everywhere except for the origin. Here, we compute

MX={φ⋅tn|φ∈𝒪X×}.

The stalk is 𝒪X× everywhere except at the origin, where it is 𝒪𝔸1,0×⊕ℕ.

Example 2.9.

Now let X=𝔸2 and D be the union of the coordinate axes. Then

MX,D ={f∈k⁡[x,y]|f⁢ is invertible outside ⁢D}
={φ⋅xa⋅yb}.

Note here that at the general point, we see Mp=𝒪X,p×. At the origin, we see 𝒪X,p×⊕ℕ2. At a general point on the x-axis, we see that xa is invertible, so we see the stalk 𝒪X,p×⊕ℕ⋅b. Similarly, we can compute the stalk at a general point on the y-axis.

Just as we can associate a sheaf to a presheaf, we will associate a log structure to a pre-log structure. First, a pushout in a category 𝒞 will be denoted by B⊔AC and is the colimit of the diagram

In the case where 𝒞 is commutative monoids, then

B⊔AC=(B⊕C)/∼,(f(a)+b,c)∼(b,g(a)+c).
Example 2.10.

Consider the morphisms 2:ℕ→ℕ and 3:ℕ→ℕ. Then the pushout is the monoid

P=ℕ⊕ℕ(3,0)∼(0,2)≃ℕ∖{1}.

If we replace 𝒞 by the category of sheaves of commutative monoids, we can form the pushout on sections and then sheafify.

Definition 2.11.

The associated log structure of a pre-log structure α:MX→𝒪X is the pushout

MX⊔α−1⁢(𝒪X×)𝒪X×.

The map to 𝒪X is given by (a,b)→α⁡(a)⁢b.

Definition 2.12.

A morphism of log schemes (X,MX)→(Y,MY) consists of

  1. (1)

    A morphism f¯:X¯→Y¯ of underlying schemes;

  2. (2)

    A map f♭:f∗⁢MY→MX, where f∗⁢MY is the log structure associated to f−1⁢MY.

Definition 2.13.

A chart for a log scheme (X,α:MX→𝒪X) is a morphism from the constant monoid PX→MX such that MX≃PXa≃PX⊕αP−1⁢(𝒪X×)𝒪X×, where αP:PX→MX→𝒪X.

Charts are useful in specifying log structures. For example, if we have PX→𝒪X, then PXa gives a log structure on X.

Example 2.14.

The trivial log structure is given by the chart P={0}.

Example 2.15.

Let X=Spec⁡k and give a log structure by αℕ:ℕ→k which sends 0 to 1 and 1 to 0. This is called the standard log point and can also be formed by restricting the divisorial log structure on 𝔸1 to the origin.

Example 2.16.

Consider the chart ℕ→𝒪𝔸1 which sends n↦tn. Then this recovers the divisorial log structure on 𝔸1 relative to the origin.

Example 2.17.

Consider the chart ℕ2→𝒪𝔸2 which sends (a,b)↦xa⁢yb. This recovers the divisorial log structure on 𝔸2 relative to the toric boundary.

Definition 2.18.

A chart for a log map f:(X,MX)→(Y,MY) is a triple (PX→MX,QY→MY,Q→P), where PX→MX and QY→MY are charts and the diagram

commutes.

Definition 2.19.

A log scheme (X,MX) is finitely generated, fine, integral, saturated if there exists an étale local chart PU→MU for a cover U→X such that P is finitely generated, fine, integral, or saturated, respectively.

2.4 Log smoothness.

Definition 2.20.

Consider a commutative diagram

where j is a strict closed immersion (here, this means that MT0=j∗⁢MT1). A morphism f:X→Y of fine log schemes is log smooth (resp. log étale) if

  1. (1)

    The underlying map f¯:X¯→Y¯ is locally of finite presentation;

  2. (2)

    For any commutative diagram as above, étale locally on T1 there exists a (resp. there exists a unique) morphism g:T1→X such that ϕ=g∘j and ψ=f∘g.

We will now give a chart local criterion for log smoothness.

Theorem 2.21 ([Kat89, Theorem 3.5]).

Let f:X→Y be a morphism of fine log schemes. Assume we have a chart Q→MY where Q is a fine monoid. Then f is log smooth if and only if étale locally on X there exists a chart for f extending Q→MY satisfying

  1. (1)

    The kernel and the torsion part of the cokernel of Qgp→Pgp are finite groups whose orders are invertible on X;

  2. (2)

    The induced morphism X¯→Y¯×Spec⁡ℤ⁡[Q]Spec⁡ℤ⁡[P] is étale in the classical sense.

Example 2.22.

Let X be an affine toric variety given by Spec⁡ℂ⁡[P] for a monoid P. Note that Pa≃MX,X∖T induces the divisorial log structure. Then consider the map f:X→pt, where the point has a trivial log structure. We note that the morphism 0→Pgp has no kernel and the cokernel is torsion-free, and the map

X¯→Spec⁡ℂ×Spec⁡ℤSpec⁡ℤ⁡[P]=Spec⁡ℂ⁡[P]

is an isomorphism, so any toric variety is log smooth over a point with trivial log structure.

From this example, we can morally think of log smoothness as being locally toric relative to the base.

Example 2.23.

Recall the family x⁢y=t with log structure relative to the central fiber over 𝔸1 with the divisorial log structure relative to 0. The map of charts we will consider is in fact Δ:ℕ→ℕ2. Taking the groupification, the map becomes Δ:ℤ→ℤ2. The kernel is trivial and the cokernel is torsion-free, so we have verified the first condition. Then we consider the map

X¯→Spec⁡ℂ⁡[t]×Spec⁡ℤ⁡[ℕ]Spec⁡ℤ⁡[ℕ2]=Spec⁡ℂ⁡[u,v,t]u⁢v−t,

which is an isomorphism, so this family is log smooth.

2.5 Stack of log structures.

The stack of log structures and its relation to log smoothness are due to Olsson [Ols03].

Let S be a fine log scheme. We will consider the category 𝖫𝗈𝗀S whose objects are fine log schemes (T,MT)→S and whose morphisms are strict morphisms (T,MT)→(T′,MT′) over S.

  1. (1)

    This category 𝖫𝗈𝗀S is a category fibered in groupoids over 𝖲𝖼𝗁/S classifying all fine log schemes mapping to S;

  2. (2)

    𝖫𝗈𝗀S is an algebraic stack locally of finite type over S;

  3. (3)

    A morphism f:X→S is log smooth if and only if X→𝖫𝗈𝗀S is smooth. The same holds with smooth replaced by étale.

2.6 Tropicalization.

Let X be a fine log scheme. Then the tropicalization of X is defined to be the colimit

Σ(X)≔⨆x∈XHom(M¯X,x,ℝ≥0)/∼,

where the equivalence relation is given by if a point x specializes to y, then the induced map σx→σy induces an equivalence from σx to its image.

Now suppose there is a stratification of X by Xi such that M¯|Xi is constant. For any Xi, all points x∈Xi satisfy x∈{ηXi}¯, so we only need to consider the generic points of the strata and then glue various faces.

Example 2.24.

Consider X with the trivial log structure. Note that for any point x∈X, we have M¯X,x=0, so σX={0}. Then Σ⁡(X)={0}.

Example 2.25.

Consider 𝔸1 relative to the origin (with divisorial log structure). It is easy to see that σ0=Hom⁡(ℕ,ℝ≥0)=ℝ≥0 and ση={0}, so the tropicalization is ℝ≥0.

Example 2.26.

Consider 𝔸2 with the toric log structure (divisorial log structure relative to x⁢y=0). Then σ(0,0)=ℝ≥02, σ(x,0)=ℝ≥0, σ(0,y)=ℝ≥0, and σ(x,y)={0}, so we obtain the fan of 𝔸2 as a toric variety treated as a cone complex.

Example 2.27.

Let XΣ be a toric variety with the divisorial log structure relative to XΣ∖T. Then

Σ⁡(XΣ)=Σ,

so a possible slogan is that tropicalizing a toric variety recovers the structure of ordinary toric geometry (minus the embedding of the fan in some real vector space).

Example 2.28.

Let X=Spec⁡k⁡[x,y,t]/(x⁢y−tℓ) with divisorial log structure over x⁢y=0. Then there is a chart given by

Q=⟨ex,ey,et|ex+ey=ℓ⁢et⟩.

Note that MX=Qa=Q⊕α−1⁢(𝒪X×)𝒪X× and M¯X=Q. Therefore, we have

σq =Hom⁡(Q,ℝ≥0)
={(ρx,ρy,ρt)∈ℝ≥03|ρx+ρy=ℓ⁢ρt}
={(ρt,ρx)∈ℝ≥02|0≤ρx≤ℓ⁢ρt}

at the singular point q, which recovers the cone which gives X as a toric variety. At the generic point ηx of x=0, we see that M¯X,ηx=ℕ⁢et, and therefore σηx=ℝ≥0. Similarly, we see that σηy=ℝ≥0. The remaining problem is gluing.

Note that M¯X,q→M¯X,ηx is given by et↦et, ex↦ℓ⁢et, and ey↦0, and therefore the map σηx→σq sends ρt to (ρt,ρx), where ρx=ℓ⁢ρt.

The morphism X→𝔸t1 giving a family of curves with nodal central fiber has tropicalization given by projecting the cone onto ℝ≥0.

2.7 Log curves.

For now, all monoids and log schemes will be fine (or even fine saturated). There are two reasons for this:

  1. (1)

    If P is a fine monoid, its dual is fs and sharp;

  2. (2)

    If X=(X¯,MX) is a fine log scheme, for any geometric point x¯→X, there exists an étale neighborhood of x¯ which has a chart.

We will now discuss various geometric properties of maps between monoids.

Definition 2.29.

A map θ:P→Q is integral if the map Spec⁡ℂ⁡[Q]→Spec⁡ℂ⁡[P] is flat.

For example, any nonzero map ℕ→ℕ and the diagonal Δ:ℕ→ℕ2 are integral. If a map is integral, then for any P→P′, the monoid P′⊕PQ is fine.

Example 2.30.

Pushouts may not be fine, for example consider

⟨a,b,c|a+c=b+c⟩=ℕ3⊕ℕ2ℕ.
Definition 2.31.

A map f:X→Y between fine log schemes is integral if at every geometric point of X, the map

(f∗⁢M¯Y)x¯→M¯X,x¯

is integral.

Definition 2.32.

A map between fs monoids P→Q is saturated if for all P→P′, the monoid P′⊕PQ is also fs.

Example 2.33.

The map Δ:ℕ→ℕ2 is saturated, but ℓ:ℕ→ℕ is not.

Definition 2.34.

A log curve over an fs log scheme S is a log smooth and integral map π:𝒞→S between fs log schemes such that the underlying geometric fibers are reduced connected curves.

Proposition 2.35 ([Kat89]).

Let f:X→Y be a log smooth and integral map between fs log schemes. Then f¯ is flat.

Theorem 2.36 ([Kat00]).

The underlying family of a log curve is a family of nodal curves.

Example 2.37.

Let P=ℕ∖{1}. Then Spec⁡(P→k⁡[P]) is log smooth over k, but Spec⁡k⁡[P] is a cusp.

Definition 2.38.

An n-pointed log curve over an fs base S consists of the data (π:𝒞→S),p→={pi}i=1n such that

  1. (1)

    The underlying family is a prestable curve;

  2. (2)

    π is a log smooth map between fs log schemes;

  3. (3)

    On the smooth locus U of π¯, we have

    M¯𝒞|U≃π∗⁢M¯S⊕⨁i=1npi⁢ℕ¯.

2.8 Canonical log structures on prestable curves.

Let 𝔐g,n be the moduli of n-pointed prestable curves. Then the singular locus is a normal crossings divisor, so there is a canonical log structure

M𝔐g,ncan=M∂𝔐g,n.

If we consider the universal family ℭg,n, we can form π−1⁢(∂𝔐g,n)⊆ℭg,n. Therefore, we have a map

π∗⁢M∂𝔐g,n→Mπ−1⁢(∂𝔐g,n).

We can also consider the divisors pi⁢(𝔐g,n)⊂ℭg,n, which also define log structures

Pi≔Mpi⁢(𝔐g,n).

Therefore, we can define a log structure

Mℭg,ncan≔Mπ−1⁢(∂𝔐g,n)⊕𝒪×⨁i=1nPi.

Then if we consider

π♭:π¯−1⁢M𝔐g,ncan→Mπ−1⁢(∂𝔐g,n)→Mℭg,ncan,

we can lift π to a map of log stacks.

Theorem 2.39 ([Kat00]).

The map π is a log smooth integral map.

Definition 2.40.

For a family (C¯/S¯,p→) of prestable curves, we can pull back along the diagram

and endow the left edge with a canonical log structure.

Remark 2.41.

Let S¯=Spec⁡k. If Scan=Spec⁡(ℕr→k), then r is the number of nodes on C¯. Working étale locally on a node q, the log structure looks like
Theorem 2.42 ([Kat00]).

Let (𝒞/S,p→) be an n-pointed log curve on an fs base S. Then there exists a unique MScan→MS such that

is a Cartesian diagram in the category of fs log schemes.

A slogan is that a log curve is a prestable curve together with MScan→MS.

Example 2.43.

Let S¯=Spec⁡k⁡[s] and T¯=Spec⁡k⁡[t]. Also choose ℓ∈ℕ. Then consider the diagram

On log structures, consider the case where the bottom left arrow corresponds to 1↦ℓ on ℕ. Then at the top left corner, the monoid becomes ℕ2⊕ℕ,ℓℕ. If we call this P, then the map k⁡[P]→k⁡[ℕ] is not a family of log curves with the canonical log structure, but is a family of log curves.

2.9 Moduli of log curves.

Definition 2.44.

A map between n-pointed log curves (𝒞,S)→(𝒞′,S′) is a pair (ℓ:𝒞→𝒞′,Θ:S→S′) such that Θ is strict and the diagram

is Cartesian. Denote by 𝔐g,nlog the fibered category parameterizing n-pointed log curves.

Proposition 2.45 ([Kat00; Ols03]).

We have 𝔐g,nlog≃𝖫𝗈𝗀(𝔐g,n,M𝔐g,ncan).

In particular, for a scheme T¯, the groupoid 𝔐g,nlog⁢(T¯) parameterizes log structures MT together with log curves 𝒞/T.

Consider a log curve π:𝒞→S,p→ over S=Spec⁡(Q→k). Denote π¯♭:π¯∗⁢M¯S→M¯𝒞. At a generic point or a general smooth point η, the map is

π¯η♭:(π−1⁢M¯S)η=Q≃M¯𝒞,η.

At a marked point pi∈{η}¯, we have M¯𝒞,pi=Q⊕ℕ. In this case we have

χη:M¯𝒞,pi→pr1M¯𝒞,η

the specialization map and the pullback

π¯pi♭:Q↪Q⊕ℕ.

At a node q, we have M¯𝒞,q=Q⊕ℕℕ2. Let ρq denote the image of 1 in Q, which is the edge length or smoothing parameter at q. Denote by η¯1 and η¯2 the generic points of the two branches of q. Then the generalization maps are

χη1:Q⊕ℕℕ2→Q(q,(a,b))↦q+a⁢ρq;
χη2:Q⊕ℕℕ2→Q(q,(a,b))↦q+b⁢ρq.

2.10 Tropicalization of log curves.

We will only consider the situation over a log point S=Spec⁡(Q→k). We will consider the category of cones 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖾, whose objects are pairs (w,Nw) such that w⊆Nw⊗ℤℝ, where w is a full-dimensional strongly convex rational polyhedral cone. The morphisms are maps (w1,Nw1)→(w2,Nw2), which consist of

χ:Nw1→Nw2

such that χℝ⁢(w1)⊆w2.

Example 2.46.

Let X be an fs log scheme and consider ((M¯X,x∨)ℝ,(M¯X,x∨)ℤ).

We will now consider the category 𝖦𝖢𝖢 of generalized cone complexes. Its objects are topological spaces |Σ| together with a presentation as the colimit of a diagram in 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖾 with all arrows being inclusions of faces. Its morphisms are continuous map |Σ|→|Σ′| such that for each (w,Nw)∈Σ, the map w→|Σ′| factors through (w,Nw)→(w′,Nw′).

Example 2.47.

If f:X→Y is a morphism of fs log schemes, the map f¯♭:f∗⁢M¯Y→M¯X induces Σ⁡(X)→Σ⁡(Y) on tropicalizations.

Definition 2.48.

A cone complex is a generalized cone complex Σ such that for each (σ,Nσ)∈Σ, the map σ→|Σ| is injective.

Theorem 2.49 ([ACP15]).

If X is fs and log smooth over ℂ¯ with Zariski log structure, then Σ⁡(X) is a cone complex.

For a monoid Q, we will denote wQ=Qℝ∨=Hom⁡(Q,ℝ≥0) and the lattice Hom⁡(Q,ℤ)=Qℤ∨. At a smooth point, we have

wη=(Qℝ∨,Qℤ∨).

At a marked point, we see that

wp=(Hom⁡(Q⊕ℕ,ℝ≥0)=Qℝ∨⊕ℝ≥0,Qℤ∨⊕ℤ).

At a node, we have

wq =(Hom⁡(Q⊕ℕℕ2,ℝ≥0),(M¯𝒞,q)ℤ∨).

Note that the cone is in fact equal to

{(m,mx,my)|m⁡(ρq)=mx+my}≃{(m,ex)|ex≤m⁡(ρq)}⊆Qℝ∨×ℝ≥0.

Now that we understand the cones associated to every point, we now need to discuss the face maps. The generalization maps corresponding to marked points are

Q⊕ℕ→pr1Q,

and the associated face maps are

wη↪wpm↦(m,0).

At a node, the two face maps are

χη1∨:Qℝ∨→wqm↦(m,m⁡(ρq))

and

χη2∨:Qℝ∨→wqm↦(m,0).
Example 2.50.

Consider a curve which is a union of two rational curves with a marked point p on one branch. Then let S¯=Spec⁡ℂ. Then we see that

Scan=Spec⁡(ℕ→ℂ),

Q=ℕ, and Qℝ∨=ℝ≥0. We also see that M¯C,q=ℕ⊕ℕℕ2 and M¯C,p=ℕ⊕ℕ.

2.11 Tropical curves.

Definition 2.51.

A family of tropical curves (G,g→,ℓ→) over a cone w,Nw consists of

  1. (1)

    A connected graph G=V⁡(G)∪E⁡(G)∪L⁡(G);

  2. (2)

    A leg ordering m→:L⁡(G)→∼{1,…,n};

  3. (3)

    A genus function g→:V⁡(G)→ℕ;

  4. (4)

    An edge length function ℓ:E⁡(G)→Hom⁡(w∩Nw,ℕ)∖{0}.

Now we will construct Σ⁡(G,ℓ). For v∈V⁡(G), we set wv=w. For e∈E⁡(G), we set

we={(s,λ)|λ≤ℓ→⁢(e)⁢(s)}⊆w×ℝ≥0.

For legs ℓ∈L⁡(G), we set wℓ=w×ℝ≥0. We now need to define the face maps. If ℓ is incident to v, then the face map is

wv↪wℓ:s↦(s,0).

If e is incident to two vertices v1,v2, then the face maps are

wv1↪we :s↦(s,ℓ→⁢(e)⁢(s))
wv2↪we :s↦(s,0).
Remark 2.52.

The choice of v1 and v2 does not change the cone complex up to isomorphism, but it does matter when we want to define contact orders for log maps. However, in general there is no canonical way to make this choice.

2.12 Punctured curves.

Punctured logarithmic curves and maps are developed in [ACGS25].

We consider a nodal curve

Spec⁡k⁡[x,y]/x⁢y→Spec⁡k

with log structures given by ℕ2 with chart (a,b)↦xa⁢yb and ℕ→k being the standard log point. Now consider C¯1=Z⁡(x)=Spec⁡k⁡[y] and mark the node by p:Spec⁡k→Spec⁡k⁡[y]. Note that

Ccan=(C¯,MC)→Scan=Spec⁡(ℕ→k).

Denote MC1∘=MC|C1. Then we see that on log structures we have the diagram

In particular, we can compute the stalk M¯C1∘|p=ℕ2, and therefore we have

π¯C1∘♭|p:ℕ→Δℕ2.

However, we should have the map

π¯C1♭|p:ℕ→i1ℕ⊕ℕ,

and therefore C1 is not a log curve. We can then consider the diagram

Therefore, we will consider extending the log structures.

Recall that for a log curve, we have M𝒞=M𝒞′⊕𝒪𝒞×P𝒞, where P𝒞 is the divisorial log structure by the markings.

Definition 2.53.

A punctured curve over an fs log scheme S consists of (𝒞∘→𝑝𝒞→𝜋S,{pi}i=1n), where (𝒞→𝜋S,p→) is a log curve and the map p:𝒞∘→𝒞 is a map of fine log schemes satisfying the following conditions:

  1. (1)

    The underlying map p¯ is an isomorphism;

  2. (2)

    On log structures, the map p♭:M𝒞↪M𝒞∘ is an isomorphism away from the pi and induces

    M𝒞→p♭M𝒞∘↪M𝒞⊕Pgp.
  3. (3)

    For any marking pi and any s∈M𝒞∘,pi∖M𝒞,pi, we have α𝒞∘⁢(s)=0.

Roughly speaking, a punctured curve is a log curve plus the data of a commutative diagram
Example 2.54.

Let (𝒞¯→S¯=Speck,p) be a smooth 1-pointed curve.

  1. (1)

    Let (𝒞/S,p) be endowed with the canonical log structure (so S has no log structure). Let M𝒞=P. Then any puncturing p♭:M𝒞↪M𝒞∘⊂Pgp must be trivial. The reason is that M𝒞∘ cannot have a section s such that α𝒞∘⁢(s)=0. If s∈P=M𝒞, then α𝒞∘⁢(s)=α𝒞⁢(s). Otherwise, if s∉P, then because α𝒞∘⁢(−s) is nonzero, so is α𝒞∘⁢(s).

  2. (2)

    Let M𝒞∘⊆(ℕ⊕𝒪𝒞×)⊕Pgp be a puncturing. Choose a local generator x of 𝒪⁡(−p). Then any s∈M𝒞∘,p has the form s=((n,φ),xm) where n∈ℕ and φ∈𝒪𝒞,p×. If m<0, then we require that α𝒞∘⁢(s)=0. This implies that α𝒞⁢((n,φ),0)=0, and therefore

    M¯𝒞∘,p⊆{(n,m)∈ℕ⊕ℤ|m≥0⁢ if ⁢n=0}.

    In fact, any fine submonoid of the right hand side containing ℕ⊕ℕ can be realized by a puncturing.

  3. (3)

    Let S=Spec⁡(ℕ→k). Consider M𝒞∘ such that M¯𝒞∘,p=ℕ2+ℕ⁡(2,−2). Because (1,−1)∉M¯𝒞∘,p, we see that M𝒞∘ is not saturated.

Lemma 2.55 ([ACGS25]).

Let Q be a sharp fs monoid. Let w≔Hom⁡(Q,ℝ≥0)=Qℝ∨. Let Q∘⊆Q⊕ℤ be finitely generated with Q⊕ℕ⊊Q∘ and Q∘∩{0}×ℤ<0=∅. Then there exists a nonzero, concave, piecewise linear function

ℓ:w→ℝ≥0

with rational slopes such that

(Q∘)ℝ∨={(s,λ)∈w×ℝ≥0|0≤λ≤ℓ⁡(s)}.
Example 2.56.

Let Q=ℕ2 and set

Q∘ =⟨((1,0),−1),((0,1),−1),((0,0),1)⟩⊂ℕ2⊕ℤ
={((a,b),m)|a+b+m≥0,a,b≥0}.

Then

(Q∘)ℝ∨={(ex,ey,et)|0≤et≤min⁡(ex,ey)}.

3 Intro to GW theory with a view to higher genus (Patrick Lei)

3.1 Introduction to GW theory.

For the virtual fundamental class construction, see [BF97]; for the axioms and quantum cohomology, see [KM94].

The goal of these lectures is to discuss Gromov-Witten theory in a way that is amenable to doing calculations in higher genus. Gromov-Witten theory concerns itself with integrals on the moduli space ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β), where X is a smooth projective algebraic variety and β∈H2⁢(X,ℤ) is an effective curve class. There is a diagram

where 𝒞 is the universal curve, σi are the sections of π which give the marked points, f is the universal stable map, and evi=f∘σi are evaluation morphisms. While ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β) is generally singular, not equidimensional, and reducible, there is a special class

[ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β)]vir∈A(c1⁢(X),β)+(dimX−3)⁢(1−g)+n⁢(ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β),ℚ),

which is known as the virtual fundamental class.

Exercise 3.1.

Use standard arguments in deformation theory to verify that the “expected dimension” of ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β) is the number given above.

Under the assumption that X is smooth and projective, ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β) is proper, so we may define GW invariants

⟨τa1⁢(α1),⋯,τan⁢(αn)⟩g,n,β≔∫[ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β)]vir∏i=1nevi∗⁡αi⋅ψiai

for αi∈H∗⁢(X). Here, the ψi are defined by ψi=c1⁢(σi∗⁢(ωπ)).

Unfortunately, calculating individual Gromov-Witten invariants is very difficult, so we will consider the even more difficult problem of studying generating series of GW invariants, for example

Fg=∑β≥0qβ⁢⟨⟩g,0,β

when X is a Calabi-Yau threefold. Here, q is a formal variable which keeps track of the curve class and we will denote the ring ℚ⟦qβ|β∈H2(X,ℤ)eff⟧ by Λ. There are some other structures we will consider. First, we may consider the quantum cohomology ring, whose product a⋆𝐭b is given by the formula

(a⋆𝐭b,c)=∑β≥0n≥0⟨a,b,c,𝐭,…,𝐭⟩0,3+n,β⁢qβn!.

Here a,b,c,𝐭∈H∗⁢(X). We will also consider the quantum connection. Let {ei} be a basis for H∗⁢(X). Then the quantum connection is the connection on the trivial bundle with fiber H∗⁢(X) over H∗⁢(X)×ℙz1 given by the formula

∇ti=∂ti+1zei⋆𝐭.

Sometimes, it is useful to also consider the connection in the z-direction given by

∇z⁢ddz≔zddz−1zEX⋆𝐭+μX,

where μX⁢(α)=deg⁡(α)−dimX2⁢α is the grading operator and

EX=c1⁢(X)+∑i(1−deg⁡(ei)2)⁢ti⁢ei

is the Euler vector field. Because we will be mostly interested in Calabi-Yau varieties, we will not consider this.

3.2 Enumerative mirror symmetry in genus zero.

The impetus for mathematicians to develop and study Gromov-Witten theory came in the early 1990s, when Candelas, de la Ossa, Green, and Parkes [COGP91] predicted the number of rational curves of low degree on a general quintic threefold by converting the problem to one of computing period integrals on a different Calabi-Yau threefold called the mirror quintic (equivalently, studying its variation of Hodge structure). In genus zero, all invariants can be recovered from the J-function J𝐭⁢(q,z)∈H∗⁢(X,Λ)⁢[z], which is defined by

(J𝐭⁢(q,z),α)≔(z+𝐭,α)+∑n,βqβn!⁢⟨αz−ψ,𝐭,…,𝐭⟩0,1+n,β

for any 𝐭∈H∗⁢(X,Λ)⁢[z] and α∈H∗⁢(X), where (−,−) is the Poincaré pairing. Therefore, the problem of computing all genus-zero Gromov-Witten invariants with descendants (these are the ψ-classes) reduces to the problem of computing the J-function.

Remark 3.2.

We expand 1z−ψ as ∑k=0∞ψk⁢z−k−1.

We should note that the J-function can be obtained via a fundamental solution to the quantum differential equation, which is given by

(S𝐭⁢(z)⁢ϕ,α)=(ϕ,α)+∑n,βqβn!⁢⟨αz−ψ,ϕ,𝐭,…,𝐭⟩0,2+n,β.

This has the property that S𝐭∗⁢(−z)⁢S𝐭⁢(z)=Id, which is usually known as the symplectic property. From this, we can recover the J-function by z⁢S𝐭∗⁢(z)⋅1=J𝐭⁢(q,z).

In physics, mirror symmetry is a duality between two different theories called the A-model and B-model, so now we will need to introduce the B-model object. In the interest of time (and notation), we will assume that X is a toric variety and that −KX is nef. Let D1,…,Dr be the complete set of torus-invariant divisors in X. Then define the I-function

I𝐭⁢(q,z)≔z⁢e𝐭/z⁢∑β≥0qβ⁢∏i=1r∏m=−∞0(Di+m⁢z)∏i=1r∏m=−∞β⋅Di(Di+m⁢z).

Note here that we expand any (Di+m⁢z)−1 which appears as 1m⁢z⁢(1−Dim⁢z+⋯), or namely, as a geometric series in Dim⁢z. In addition, the I-function is annihilated by a differential equation known as the Picard-Fuchs equation, which is some hypergeometric type equation.

Example 3.3.

If 𝐭=0 and X=ℙ1, we obtain

I⁡(q,z) =z⁢∑d≥0qd⁢1∏m=1d(H+m⁢z)2
=z⁢∑d≥0(qz2)d⁢1(d!2)+O⁡(H),

so in fact we see the Bessel function of the first kind as the leading term.

If X is a complete intersection in a toric variety Y cut out by line bundles L1,…,Lk, all of which satisfy H1⁢(f∗⁢Li)=0 for any genus zero stable map to Y (this is called being convex), then the quantum Lefschetz theorem [CG07] allows us to replace [ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β)]vir with e⁡(⨁π∗⁢f∗⁢Li)∩[ℳ¯g,n⁢(Y,β)]vir and perform all computations on Y. In this case, the I-function is defined to be

I𝐭⁢(q,z)≔z⁢e𝐭/z⁢∑β≥0qβ⁢∏i=1k∏m=−∞Li⋅β(Li+m⁢z)∏i=1k∏m=−∞0(Li+m⁢z)⁢∏i=1r∏m=−∞0(Di+m⁢z)∏i=1r∏m=−∞β⋅Di(Di+m⁢z),

where we abuse notation and conflate the Li with their first Chern classes.

Example 3.4.

For the quintic threefold, which is cut out by a section of 𝒪ℙ4⁢(5), the I-function at 𝐭=0 is given by

I⁡(q,z)=z⁢∑d≥0qd⁢∏m=15⁢d(5⁢H+m⁢z)∏m=1d(H+m⁢z)5.

The content of the genus zero mirror theorem is a correspondence between these two objects. More precisely, in the case where −KX is nef, they are related by a change of variables.

Theorem 3.5 ([Giv98; LLY97]).

Write the I-function with 𝐭=0 as I0⁢(q)⋅z+I1⁢(q)+O⁡(z−1). Then we have

Jτ⁡(𝐭)⁢(q,z)=I𝐭⁢(q,z)I0⁢(q),

where τ⁡(𝐭)=𝐭+I1⁢(q)I0⁢(q).

Example 3.6.

When X=ℙ1, note that I0⁢(q)=1 and I1⁢(q)=0, so in fact, we have the equality

J𝐭⁢(q,z)=I𝐭⁢(q,z).
Example 3.7.

When X is the quintic threefold, we will rewrite the components of the I-function as I0⁢(q)⋅z+I1⁢(q)⁢H+O⁡(z−1) for convenience. We have

I0⁢(q)=∑d≥0(5⁢d)!(d!)5⁢qd,I1⁢(q)=∑d≥0(5⁢d)!(d!)5⁢(5⁢∑m=d+15⁢d1m)⁢qd,

so there is a nontrivial mirror map in this case. Specializing to 𝐭=0, we see that τ=I1⁢(q)⁢HI0⁢(q), so we obtain

Jτ⁢(q,z)=I⁡(q,z)I0⁢(q).

By the divisor equation, the left hand side also equals J⁡(q⁢eI1/I0,z), and we will also refer to this as the mirror map. Therefore, we can use the mirror theorem to compute ⋆τ. The quantum connection in the direction of H2 becomes the ODE

(H+zD)Sτ(z)∗=Sτ(z)∗⋅I11H⋆τ,

where D≔q⁢ddq (here, the coordinate is log⁡q) and I11≔1+D⁡(I1⁢(q)I0⁢(q)). An explicit computation using the mirror theorem and the results of Zagier–Zinger [ZZ08] yields

I11⁢H+⋯ =Sτ⁢(z)∗⁢(I11⁢H⋆τ𝟏)
(1+D⁡(I1I0+D⁡(I2I0)I11))⁢H2+⋯ =Sτ⁢(z)∗⁢(I11⁢H⋆τH)
I11⁢H3 =Sτ⁢(z)∗⁢(I11⁢H⋆τH2).

Because Sτ begins with the identity, this computes H⋆τ.

3.2.1 Oscillating integrals.

We will now reinterpret the genus zero mirror theorem, and we will return to this interpretation when we discuss higher genus invariants. In particular, we will interpret the I-function as an integral on some mirror family to X, which for us will be a toric variety. Let

0→Λ→ℤr→N→0

be the fan sequence of X. Applying Hom⁡(−,ℂ×), we obtain the exact sequence

1→(ℂ×)dimX→(ℂ×)r→Hom⁡(Λ,ℂ×)→1.

Suppose that the map Λ→ℤr is given by the matrix (mi⁢j)i=1,…,rj=1,…,ρ⁡(X). Then we consider the variety

Eq=(∏i=1rxjmi⁢j=qi|i=1,…,ρ(X))

which is mirror to X and consider the superpotential f=x1+⋯+xr. If we wish to consider the equivariant theory with equivariant parameters λ1,…,λr acting on each homogeneous coordinate of X, we will consider fλ=∑i=1r(xi−λi⁢log⁡xi).

Example 3.8.

When X=ℙn, the mirror to X is the superpotential ∑i=1n+1(xi−λi⁢log⁡xi) on the variety Eq=(x1⁢⋯⁢xn+1=q).

We now choose an appropriate Lefschetz thimble Γα near each critical point (xα) of the (equivariant) superpotential and consider the integral

Iα=∫Γαefλ/z⁢∏i=1rdxixi.

This corresponds in the I-function to replacing each Di in the expression by Di−λi (turning on the equivariant parameters) and in the J-function to considering the fully equivariant GW theory of X. In genus zero, the limit as λi→0 exists, so we can safely recover the original mirror theorem from the following:

Theorem 3.9 ([Giv96]).

This integral is annihilated by the same Picard-Fuchs equation as the I-function, and up to various prefactors, its asymptotic expansion as z→0− along the negative real axis coincides with the restriction of the I-function corresponding to the T-fixed point on X which corresponds to the critical point (xα).

3.2.2 The Lagrangian cone.

The quantum cohomology of X is an example of a Frobenius manifold, which we will see later can be produced from any cohomological field theory. Write V=H∗⁢(X) and let (eμ) be a basis for V, so we can write 𝐯=∑μ,ntnμ⁢eμ⁢zn∈V⁡⟦z⟧. The structure of a Frobenius manifold comes from the function

ℱ0⁢(𝐯)=∑n,β,μqβn!⁢⟨𝐯⁡(ψ),…,𝐯⁡(ψ)⟩0,n,β,

which is also called the genus zero descendant potential of X. It satisfies the string equation, dilaton equation, and topological recursion relations:

∂∂t01⁢ℱ0 =12⁢(𝐯0,𝐯0)+∑n=0∞∑μtn+1μ⁢∂∂tnμ⁢ℱ0;
∂∂t11⁢ℱ0 =∑n=0∞∑μtnμ⁢∂∂tnμ⁢ℱ0−2⁢ℱ0;
∂3∂tk+1α⁢⁡∂tmβ⁢⁡∂tnγ⁢ℱ0 =∑μ,ν∂2∂tkα⁢⁡∂t0μ⁢ℱ0⋅ημ⁢ν⋅∂3∂t0ν⁢⁡∂tmβ⁢⁡∂tnγ⁢ℱ0.

To state the following result, we consider the infinite-dimensional vector space V⁢⦇z−1⦈ (or a completion of this) with the symplectic form

ω⁡(𝐟⁡(z),𝐠⁡(z))≔Resz=0⁡(𝐟⁡(−z),𝐠⁡(z)).

We also consider the new variable2 𝐪=𝐯−z, so ℱ0 is now a function near 𝐪=−z.

Theorem 3.10 (Givental [Giv04]).

ℱ0 satisfies the above PDEs if and only if the graph ℒ of dℱ0 is a Lagrangian cone with vertex at 𝐪=0 such that its tangent spaces L are tangent to ℒ exactly along z⁢L⊂L.

We may recover the Lagrangian cone ℒ by the following procedure. We find a fundamental solution

S=Id+S1⁢z−1+S2⁢z−2+⋯

to the quantum connection, which satisfies the equation

z⁢∂∂tμ⁢S=eμ⋆S.

Then, setting J≔z⁢S∗⁢(z)⁢𝟏, we can then recover the Lagrangian cone by the following procedure:

  • •

    The derivatives ∂∂tμ⁢J form a basis of L∩V⁢⟦z−1⟧;

  • •

    This implies that z⁢∂2∂tμ⁢⁡∂tν⁢J∈L∩V⁡⟦z−1⟧. Writing these in terms of the first derivatives and using the fact that J solves the quantum connection, we recover the Frobenius structure and hence the Lagrangian cone.

Using this, we can interpret the genus zero mirror theorem as:

Theorem 3.11 ([Giv98]).

The I-function I𝐭⁢(q,z) lies on the Lagrangian cone of X.

3.3 Moduli of curves and CohFTs.

The notion of a cohomological field theory was introduced by Kontsevich–Manin [KM94].

We will denote by ℳ¯g,n the moduli space of stable curves of genus g with n marked points. This is nonempty if and only if 2⁢g−2+n>0, in which case it is a Deligne-Mumford stack of dimension 3⁢g−3+n. There is a combinatorial structure to the collection of ℳ¯g,n, which is given by a collection of morphisms.

  • •

    There is the gluing morphism

    q:ℳ¯g,n+1×ℳ¯h,m+1→ℳ¯g+h,n+m,

    which takes two curves and glues them along the last marked point to form a node;

  • •

    There is the self-gluing morphism

    s:ℳ¯g−1,n+2→ℳ¯g,n,

    which glues the last two marked points.

There is of course another interesting map, which is the forgetful map

pr:ℳ¯g,n+1→ℳ¯g,n

given by deleting the last marked point and then stabilizing. We are now able to define our enumerative theories of interest, which include Gromov-Witten theory.

Definition 3.12.

Given a vector space V with a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form η and a unit element 𝟏∈V, a Cohomological Field Theory (CohFT) Ω on V is a collection Ωg,n of Sn-equivariant linear maps

Ωg,n:V⊗n→H∗⁢(ℳ¯g,n)

which satisfy the basic identity

Ω0,3⁢(𝟏,u,v)=η⁡(u,v)

and the following combinatorial identities (we will let eμ be a basis of V such that e1=𝟏 and eμ be the dual basis):

q∗⁢Ωg+h,n+m⁢(𝐯1,𝐯2) =∑μΩg,n+1⁢(𝐯1,eμ)⋅Ωh,m+1⁢(𝐯2,eμ);
s∗⁢Ωg,n⁢(𝐯) =∑μΩg,n+2⁢(𝐯,eμ,eμ).

If in addition the identity

pr∗⁡Ωg,n⁢(𝐯)=Ωg,n+1⁢(𝐯,𝟏)

is satisfied, then we say the CohFT has a flat unit (or satisfies the string equation).

All of this can be generalized to super vector spaces, but for simplicity we will not deal with this case.

Example 3.13.

The most important example of a CohFT is the Gromov-Witten theory of a smooth projective variety X. Here, recall that the source of a stable map is a prestable curve, so there is a stabilization morphism

st:ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β)→ℳ¯g,n

which forgets the map and stabilizes the curve. Then, working over the Novikov ring, we will set V=H∗⁢(X), η to be the Poincaré pairing, and 𝟏 to be the fundamental class of X. The linear maps Ωg,nX are given by the formulae

Ωg,nX⁢(𝝉)≔∑βqβ⁢st∗⁡(∏i=1nevi∗⁡(τi)∩[ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β)]vir),

where evi:ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β)→X is the i-th evaluation map.

Example 3.14.

Let π:𝒞g,n→ℳ¯g,n be the universal curve. Then the Hodge bundle is the vector bundle

𝔼g,n≔π∗⁢ωπ.

We then consider the vector space V=ℂ with the usual pairing and define the CohFT Ω𝔼 by the formula

Ωg,n𝔼≔c⁡(𝔼g,n).

The gluing axioms are satisfied by the equation q∗⁢𝔼g+h=𝔼g⊕𝔼h and the exact sequence

0→𝔼g−1→𝔼g→𝒪→0.

Here, because genus zero components do not contribute to global sections of ω and 𝔼 does not depend on the marked points, this CohFT has a flat unit.

Remark 3.15.

We will see later that this is related to the GW CohFT of a point by the quantum Riemann-Roch theorem.

Given a CohFT Ω, we may produce invariants by pairing the classes Ωg,n⁢(𝐯) with various cohomology classes on ℳ¯g,n. The most important ones to consider are the classes

ψ¯i≔c1⁢(si∗⁢ωπ),

where si:ℳ¯g,n→𝒞g,n is the i-th marked point.

Remark 3.16.

In Gromov-Witten theory, these are called ancestors. There are also descendants, which are given by the same formula except using the moduli space 𝔐g,n of prestable curves instead of ℳ¯g,n, where we factor the morphism st defined above as

ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β)→forget map𝔐g,n→stabilizeℳ¯g,n.

The descendant classes are denoted by ψi.

Example 3.17.

We will calculate an invariant which will appear in the GW theory of Calabi-Yau threefolds. For any CohFT Ω, consider the invariant

⟨𝟏⁢ψ¯1⟩1,1Ω≔∫ℳ¯1,1Ω1,1⁢(𝟏)⁢ψ¯1.

Using the second gluing equation, the degree zero part of Ω1,1⁢(𝟏) is equal to

∑μΩ0,3⁢(𝟏,eμ,eμ)=∑μη⁡(eμ,eμ),

which yields the (graded) dimension χ⁡(V) of V (for example, if V=H∗⁢(X) for a Calabi-Yau threefold X, this is the topological Euler characteristic of X). Therefore, we obtain

⟨𝟏⁢ψ¯1⟩1,1Ω=dimV24.
Example 3.18.

Consider the GW CohFT of a point. This is given by V=ℂ with the usual pairing and the formula

Ωg,n=1.

Then we define the invariants

⟨ψ¯1a1⁢⋯⁢ψ¯nan⟩g,n≔∫ℳ¯g,nΩg,n⋅ψ¯1a1⁢⋯⁢ψ¯nan.
Theorem 3.19 (Kontsevich [Kon92]).

The function

𝒟≔exp⁡(∑g,nℏg−1n!⁢∑a1+⋯+an=3⁢g−3+n⟨ψ¯1a1⁢⋯⁢ψ¯nan⟩g,n⁢ta1⁢⋯⁢tan)

is annihilated by the operators

L−1≔ −∂∂t0+ℏ−12⁢t02+∑i=0∞ti+1⁢∂∂ti;
L0≔ −32⁢∂∂t1+∑i=0∞2⁢i+12⁢ti⁢∂∂ti+116;
Ln≔ −(2⁢n+3)!!2n+1⁢∂∂tn+1+∑i=0∞(2⁢i+2⁢n+1)!!(2⁢i−1)!!⁢2n+1⁢ti⁢∂∂ti+n
+ℏ2⁢∑i=0n−1(2⁢i+1)⁢(2⁢i−1)⁢⋯⁢(2⁢i+1−2⁢n)2n+1⁢∂2∂ti⁢⁡∂tn−1−i.
Remark 3.20.

This result (Virasoro constraints for a point) is equivalent to 𝒟 being a tau-function for the KdV hierarchy and has been generalized by various authors.

3.4 R-matrix action.

In the early 2000s, Givental discovered a remarkable property of axiomatic enumerative theories, namely that one can transform CohFTs by the action of matrices R⁡(z)=R0+R1⁢z+R2⁢z2+⋯∈Hom⁡(V,V′)⁢⟦z⟧ which satisfy the property

R∗⁢(−z)⁢R⁢(z)=IdV.

Traditionally, the literature requires that V=V′ and R0=Id, but the MSP group has removed this restriction and also allows dimV<dimV′.

In order to define the action of R on a CohFT Ω defined on V, we need to review some of the combinatorial structure of ℳ¯g,n. For a curve C∈ℳ¯g,n⁢(ℂ), we may consider the dual graph of C, which has vertices, edges, and legs, which are defined as follows:

  • •

    The vertices correspond to irreducible components of C and are labelled by a non-negative integer, which is the genus;

  • •

    The edges correspond to nodes of C (in particular, we allow loops);

  • •

    The legs correspond to marked points.

Any graph which appears as the dual graph of a stable curve is called a stable graph.

The first type of action on CohFTs is a translation action. Let T∈V⁢⟦z⟧. For a CohFT Ω, we define

(T⁢Ω)g,n⁢(𝐯)≔∑m1m!⁢p∗⁢Ωg,n+m⁢(𝐯,T,…,T)

whenever the infinite sum makes sense.

Example 3.21.

If ΩX is the GW CohFT of a smooth projective variety X and τ∈H2⁢(X) is a divisor class, then the infinite sum makes sense and we can define the shifted GW CohFT ΩX,τ of X. For example, if X is the quintic threefold and τ=I1I0⁢H, then shifting to τ is the same as the mirror map q↦Q⁡(q)=q⁢eI1I0.

The second type of action is the action of a matrix R as in the beginning of this section. Let Gg,n denote the set of all stable graphs of genus g with n legs. Then we define

(R⁢Ω)g,n≔∑Γ∈Gg,n1|Aut⁡Γ|⁢ContΓ,

where ContΓ is defined by the following construction:

  • •

    At the i-th leg, we place the map

    R⁢(−ψ¯i)∗∈Hom⁡(V′,V)⁢⟦ψ¯i⟧;
  • •

    At every edge, we place the bivector

    V⁡(ψ¯1,ψ¯2)≔∑μeμ⊗eμ−R⁢(−ψ¯1)∗⁢eμ⊗R⁢(−ψ¯2)∗⁢eμψ¯1+ψ¯2;
  • •

    At every vertex, we place the linear map

    Ωgv,nv:V⊗nv→H∗⁢(ℳ¯gv,nv);
  • •

    Finally, we consider the pushforward in cohomology along the gluing morphism ∏vℳ¯gv,nv→ℳ¯g,n.

Definition 3.22.

Let R be as above. Then we define the translation

TR≔z⁡(𝟏−R⁢(−z)∗⁢𝟏′)∈z⁢V⁢⟦z⟧.

Whenever it makes sense, we define

R.Ω≔R⁢T⁢Ω.
Theorem 3.23 (Chang-Guo-Li [CGL26, Theorem 2.7]).

Suppose we work with coefficients in ℂ⁢⟦q⟧. Then if

TR∈z2⁢V⁢⟦z⟧+z⁢q⁢V⁢⟦z⟧,

R.Ω is a well-defined CohFT. Moreover, if dimV=dimV′, 𝟏′ is a unit for R.Ω.

We would like to remark a bit more about the translation action when R0≠Id. For simplicity, we will assume that V=V′ and R0⁢𝟏=c⋅𝟏 for some constant c. Then we set T~R≔z⁡(𝟏−c⁢R⁢(z)−1⁢𝟏) and use the dilaton equation to compute

TR⁢Ωg,n⁢(𝐯) =∑m=0∞1m!⁢p∗⁢Ωg,n+m⁢(𝐯,TR,…,TR)
=∑k,ℓ≥01k!⁢ℓ!⁢p∗⁢Ωg,n+k+ℓ⁢(𝐯,((1−c−1)⁢𝟏⋅ψ)⊗k,(c−1⁢T~R)⊗ℓ)
=∑k,ℓ≥0(1−c−1)k⋅c−ℓℓ!⁢(2⁢g−2+n+k+ℓ−1k)⁢p∗⁢Ωg,n+ℓ⁢(𝐯,T~R⊗ℓ)
=∑m=0∞c2⁢g−2+nm!⁢p∗⁢Ωg,n+m⁢(𝐯,T~R,…,T~R)

whenever this makes sense.

3.5 Reconstruction theorem.

Recall that every CohFT defines a Frobenius algebra. We will call a CohFT semisimple if the corresponding Frobenius algebra is semisimple.

Theorem 3.24 (Teleman [Tel12]).

Let Ω be a semisimple CohFT with flat unit and ω be its topological part. Then there exists a unique

R=Id+R1⁢z+⋯∈End⁡(V)⁢⟦z⟧

such that

Ω=R.ω.
Example 3.25.

Recall the Hodge bundle CohFT from before. Recall that it is given by the formula

Ωg,n𝔼=c⁡(𝔼)=1+λ1+⋯+λg.

Taking the degree zero part, we see that ω𝔼 is the GW CohFT of a point. Using Mumford’s computation

ch⁡(𝔼)=g+∑k=1∞B2⁢k(2⁢k)!⁢(κ2⁢k−1+12⁢ι∗⁢∑i=02⁢k−2ψ¯1i⁢(−ψ¯2)2⁢k−2−i),

where κm=p∗⁢ψ¯n+1m+1, B2⁢k are the Bernoulli numbers, and ι is the inclusion of the boundary up to a 2:1 étale cover, and the formula

c⁡(E)=exp⁡(−∑k(−1)k⁢(k−1)!⁢chk⁡(E))

for any vector bundle E (or by just using the quantum Riemann-Roch theorem3 directly), we obtain the R-matrix

R⁡(z)=exp⁡(∑k=1∞B2⁢k2⁢k⁢(2⁢k−1)⁢z2⁢k−1)=1+112⁢z+⋯.

As a sanity check, we will compute Ω1,1𝔼 using the R-matrix. First, we consider the stable graphs in Figure 2.

The first graph Γ1 gives us the contribution

ContΓ1 =T⁢ω1,1𝔼⁢(R⁢(z)−1⁢𝟏)
=ω1,1𝔼⁢(R⁢(z)−1⁢𝟏)+p∗⁢ω1,1𝔼⁢(R⁢(z)−1⁢𝟏,TR⁢(z)).

Using the formula B2=16 and the fact that dimℳ¯1,1=1, this becomes

1−112⁢ψ1+112⁢κ1.

The second graph does not receive tail contributions because dimℳ¯0,3=0. The constant term of the edge contribution is 112, so considering the automorphism and pushing forward to ℳ¯1,1 gives us

ContΓ2=112⁢Δ,

where Δ denotes the boundary divisor (with the correct stack structure). Because ψ1=κ1 in this case, we obtain

1+λ1=1+112⁢(κ1−ψ1+Δ)=1+112⁢Δ.

3.6 Operator formalism and geometric quantization.

We will return to the symplectic formalism of Givental. This is more convenient for certain computations, but it is in fact equal to what we have before, at least when we want to calculate generating functions. Recall that we had a Frobenius manifold structure on V and we considered the vector space 𝒱≔V⁡⦇z−1⦈ with symplectic form

(𝐟⁡(z),𝐠⁡(z))≔Resz=0⁡η⁡(𝐟⁡(−z),𝐠⁡(z)).

If we consider the polarization given by 𝒱+=V⁡[z] and 𝒱−=z−1⁢V⁢⟦z−1⟧, then letting 𝐪 be as before (with the dilaton shift), let 𝐩 be coordinates on 𝒱− such that (𝐪,𝐩) form a system of Darboux coordinates for 𝒱.

Definition 3.26.

We will call any formal function of the form

𝒟=exp⁡(∑g=0∞ℏg−1⁢ℱg)

an asymptotic element of the Fock space.

Then given such an asymptotic element of the Fock space, we will quantize (infinitesimal) symplectic transformations on 𝒱 by the following formulae:

pa⁢pb̂≔ℏ⁢∂qa∂qb,pa⁢qb̂≔qb⁢∂qa,qa⁢qb̂=qa⁢qbℏ.

In particular, this will allow us to understand expressions like R^⁢𝒟. However, we need to be careful because our formulae will involve both the fundamental solution Sτ and the R-matrix, and Sτ is a power series in z−1.4

Theorem 3.27 (Givental [Giv01a]).

An operator of the form S⁡(z−1)=Id+S1⁢z−1+⋯ acts on (asymptotic) elements of the Fock space by the formula

S^−1⁢𝒟⁢(𝐪)=e12⁢ℏ⁢W⁢(𝐪,𝐪)⁢𝒟⁢([S⁢𝐪]+),

where W=∑η⁡(Wm⁢n⁢qm,qn) is defined by the formula

S⁢(w−1)∗⁢S⁢(z−1)−Idw−1+z−1=∑Wm⁢nwm⁢zn.

Operators of the form R⁡(z)=Id+R1⁢z+⋯ act by the formula

R^⁢𝒟⁢(𝐪)=eℏ2⁢V⁢(∂𝐪,∂𝐪)⁢𝒟⁢(R−1⁢𝐪),

where V=∑η⁡(pm,Vm⁢n⁢pn) is defined by

R⁢(w)∗⁢R⁢(z)−Idw+z=∑Vm⁢n⁢wm⁢zn.

For a semisimple CohFT, there is a system of canonical coordinates uα such that the 1-form du is a homomorphism of algebras Tv⁢V→ℂ. Then near a semisimple point, there is an asymptotic solution to the quantum connection of the form

Ψ⋅R⋅eUz,

where Ψ switches from flat coordinates to canonical coordinates and U=diag⁡(uα) is the matrix of canonical coordinates. Finally, define

C=12⁢∫u∑R1α⁢α⁢duα.

A corollary of Teleman’s reconstruction theorem is the formula

𝒟X=eC⁡(u)⁢S^τ−1⁢Ψ^⁢R^⁢eUẑ⁢∏i=1dimV𝒟pt

for the Gromov-Witten theory of any smooth projective variety with semisimple quantum cohomology.

Example 3.28.

As a final example, we will apply Teleman’s theorem to compute F1 of any semisimple CohFT. Let eμ denote an idempotent basis for the quantum product. We will compute

∫ℳ¯1,1Ω1,1⁢(eβ).

Using the reconstruction theorem, we obtain

∫ℳ¯1,1Ω1,1⁢(eβ)= ∫ℳ¯1,1TR⁢ω1,1⁢(R⁢(ψ¯)−1⁢eβ)+12⁢TR⁢ω0,3⁢(R⁢(ψ¯)−1⁢eβ,V⁡(ψ¯2,ψ¯3))
= ∫ℳ¯1,1TR⁢ω1,1⁢(eβ)−∫ℳ¯1,1TR⁢ω1,1⁢(R1⁢eβ)⁢ψ¯
+12⁢∑μω0,3⁢(eβ,R1⁢eμ,eμ)
= ∫ℳ¯1,1(ω1,1⁢(eβ)+p∗⁢(ω1,2⁢(eβ,R1⁢𝟏)⁢ψ¯22))
−∫ℳ¯1,1(ω1,1⁢(R1⁢eβ)⁢ψ¯1+p∗⁢(ω1,2⁢(R1⁢eβ)⁢ψ¯22)⁢ψ¯1)
+12⁢∑μη⁡(eβ⋆eμ,R1⁢eμ)
= 124⁢∑μ(ω0,4⁢(eμ,eμ,eβ,R1⁢𝟏)−ω0,3⁢(eμ,eμ,R1⁢eβ))
+12⁢η⁢(eβ,R1⁢eβ)
= 124⁢∑μ∑νω0,3⁢(eμ,eμ,eν)⁢ω0,3⁢(eν,eβ,R1⁢𝟏)
−124⁢∑μω0,3⁢(eμ,eμ,R1⁢eβ)+12⁢(R1)β⁢β
= 124⁢(η⁡(eβ,R1⁢𝟏)−∑μη⁡(eμ,R1⁢eβ))+12⁢(R1)β⁢β.

Using the identities

η⁡(R1⁢𝟏,eβ)−∑μη⁡(R1⁢eβ,eμ) =∑μΔμ⁢∫ℳ¯0,4Ω0,4⁢(eμ,eμ,eμ,eβ)
=−12⁢∑μΔμ⁢∂uβΔμ−1
=12⁢∑μ∂uβlog⁡Δμ,

where Δμ≔η⁢(eμ,eμ)−1, we obtain the result

∫ℳ¯1,1Ω1,1⁢(eβ)=148⁢∑μ∂uβlog⁡Δμ+12⁢(R1)β⁢β,

which can be placed in the suggestive form

dF1Ω=∑μ(d⁢log⁡Δμ48+12⁢(R1)μ⁢μ⁢duμ).

This recovers a result which was already known to Givental.

3.7 How to compute the R-matrix.

We will conclude by explaining how to compute the R-matrix, starting in the setting where the Frobenius manifold is conformal (for example the Gromov-Witten theory of a smooth projective variety, r-spin curves, etc). In this example, we will consider the Frobenius manifold for 3-spin curves, following [PPZ15]. Let V be 2-dimensional with coordinates x and y, where x corresponds to the unit. The metric is given by

η=(0110)

and the primary genus zero potential is F⁡(x,y)=12⁢x2⁢y+172⁢y4. There is an Euler vector field

E=x⁢∂∂x+23⁢y⁢∂∂y,

which acts with weights −1 and −23 on ∂x and ∂y, respectively. The conformal dimension is δ=13, and we will define the degree operator

μ⁡(v)=[E,v]+(1−δ2)⁢v.

Here, ∂x has degree −16 and ∂y has degree 16.

To make our lives easier, we will set ϕ=y3 and define

∂^x=ϕ1/4⁢∂x,∂^y=ϕ−1/4⁢∂y,

and then compute in this frame. In this setting, quantum multiplication is given by

∂^x⋆∂^x=ϕ1/4⁢∂^x,∂^x⋆∂^y=ϕ1/4⁢∂^y,∂^y⋆∂^y=ϕ1/4⁢∂^x.

The last thing we need is that quantum multiplication by E is given by

E⋆−=(x2⁢ϕ3/22⁢ϕ3/2x).

We will now compute the R-matrix R=1+R1⁢z+⋯ by using the recursive equation

[Rk+1,E⋆−]=(k+μ)Rk.

Setting Rk=(akbkckdk), we obtain the equation

[(ak+1bk+1ck+1dk+1),(x2⁢ϕ3/22⁢ϕ3/2x)]=16⁢(6⁢k−16⁢k+1)⁢(akbkckdk).

The unique solution of this is in fact

ak =11728k⁢ϕ3⁢k/2⁢1+6⁢k1−6⁢k⁢(6⁢k)!(3⁢k)!⁢(2⁢k)!⁢δk,even,
bk =11728k⁢ϕ3⁢k/2⁢1+6⁢k1−6⁢k⁢(6⁢k)!(3⁢k)!⁢(2⁢k)!⁢δk,odd,
ck =11728k⁢ϕ3⁢k/2⁢(6⁢k)!(3⁢k)!⁢(2⁢k)!⁢δk,odd,
dk =11728k⁢ϕ3⁢k/2⁢(6⁢k)!(3⁢k)!⁢(2⁢k)!⁢δk,even.

If you are familiar with tautological relations on the moduli space of curves, you will see that the series ak+bk and ck+dk enter in the formulation of the Faber-Zagier relations and the formulation of Pixton’s relations.

In the case where the Frobenius manifold is not conformal (for example in equivariant Gromov-Witten theory), we will need to use an oscillating integral or some other technique to fix initial values in the R-matrix. We will give an example computation here, which is due to Givental [Giv01b]. In this setting, X=ℙn, but the argument can be made to work for any Fano toric variety. Recall that the equivariant mirror of ℙn is the superpotential

W=x1+⋯+xn+1+∑i=1n+1λi⁢log⁡xi

(here, we change the sign of the equivariant parameters for convenience). Therefore, the oscillating integrals will look like

I=∫Γ⊂Eq=(x1⁢⋯⁢xn+1=q)eW/z⁢∏i=1n+1dxixi.

This is annihilated by the operator

∏i=1n+1(z⁢q⁢ddq−λi)−q,

which is exactly the Picard-Fuchs equation satisfied by the I-function of projective space.

To expand this integral near the critical points, we first need to compute the critical points. Here, using coordinates t=log⁡q and Ti=log⁡xi, we obtain the equation

xi=L−λi,

where L is the Lagrange multiplier. These satisfy the equation

∏i=1n+1(L−λi)=q,

and therefore for generic values of λ, near q=0, the possible values Li of the Lagrange multiplier are distinguished by which of the λi they begin with. Note that the function W, the values of the Lagrange multipliers, and therefore the critical points, all depend continuously on λ, so they admit non-equivariant limits at λ=0 when q≠0.

When q=0, the matrix Ψ transitions from the flat basis Hi to the basis

Li⁢(H)=∏j≠iH−λj(λi−λj)1/2,

which are the leading terms of the canonical coordinates (simply compute the fixed points of the torus action via equivariant localization, and we will obtain this Lagrange interpolation). Therefore, we need to compute Lj⁢(z⁢q⁢ddq)⁢I in the q=0 limit. A direct computation shows that applying Li⁢(z⁢q⁢ddq) to the integral introduces an additional factor proportional to qxi to the integrand of the oscillating integral. Because we can permute the indices, we will compute only the case where i=n+1. Another direct computation shows that the integral vanishes at q=0 unless j=n+1, so in fact we see that R is diagonal in the classical limit. When j=n+1, we have

qxn+1=x1⁢⋯⁢xn,

and the integral becomes

∫Γe(∑i=1nxi+(λi−λn+1)⁢log⁡xi)/z⁢dx1⁢⋯⁢dxn=∏i=1n∫ℝexi/z⁢xi(λi−λn+1)/z⁢dxi,

which is simply a product of gamma functions.

Lemma 3.29.

We have the asymptotics

log⁡Γ⁡(1+s)∼s⁢log⁡(se)+12⁢log⁡(2⁢π⁢s)+∑k=1∞B2⁢k2⁢k⁢s1−2⁢k2⁢k−1.

Using this, we see that at q=0, the diagonal matrix element of the R-matrix is given by

log⁡R=∑k=1∞B2⁢k2⁢k⁢z2⁢k−12⁢k−1⁢∑i=1n(λi−λn+1)1−2⁢k.

By a result of Givental, this implies that this R-matrix recovers the equivariant GW theory of ℙn, and as a corollary, because the non-equivariant limit exists, we obtain Virasoro constraints for ℙn.

4 Decomposition theorem for semi-small maps (Xueqing Wen)

Question 4.1.

Let X be a (manifold, variety, analytic space, etc). How can we compute H∗⁢(X,ℂ)?

Unfortunately, this question is too hard, so we will replace it with a new question.

Question 4.2.

How can we detect H∗⁢(X,ℂ) using smaller spaces?

Theorem 4.3 (Künneth formula).

We have H∗⁢(X×Y,ℂ)=H∗⁢(X,ℂ)⊗H∗⁢(Y,ℂ).

Unfortunately, most spaces are not products, so we consider the following question.

Question 4.4.

Let f:X→Y be a morphism. Can we detect the cohomology of X using the cohomology of Y and the cohomology of the fibers of f?

This question is still very difficult, but at least we can study it. We will begin with the case where f is a fiber bundle between compact manifolds. The answer is of course the Leray or Serre spectral sequences, but before we get there, we need some preliminaries.

Definition 4.5.

A ℂ¯Y-local system on Y is a locally constant sheaf ℒ of vector spaces on Y.

For example, if Y is connected, then local systems correspond to representations of π1⁢(Y). Also, note that if Y is an algebraic variety, we will need to work with its analytification.

Example 4.6.

Let f be a fiber bundle with fiber F as above. Then Ri⁢f∗⁢ℂ¯X is a local system on Y with fiber Hi⁢(F,ℂ).

Proposition 4.7.

We have

H∗⁢(X,ℂ)=H∗⁢(X,ℂ¯X)=H∗⁢(pt,R⁢aX⁣∗⁢ℂ¯X).
Theorem 4.8 (Leray/Serre spectral sequence).

We have a spectral sequence

E2p,q=Hp⁢(Y,Rq⁢f∗⁢ℂ¯X)⇒Hp+q⁢(X,ℂ).

We will now consider the setting where f:X→Y is a smooth projective map between smooth projective varieties.

Theorem 4.9 (Deligne [Del68]).

We have the non-canonical isomorphism

R⁢f∗⁢ℂ¯X=⨁q≥0Rq⁢f∗⁢ℂ¯⁢[−q].

At the level of cohomology, we have

H∗⁢(X,ℂ)=⨁q≥0H∗−q⁢(Y,Rq⁢f∗⁢ℂ¯).

This is a consequence of the hard Lefschetz theorem for projective varieties and also states that the Serre spectral sequence degenerates at the E2 page. In topology, this fails for the Hopf fibration.

We will now consider the setting where f:X→Y is a proper map between algebraic varieties. Then we have a Whitney stratification5 Y=⨆λYλ such that f−1⁢(Yλ)→Yλ is a C∞ fibration in possibly singular varieties.

Definition 4.10.

A ℂ¯Y-module ℱ on Y is called a constructible sheaf if there exists a Whitney stratification Y=⨆Yλ such that ℱ|Yλ is a local system for all λ.

With this definition, we may consider the derived category 𝒟cb⁢(Y) of constructible sheaves on Y. This assignment admits a six functor formalism, where the functors are f∗,f∗,f!,f!,⊗,ℋom, and satisfies Verdier duality via the functor

DY:𝒟cb⁢(Y)→𝒟cb⁢(Y).
Definition 4.11.

A complex ℱ∙∈𝒟cb⁢(Y) is a perverse sheaf if it satisfies the following conditions:

  1. (1)

    (Support condition) We have dimsupp⁡ℋ−i⁢(ℱ∙)≤i for all i;

  2. (2)

    (cosupport condition) We have dimsupp⁡ℋ−i⁢(DY⁢ℱ∙)≤i for all i.

Remarks 4.12.
  1. (1)

    Perverse sheaves are not sheaves, but are complexes in degrees [−dimY,0].

  2. (2)

    They have two origins. One is intersection homology, and the other is the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence.

We will need to use the following fact: the category 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏⁡(Y) of perverse sheaves on Y is an abelian category and is moreover the heart of a t-structure on 𝒟cb⁢(Y). In particular, for any 𝒢∈𝒟cb⁢(Y), we can consider the perverse cohomology ℋip⁢(𝒢)∈𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏⁡(Y).

Theorem 4.13 (Beilinson-Bernstein-Deligne-Gabber [BBD82]).

Let f:X→Y be a proper morphism between algebraic varieties. Assume that X is smooth and connected.6 Then

R⁢f∗⁢ℂ¯X⁢[dimX]=⨁iℋip⁢(R⁢f∗⁢ℂ¯X)⁢[−i].

Moreover, each ℋip⁢(R⁢f∗⁢ℂ¯X) is semi-simple (meaning each subobject is a direct summand).

Definition 4.14.

Let f:X→Y be a proper surjective morphism with X smooth and irreducible. Let Y=⨆Yλ be a stratification such that f−1⁢(Yλ)→Yλ is a C∞-fibration. We say that f is semi-small if for all yλ∈Yλ, we have codimY⁡Yλ≥2⁢dimf−1⁢(yλ). If equality holds, we say that Yλ is relevant. If the only relevant stratum is the dense one, then we say that f is small.

Theorem 4.15 ([CM02]).

If f:X→Y is semi-small, then R⁢f∗⁢ℂ¯X⁢[dimX] is a perverse sheaf on Y.

Proof.

For yλ∈Yλ⊆Y, we see that

R⁢f∗⁢ℂ¯X|yλ=⨁Hi⁢(f−1⁢(yλ),ℂ).

Note that this vanishes if i>2⁢dimf−1⁢(yλ)≤codimY⁡(Yλ). If we vary over all strata Yλ, we obtain the support condition. Because f is proper, we have Rf∗=f!, and by using DYRf∗=f!DX, we obtain the cosupport condition. □

Examples 4.16.

We now give some examples of semi-small maps.

  1. (1)

    Any generically finite proper map between surfaces is semi-small.

  2. (2)

    Let Y={x⁢y=tℓ+1}⊆ℂ3. Then there is a crepant resolution f:Y~→Y of singularities, and the fiber over the singular point is a chain of ℙ1s, so it is semi-small (see also the previous example).

Theorem 4.17 (Kaledin [Kal06]).

A projective birational map from a nonsingular holomorphic symplectic variety is semi-small.

Example 4.18.

For example, the Springer resolution and the Grothendieck-Springer resolution are semi-small. In addition, the Hilbert-Chow morphism for the Hilbert scheme of points on a surface is semi-small.

Let f:X→Y be semi-small and consider a stratification Y=⨆Yλ. If Yλ is relevant, consider

ℒλ=Rdλ⁢f∗⁢ℂ¯f−1⁢(Yλ),

where dλ=2⁢dimf−1⁢(yλ). Then ℒλ is semi-simple. Here, note that ℒ|λ=Hdλ(f−1(yλ),ℂ). Now let IC⁡(ℒλ) be the intermediate extension of ℒλ⁢[dimYλ] on Y¯λ, which is a perverse sheaf.

Theorem 4.19 ([CM02]).

Let f:X→Y=⨆Yλ be semi-small. Then there is a canonical decomposition

R⁢f∗⁢ℂ¯X⁢[dimX]=⨁Yλ⁢ relevantIC⁡(ℒλ).
Example 4.20.

Let G be a reductive group with Lie algebra 𝔤 and choose a Borel B. Then

G×B𝔟=𝔤~→𝜋𝔤

is small. Therefore, we have

R⁢π∗⁢ℂ¯𝔤~⁢[dim𝔤]=IC⁡(ℒ).

Recall that 𝔤~rs→𝔤rs is a W-torsor. Then for a∈𝔤rs, we have ℒ|a≅ℂ[W], and therefore ℒ=R0⁢π∗⁢ℂ¯𝔤~rs. This implies that W acts on ℒ, and this action can be extended to IC⁡(ℒ) and also on R⁢π∗⁢ℂ𝔤~, and in particular acts on the fiber R⁢π∗⁢ℂ𝔤~|a for any a∈𝔤.

Example 4.21.

Consider the Springer resolution μ:T∗⁢(GL3/B)→𝒩=𝕆(13)⊔𝕆(2,1)⊔𝕆(3). This map is semi-small, but unfortunately all nilpotent orbits are relevant. Note that the fiber above the (2,1) orbit is a union of two ℙ1s glued at a node, the fiber above the (3) orbit is a point, and the fiber above the (13) orbit is GL3/B.

We see that ℒ(3) must be trivial because μ is an isomorphism above this orbit. Then ℒ(2,1)=R2⁢μ∗⁢ℂ¯ is a rank 2 local system on 𝕆(2,1). Finally, ℒ(13)=R6⁢μ∗⁢ℂ¯ is a rank 1 local system on 𝕆(13)=pt. Therefore, we have

R⁢μ∗⁢ℂ¯T∗⁢GL3/B⁢[6]=IC⁡(ℒ(3))⊕IC⁡(ℒ(2,1))⊕IC⁡(ℒ(13)).

Restricting to b∈𝕆(3), we obtain ℒ(3)=H0⁢(pt). Restricting to a∈𝕆(2,1), we obtain

H0⁢(X,ℂ)⊕H2⁢(X,ℂ)=IC⁡(ℒ(3))|(a)⊕IC⁡(ℒ(2,1))|(a).

Restricting to 0=𝕆(13), we obtain

H∗⁢(GL3/B,ℂ)=ℂ⁡[W] =IC⁡(ℒ(3))|0⊕IC⁡(ℒ(2,1))|0⊕ℒ(13)|0
=H0⁢(GL3/B,ℂ)⊕(a summand of dimension ⁢4)⊕H6⁢(GL3/B,ℂ).

As representations of W=S3, these correspond to the trivial representation, two copies of the standard representation, and the sign representation. For the Springer-theoretic construction and these decompositions, see [BM83].

5 Quantum K-theory (Xiaohan Yan and You-Cheng Chou)

5.1 Overview.

Gromov-Witten invariants are some way of “counting” curves in a smooth projective variety X. GW theory produces numbers of the form

⟨α1,…,αn⟩g,n,β∈ℚ

for various classes αi∈H∗⁢(X), genus g, number n of marked points, and curve class β∈H2⁢(X,ℤ). This has been used to study mirror symmetry, and outside of mirror symmetry has produced birational invariants. Our goal now is to lift this entire story to K-theory. Quantum K-theory produces numbers

⟨V1,…,Vn⟩g,n,β∈ℤ

for V1,…,Vn∈K⁡(X). These satisfy various difference equations7 and have found various applications in 3D mirror symmetry and representation theory.

5.2 K-theory.

Definition 5.1.

Let X be a smooth projective variety. Then the K-theory K⁡(X) of X is the Grothendieck group of vector bundles on X with the relation that if

0→V1→V2→V3→0

is a short exact sequence, then V2=V1+V3.

Remark 5.2.
  1. (1)

    K⁡(X) is a ring with the operations of direct sum and tensor product;

  2. (2)

    The Chern character gives an isomorphism K⁡(X)→A∗⁢(X), at least working over ℚ.

Example 5.3.

Let X=ℙn and set P=𝒪⁡(−1). Then we have

K⁡(X)=ℂ⁡[P±1]/(P−1)n+1→chA∗⁢(X)=ℂ⁡[H]/Hn+1.

For a Deligne-Mumford stack which is not assumed to be smooth, then there are two versions

K0⁢(X)⊃K0⁢(X),

where K0 means coherent sheaves and K0 means perfect complexes. These coincide on a smooth projective variety, so from now on K⁡(X) will mean K0⁢(X). There is a tensor product

K0⁢(X)⊗K0⁢(X)→K0⁢(X)

and a pushforward

f∗:K⁡(X)→K⁡(Y)V↦∑(−1)i⁢Ri⁢f∗⁢V

along proper morphisms. If f is a perfect morphism (for example flat, regular embedding, etc), then there is a pullback

f∗:K⁡(Y)→K⁡(X)W↦∑(−1)i⁢Torif−1⁢𝒪Y⁡(𝒪X,f−1⁢W).

5.3 Moduli of curves.

Recall the moduli space

M¯g,n(X,β)={f:(Σ,p1,…,pn)→X|g(Σ)=g,f∗[Σ]=β,|Autf|<∞}

of stable maps to X. This has evaluation maps

evi:M¯g,n⁢(X,β)→X(f,Σ,p¯)↦f⁡(pi).

There are also the universal cotangent lines Li=σi∗⁢ω𝒞/M¯.

The moduli space is a proper DM stack which has a perfect obstruction theory, which produces a virtual structure sheaf 𝒪g,n,βvir. This comes from the structure of a virtual tangent bundle, where

𝕋(f,Σ,p¯)⁢M¯g,n⁢(X,β)=χ⁡(Σ,f∗⁢TX)−χ⁡(Σ,TΣ⁢(−p1−⋯−pn)).

Roughly, if M¯ is the zero locus of a section of a vector bundle E on a variety Y, then 𝒪vir=𝒪Y⊗Eu⁡(E), where the K-theoretic Euler class is Eu⁡(E)=∑(−1)i⁢Λi⁢E∨.

5.4 KGW invariants.

For quantum K-theory, see [Lee04]; for the permutation-equivariant theory, see [Giv17; Giv15b]. Toën [Toë99] proves the Riemann–Roch formula for Deligne–Mumford stacks used below.

Definition 5.4.

K-theoretic GW invariants are defined by

⟨V1,…,Vn⟩g,n,β≔χ⁡(M¯g,n⁢(X,β);𝒪vir⊗⨂i=1nevi∗⁡Vi).

If V1,…,Vn are actual vector bundles, then the invariant is an integer, but generally we will consider K0 with coefficients in a field of characteristic zero. We may also define gravitational descendents

⟨V1⁢L1k1,…,Vn⁢Lnkn⟩g,n,β≔χ⁡(M¯g,n⁢(X,β);𝒪vir⊗⨂i=1n(evi∗⁡Vi)⁢Liki).

Using the action of Sn on M¯g,n⁢(X,β) given by permuting the marked points, then the objects ⨂i=1nevi∗⁡V and ⨂i=1nLik are Sn-equivariant.

Definition 5.5.

We define permutation-invariant K-theoretic GW invariants by

⟨V⁢L1k,…,V⁢Lnk⟩g,n,βSn ≔χ⁡([M¯g,n⁢(X,β)/Sn];𝒪vir⊗⨂i=1n(evi∗⁡V)⁢Lik)
=dimχSn⁢(M¯g,n⁢(X,β);𝒪vir⊗⨂i=1n(evi∗⁡V)⁢Lik)Sn.

Given t⁡(q)=∑n∈ℤtn⁢qn∈K⁡(X)⁢[q,q−1], we can define

⟨t⁡(L1),…,t⁡(Ln)⟩g,n,βSn≔χ⁡([M¯g,n⁢(X,β)/Sn],⋯).

More generally, if H=Sa1×⋯×Sam⊂Sn, we can define

⟨t1⁢(L1),…,t1⁢(La1),t2⁢(La1+1),…,t2⁢(La1+a2),…⟩g,n,βH.
Remark 5.6.

We would like to discuss some relation to ordinary GW invariants. Recall that Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch states that

χ⁡(M;V)=∫Mch⁡(V)⁢td⁡(TM).

In the case where M is a smooth DM stack, Töen proved the formula

χ⁡(M;V)=∫I⁢Mch~⁢(V)⁢td~⁢(TM),

where I⁢M=M×Δ,M×M,ΔM is the inertia stack of M and the tildes mean taking the orbifold Chern character and Todd class.

Example 5.7.

If M=B⁢μr, then I⁢M=⨆g∈μrB⁢μr. If M=ℙ⁡(1,r) is a weighted ℙ1, then I⁢M=M⊔⨆g≠1∈μrB⁢μr.

Example 5.8.

Let M=B⁢G for a finite abelian group G and V be a vector bundle on B⁢G, which is the same thing as a representation of G. Then χ⁡(M,V)=dimVG. On the other hand, we have

∫I⁢Mch~⁢(V)⋅td~⁢(TM)=∫I⁢Mtrg⁡V=∑g∈G1|G|⁢trg⁡V=dimVG,

so we have verified Riemann-Roch in this setting.

5.5 Axiomatic properties.

Lemma 5.9 ([Giv15b]).

We have the string equation

⟨1,x1⁢(L),…,xk⁢(L),t,…,t⟩g,1+k+n,βSn=⟨x1⁢(L),…,xk⁢(L),t⊗n⟩g,k+n,βSn
+∑i⟨⋯,xi⁢(L)−xi⁢(1)L−1,…,t⊗n⟩g,k+n,βSn.
Proof.

The proof is the same as in GW theory and comes from computing π∗⁢Li along the map π:M¯g,n+1⁢(X,β)→M¯g,n⁢(X,β). □

Lemma 5.10 ([Giv15b]).

We have the dilaton equation

⟨L−1,x1⁢(L),…,xk⁢(L),t⊗n⟩g,1+k+n,βSn= (k−2)⁢⟨x1⁢(L),…,xk⁢(L),t⊗n⟩g,k+n,βSn
+⟨x1⁢(L),…,xk⁢(L),t,t⊗n−1⟩g,k+n,βSn−1.
Proof.

We use the fact that

π∗⁢L=k+IndSn−1Sn⁡(1)−1,

where π forgets the first marked point and L=ωπ⁢(p1+⋯+pn). This follows from the fact that there is a residue map

H0⁢(L)→Res⨁i=1k+nℂ⁢pi→∑ℂ.

The middle term is a direct sum of k trivial representations and one standard representation. □

Notation 5.11.

Fix τ,t∈K⁡(X). We will denote

⟨⟨x1⁢(L1),…,xk⁢(Lk)⟩⟩g,k≔∑m,n,βQβm!⁢⟨x1⁢(L1),…,xk⁢(Lk),τ⊗m,t⊗n⟩g,k+m+n,βSn.

We will let {ϕα} be a basis of K⁡(X) and {ϕα} be the dual basis. Then define the pairing

gα⁢β=χ⁡(X,ϕα⊗ϕβ).

This is not quite the right pairing, so we will consider

Gα⁢β=gα⁢β+⟨⟨α,β⟩⟩0,2.

We will let gα⁢β=(gα⁢β)−1 and Gα⁢β=(Gα⁢β)−1.

Lemma 5.12 ([Giv00]).

Given A,B,C,D∈K⁡(X)⁢[q,q−1], we have the WDVV equation

∑α,β⟨⟨A⁡(L),B⁡(L),ϕα⟩⟩0,3 Gα⁢β⁢⟨⟨C⁡(L),D⁡(L),ϕβ⟩⟩0,3
