=∑α,β⟨⟨A⁡(L),C⁡(L),ϕα⟩⟩0,3⁢Gα⁢β⁢⟨⟨B⁡(L),D⁡(L),ϕβ⟩⟩0,3.
Proof.

Pull back the equality of the boundary divisors on M¯0,4=ℙ1. In K-theory, we need to apply the inclusion-exclusion principle when relating 𝒪D to 𝒪Ci when D=⋃Ci, which accounts for the appearance of Gα⁢β. □

5.6 Loop space formalism.

Definition 5.13.

The loop space (𝒦,Ω) consists of

𝒦=K⁡(X)⁢(q)⁢⟦Q⟧

with the symplectic form

Ω⁡(f,g)=−Resq=0,∞⁡⟨f⁡(q−1),g⁡(q)⟩X⁢dqq.
Remark 5.14.

There is a polarization 𝒦=𝒦+⊕𝒦−, where

𝒦+=K⁡(X)⁢[q,q−1]⁢⟦Q⟧

and

𝒦−={fg|f,g∈K⁡(X)⁢⟦Q⟧⁢[q],g⁡(0)≠0,deg⁡f<deg⁡g}.

For example, 11−q∈𝒦−.

Definition 5.15.

The big J-function J:𝒦+→𝒦 is given by

𝐭=𝐭⁡(q)↦1−q+𝐭⁡(q)+∑β,αQβ⁢ϕα⁢⟨ϕα1−q⁢L,𝐭⁢(L)⊗n⟩0,1+n,βSn.
Remark 5.16.

Note that applying Riemann-Roch, we have

χ⁡([M¯/Sn],11−q⁢L) =∫I⁡[M¯/Sn]ch⁡(11−q⁢L)⁢td.

Each term becomes of the form ch⁡(trg⁡11−q⁢L), which gives us something of the form ch⁡(11−q⁢ζ⁢L) for some root of unity ζ. Then we can expand

11−q⁢ζ⁢L=1(1−q⁢ζ)−q⁢ζ⁢(L−1)=∑k(q⁢ζ)k(1−q⁢ζ)k+1⁢(L−1)k.
Definition 5.17.

The Givental cone is defined to be ℒ≔Im⁡J⊂𝒦, where we are considering the germ near 1−q in the Q-adic topology.

Example 5.18.

Let X=ℙn. Then we see that

J⁡(0)=(1−q)⁢∑d≥0Qd∏ℓ=1d(1−P⁢qℓ)n+1,

where P=𝒪⁡(−1). As before, we can expand

11−P⁢qℓ=1(1−qℓ)−qℓ⁢(P−1)=∑k=0∞qℓ⁢k(1−qℓ)k+1⁢(P−1)k.
Proposition 5.19 ([Giv15b]).

In fact, ℒ is actually a cone in 𝒦 and we have

ℒ=⋃t∈K⁡(X)⁢⟦Q⟧(1−q)⁢St−1⁢(q)⁢𝒦+.

We may also introduce a “huge” J-function

J⁡(𝐭,τ)=1−q+𝐭⁡(q)+τ+∑β,k,αQβk!⁢ϕα⁢⟨ϕα1−q⁢L,𝐭⁢(L)⊗n,τ⊗k⟩0,1+n+k,βSn.

If we fix 𝐭⁡(q), then J⁡(τ) comes from a fundamental solution of a differential equation on the Frobenius manifold in τ. In addition, ℒ𝐭=Im⁡J⁡(τ) is actually a Lagrangian cone.

Example 5.20.

Consider f:ℂ⁡[Λ1±,Λ2±]→ℂ⁡[Λ1±,Λ2±] which is given by the Adams operation

t↦tr(1⁢⋯⁢n)⁡t⊗n=Ψn⁢(t).

Therefore, this sends Λ1↦Λ1n and Λ2↦Λ2n. However, it is not clear how to take derivatives in t because we would need n⁢v⁢tn−1=Ψn⁢(v), so the J-function does not satisfy a quantum differential equation in 𝐭.

5.7 Equivariant K-theory and localization.

For the fixed-point recursion and the projective-space calculation, see [Giv15a].

Let a torus T=(ℂ×)r act on a smooth projective variety X.

Definition 5.21.

The equivariant K-theory KT⁢(X) is the Grothendieck group of T-equivariant vector bundles on X.

Example 5.22.

For example, we have

KT⁢(pt)=Rep⁡(T)=ℂ⁡[Λ1±,…,Λr±],

where the Λi are the 1-dimensional representations with weight (0,…,1,…,0).

Remark 5.23.

For any X, KT⁢(X) is a KT⁢(pt)-algebra.

Example 5.24.

Consider the fully equivariant K-theory of ℙn. Then we have

KT⁢(ℙn)=ℂ⁡[P±,Λ0±,…,Λn±]/∏i=0n(P−Λi).

When we specialize Λi=1, we recover the non-equivariant K-theory.

Definition 5.25.

We can define the equivariant Euler characteristic as the pushforward

χT=π∗:KT⁢(X)→KT⁢(pt).
Example 5.26.

For example, we have χT⁢(𝒪ℙ1⁢(1))=Λ0−1+Λ1−1. Similarly, we have

χT⁢(𝒪⁡(2))=Λ0−2+Λ0−1⁢Λ1−1+Λ1−2.
Notation 5.27.

Note that Frac⁡(T)=Frac⁡(Rep⁡(T)). Then we will set

KTloc⁢(X)≔Frac⁡(T)⊗Rep⁡(T)KT⁢(X).

We will need the following fact. Let F be the fixed point set of T on X and consider ι:F↪X. Then there is an isomorphism of Frac⁡(T)-algebras

KTloc⁢(X)→ι∗KTloc⁢(F).
Remark 5.28.

The inverse is given by

(ι∗)−1=⨁i=1rιi⁣∗Eu⁡(NFi/X),

where Eu⁡(V)≔∑j=0rk⁡V(−1)j⁢Λj⁢V∗ is the K-theoretic Euler class.

Example 5.29.

On ℙn, we have n+1 isolated fixed points Fi, and then we obtain

ιi⁣∗⁢𝒪FiEu⁡(NFi/ℙn)=∏j≠iP−ΛjΛi−Λj.

These are idempotents of KTloc⁢(ℙn).

Using equivariant localization, we obtain

χT⁢(X;V)=∑iχ⁡(Fi;ιi∗⁢VEu⁡(NFi/X)).
Remark 5.30.

In the Λ=1 limit, we can recover the non-equivariant Euler characteristic.

Example 5.31.

Let X=ℙ1. Then we compute

χT⁢(ℙ1,𝒪⁡(1)) =χ⁡(F0,𝒪⁡(1)|F0Eu⁡(TF0/ℙ1))+χ⁡(F1,𝒪⁡(1)|F1Eu⁡(TF1/ℙ1))
=Λ0−11−Λ0Λ1+Λ1−11−Λ1Λ0
=Λ0−1+Λ1−1.

From now on, we will assume that X is a GKM manifold. Our goal now is to use localization on M¯g,n⁢(X,β) to study the big J-function of X. Any T-fixed stable map f:(Σ,p¯)→X has two types of irreducible components. There are those components which map entirely to fixed points and those components who map via ramified covers of 1-dimensional orbits. Unfortunately, we cannot compute the big J-function via virtual localization, but we can still study it.

Let f=f⁡(q)∈𝒦=KTloc⁢(X)⁢(q)⁢⟦Q⟧. Denote the fixed points by Fα for α=1,…,r with inclusions ια:Fα↪X. Then denote

fα⁢(q)=ια∗⁢f⁢(q)∈KTloc⁢(pt)⁢(q)⁢⟦Q⟧.

Then f∈ℒ if and only if for all α, the following conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    Given λ∈TFα⁢X and m∈ℕ+, fα⁢(q) has at most simple poles at q=λ1/m, and

    Resq=λ1/m⁡fα⁢(q)⁢dqq=−Qmm⋅Eu⁡(TFα/X)Eu⁡(Tϕα,α′,mvir⁢M¯0,2⁢(X,m⋅β⁡(α,α′)))⋅fα′⁢(λ1/m).

    Here, λ∈TFα⁢X means that λ is a 1-dimensional subrepresentation of TFα⁢X. Moreover, β⁡(α,α′) is the degree of the 1-dimensional orbit of T determined by the weight λ and ϕα,α′,m parameterizes m:1 covers of this 1-dimensional orbit.

  2. (2)

    fα⁢(q) has its other poles at 0,∞, and roots of unity, and is regular elsewhere. In addition, there are various minor conditions.

Example 5.32.

Let X=ℙn. Then

JTX⁢(0)=(1−q)⁢∑d≥0Qd∏i=0n∏ℓ=1d(1−PΛi⁢qℓ)∈KT⁢(X)⁢(q)⁢⟦Q⟧.

This then implies that

JTX⁢(0)|Fj=(1−q)⁢∑d≥0Qd∏i=0n∏ℓ=1d(1−ΛjΛi⁢qℓ),

so the poles are at q=(ΛiΛj)1/ℓ. Note also that

TFj⁢X=Λ0Λj+⋯+ΛnΛj−1.

5.8 Quantum K/GV correspondence.

The quintic correspondence was conjectured in [GS22] and proved in [CL22]. The following Calabi–Yau threefold formula is due to Chou–Lee [CL25].

Our goal here will be to compute JK⁢(0) on a Calabi-Yau threefold. The following result was conjectured by Jockers-Mayr and by Garoufalidis-Scheidegger.

Theorem 5.33 ([CL25]).

We have

JK⁢(0) ≔(1−q)+∑β,αQβ⁢Φα⁢⟨Φα1−q⁢L⟩0,1,βX,K
=(1−q)+∑β∑r=1∞GVβ⁢Qr⁢β⁢[∑j=1n1Φ1⁢j⁢a⁢(r,qr)+Φ01⁢b⁢(r,qr)],

where {Φα}α=1N is a basis of K0⁢(X) decomposed such that

{Φα}α=1N=⨆i=03{Φi⁢j}j=1ni

such that the collection ch⁡(Φi⁢j) for fixed i form a basis of H2⁢i⁢(X). We then select a dual basis {Φα}α={Φi⁢j}i,j. Moreover, we set the multiple cover formulae

a⁡(r,qr) =r−11−qr+1(1−qr)2,
b⁡(r,qr) =r2−11−qr+3(1−qr)2−2(1−qr)3.

Finally, GV denotes Gopakumar-Vafa invariants, which are defined in genus zero by

GW0,β=∑r|β1r3⁢GVβ/r.

By Möbius inversion, we see that

GVβ=∑r|βμ⁡(r)r3⁢GW0,β/r.
Corollary 5.34 ([CL25]).

We have

⟨1⟩0,1,βK=∑r|βr2⁢GVβ/r.

Applying Möbius inversion, we obtain8

GVβ=∑r|βr2⁢μ⁢(r)⁢⟨1⟩0,1,β/rK∈ℤ.

In addition, we can recover the usual GW invariants by9

limq→1(1−q)3⁢⟨11−q⁢L⟩0,1,βX,K=∑r|β−2r3⁢GVβ/r=−2⁢GWβ=⟨ψ⟩0,1,βGW.

Naively, we can think of JK⁢(0)∈ℤ⁡⟦q⟧⁢⟦Q⟧, but to be a bit more precise, we can consider

JK⁢(0)∈1−q+𝒦−.

Here, we expand 11−q⁢L=∑qi⁢Li. We also need to consider the fact that if M is a DM stack and L is a line bundle on M, then the function

fΦ⁢(q)≔χ⁡(M,Φ1−q⁢L)∈ℤ⁡⟦q⟧

converges to a rational function for |q|<ε. Note that there are poles only at roots of unity.

This fact can be proved using the orbifold Riemann-Roch theorem. Decompose the inertia as

I⁢M =⨆i∈IMi
=⨆ζMζ,

where Mζ is the union of twisted sectors such that g acts on L with eigenvalue ζ. Using this, we can compute

χ⁡(M,11−q⁢L) =∑i∈I∫Mitd⁡(Mi)⁢ch⁡(Trg⁡(11−q⁢L)λ−1⁢(NMi/M∗))
=∑ζ∫Mζtd⁡(Mζ)⁢∑k≥0(ζ⁢q)k(1−ζ⁢q)k+1⁢(ch⁡(L)−1)kch⁡λ−1⁢(N∗),

and therefore all poles must be at roots of unity. Here, we use the expansion

11−ζ⁢q⁢L=∑k≥0(ζ⁢q)k(1−ζ⁢q)k+1⁢(L−1)k

and take the Chern character.

Example 5.35.

Let L=𝒪⁡(1) on ℙ1. Then we have

χ⁡(ℙ1,11−q⁢L) =χ⁡(ℙ1,11−q+q(1−q)2⁢(L−1))
=∑i≥0qi⁢(i+1)
=1(1−q)2.
Example 5.36.

We will now consider weighted projective space. Then we have

χ⁡(ℙ⁡(w0,…,wn),11−q⁢L) =∏i=0n11−qwi.

5.9 Adelic characterization.

Recall that there is a relationship between GW and GV invariants using an explicit formula in all genus. On the other hand, we can recover GW invariants from KGW invariants via the q→1 limit. In the other direction, we need the Givental–Tonita adelic characterization [GT14]. The idea is that if we have a rational function f, then we can recover it from the Laurent expansions

fq=ζ=∑fζ,k⁢(1−ζ−1⁢q)k

at roots of unity ζ.

We will study the inertia stack I⁢M¯0,1⁢(X,β). One can keep track of the components via Figure 3 or via Figure 4.

We will now explain Figure 4. Let L1 be the cotangent line at the first marked point and let g be the automorphism of a point of I⁢M¯0,1⁢(X,β). Then ζ is defined by the condition that g acts on L1 with eigenvalue ζ. In both pictures, the bullet denotes the first marked point and its image in X, while a thick component is one which is a multiple cover of its image.

First, suppose that ζ=1. Then the black component is the maximal connected component containing the first marked point on which g acts as the identity. The red and blue components are precisely those on which g acts nontrivially, and we refer to them as arms.

Now suppose that ζ is an r-th root of unity for some r≥2. In this case, the nodes of the black component are required to be balanced with respect to the g-action, so we cut off the nonbalanced part, which is colored blue, and refer to it as the tail. On what remains, the black component is the maximal connected component containing the first marked point on which gr acts as the identity. Finally, after taking out the black component and the tail, we refer to the remaining components as legs.

The following definition is due to Givental. We write

⟨Φ1−q⁢L⟩0,1,βX,K≔∑ζ⟨Φ1−q⁢L⟩0,1,βXζ,

where the Xζ term is simply the contribution of Mζ under the Riemann-Roch theorem. Now, we will define arms, legs, and tails. Here, we define the arms

arm⁡(q)≔∑β,α,ζ≠1Qβ⁢Φα⁢⟨Φα1−q⁢L⟩0,1,βXζ,

the legs

legζ⁢(q)≔legr⁢(q)=Ψr⁢(arm⁡(q)),

and the tails

tailζ⁢(q)≔∑β,α,ζ′≠ζQβ⁢Φα⁢⟨Φα1−q⁢L⟩0,1,βXζ′.
Proposition 5.37 ([GT14]).

The Laurent expansion of the J-function at q=1 is given by

JK⁢(0)q=1 =Jfake⁢(arm⁡(q))
≔1−q+arm⁡(q)+∑n,β,αQβ⁢Φαn!⁢⟨Φα1−q⁢L,arm⁡(L),…,arm⁡(L)⟩0,n+1,βfake,

where the fake invariants are computed by applying Riemann-Roch and only considering the contribution of the untwisted sector.

Proposition 5.38 ([GT14]).

At any other root of unity ζ≠1, we have

JK⁢(0)q=ζ=(1−q)+tailζ⁢(q)
+∑n,β,αQr⁢β⁢Φαn!⁢[Φα1−ζ⁢q⁢L1/r,legr⁢(L),…,legr⁢(L),1−ζ−1⁢L1/r+tailζ⁢(ζ−1⁢L1/r)]stem,

where the stem is some fake invariant of X×B⁢μr defined on the moduli space

M¯0,n+2,βX⁢(ζ)≔M¯0,n+2⁢(X×B⁢μr,β,(g,1,…,1,g−1)).

It is defined by the formula

[⋯]stem≔∫[M¯0,n+2,βX⁢(ζ)]virtd⁡(TM¯)⁢ch⁡(Tr⁡(⋯)Tr⁡(λ−1⁢(N∗))),

where N denotes the normal bundle of M¯0,n+2,βX⁢(ζ)⊂M¯0,n⁢r+2⁢(X,r⁢β).

Remark 5.39.

If we can calculate the fake and stem theories, then we can compute genus zero quantum K invariants.

5.10 Quantum K-theory of a point.

One natural question is to study higher genus quantum K-theory. We will begin with the simplest target, which is a point. One motivation for studying higher-genus would be to try to prove integrality of the Klemm-Pandharipande definition of GV invariants for Calabi-Yau fourfolds or the Pandharipande-Zinger definition of GV invariants for Calabi-Yau fivefolds (in this situation, we only need to consider genus 1). One reason we need to consider the quantum K-theory of a point is because in I⁢M¯1,1⁢(X,β), there are some components where an entire curve of genus 1 is contracted to a point.

Question 5.40.

What is the K-theoretic Witten-Kontsevich theorem?10

We will first recall the cohomological Witten’s conjecture. We will begin with the operator

L=∂x2+u⁡(x)

and deform it to

L~=∂x2+u⁡(x,T3,T5,…),

where we should think of x=T1 and u⁡(x)=u⁡(x,0,0,…). Formally, write

L1/2=∂x+∑k>0a−k⁢(x)⁢∂x−k

using the property

∂n∘f=∑m=0∞(nm)⁢f(m)⁢∂n−m

for all integers n∈ℤ. In particular, we construct the (2-)KdV hierarchy by the equation

∂L~∂T2⁢k+1=[(L~2⁢k+12)≥0,L~]

for all k≥0. We define a τ-function to be a function τ such that

2⁢∂2∂x2⁢log⁡τ⁡(x,T3,T5,…)=u⁡(x,T3,T5,…).

Now perform the above process using u=2⁢x. Define the function

F⁡(t0,t1,…)≔∑n≥0∑k0,…,kn⟨τ0k0⁢⋯⁢τnkn⟩⁢t0k0⁢⋯⁢tnknk0!⁢⋯⁢kn!.

Note that because the genus is determined entirely by the number of insertions and the degree of the insertions, the notation

⟨τ0k0⁢⋯⁢τnkn⟩

uniquely determines a descendant GW invariant of a point.

Theorem 5.41 (Kontsevich [Kon92]).

F is a τ-function of the KdV hierarchy constructed starting with L=∂x2+2⁢x under the change of variables ti=(2⁢i+1)!!⁢T2⁢i+1.

One application of this theorem is to consider virtual localization. For example, suppose we consider M¯g,0⁢(X,d⁡[C]) where C is a unique rational curve in a Calabi-Yau threefold with normal bundle N=𝒪⁡(−1)⊕𝒪⁡(−1). Then in this setting we can reduce to the local model and compute

∫[M¯g,0⁢(ℙ1,d)]virctop⁢(R1⁢π∗⁢N)=∑m⊢d(−1)d−L⁡(m)|Aut⁡(m)|⁢∫M¯g,L⁡(m)1+⋯+cg⁢(ℋ)∏i(1−mi⁢ψi)

via virtual localization. If we would like a similar result in K-theory, then we will need to consider terms of the form

χ⁡(M¯g,L⁡(m)/Aut⁡(m),λ−1⁢(ℋ)1−mi⁢Li),

so we will need to consider the permutation-equivariant quantum K-theory of a point.

We now proceed with a literature review. First, Lee [Lee97] computed the formula

⟨11−q1⁢L,…,11−qn⁢L⟩0,npt,K=(∏i=1n11−qi)⁢(1+∑i=1nqi1−qi)n−3.

Later, Lee–Qu [LQ14] gave a way to compute

⟨11−q1⁢L,…,11−qn⁢L⟩1,npt,K

in principle. Givental [Giv17] computed the formula

∑n≥2⟨11−q⁢L,1,…,1⟩0,1+nSn=(1−q)⁢exp⁡(∑k>0Ψkk⁢(1+q1−q)).

Finally, Milanov [Mil25], in a preprint first posted in 2024, computed

∑n≥0 ⟨11−q1⁢L,…,11−qr⁢L,1,…,1⟩0,r+nSn
=(∏i=1r11−qi)⁢(1+∑i=1rqi1−qi)⁢exp⁡(∑k>0Ψkk⁢(1+∑i=1rqi1−qi)).

The following pluri-Hodge recursions and the new genus-one calculations based on them are due to You-Cheng Chou and were presented in this lecture.

Let s∈ℤ and define the pluri-Hodge sheaf ℋs≔R0⁢π∗⁢(ωπs). Considering the map M¯g,n+1→𝜋M¯g,n, we will denote the upstairs cotangent lines by Li and the downstairs ones by ℓi.

Lemma 5.42.

For all integers s and di, we have

π∗⁢(ωπs⁢(∑i=1ndi⁢Di))=ℋs−ℋ1−s∗+∑i=1n∑k=1diℓi−k+s.
Remark 5.43.

Note that if f⁡(q)∈ℤ⁡[q], then exp⁡∑kΨkk⁢(f⁡(q))∈ℤ⁡⟦q⟧. The reason is that this operation sends f=∑i=1nai⁢qi to ∏i=1n1(1−qi)ai.

Proof.

When all di are zero, we see that

R0⁢π∗⁢ωπs−R1⁢π∗⁢ωπs=ℋs−ℋ1−s∗

by Serre duality. The next step is to show that

π∗⁢ωπs⁢((r+1)⁢Di)=π∗⁢ωπs⁢(r⁢Di)+ℓis−r−1.

Here, we first consider the exact sequence

0→𝒪⁡(−Di)→𝒪→𝒪Di→0

and twist by ωπs to obtain

0→ωπs⁢(r⁢Di)→ωπs⁢((r+1)⁢Di)→ωπs⁢((r+1)⁢Di)⊗𝒪Di→0

and then compute the pushforward. □

Lemma 5.44.

Let fi be rational functions, for example 11−q⁢L. Then

⟨f1⁢(L),…,fn⁢(L),Ln+1r⟩g,n+1= ∑i=1n⟨f1⁢(L),…,D⁡(fi⁢fn+1),…,fn⁢(L)⟩g,n
+⟨f1⁢(L),…,fn⁢(L)|ℋr−ℋ1−r∗⟩g,n,

where fn+1=Ln+1r and (D⁢f)⁢(x)≔f⁡(x)−f⁡(1)x−1.

To prove this, we need to consider the pushforward

π∗⁢(L1d1⁢⋯⁢Ln+1dn+1) =π∗⁢(π∗⁢(ℓ1d1⊗⋯⊗ℓndn)⊗ωπdn+1⁢(∑i(di+dn+1)⁢Di)).

Here, we use the fact that Li=(π∗⁢ℓi)⁢(Di) and Ln+1=ωπ⁢(D1+⋯+Dn). Applying the previous lemma, we see that the pushforward becomes

(ℓ1d1⁢⋯⁢ℓndn)⁢(ℋdn+1−ℋ1−dn+1∗+∑i=1n∑k=1di+dn+1ℓi−k+dn+1).

Now, Lee’s formula computes the correlators

⟨(L−1)k1,…,(L−1)kn⟩0,n=(n−3)!∏i=1nki!⁢(n−3−∑iki)!

via the expansion

11−q⁢L=11−q⁢∑k≥0qk⁢(L−1)k(1−q)k.

Note here that there is no Hodge bundle in genus 0, so in fact the lemma can be used to obtain Lee’s formula.

Lemma 5.45.

We have

ℋr−ℋ1−r∗=π∗⁢(ℋr−ℋ1−r∗)−∑i=1n(D2⁢(π∗⁢ℓi)r)⁢𝒪Di.

The lemmas collectively imply that we can reduce to the case of a single marking at the cost of making the insertions very complicated and introducing pluri-Hodge terms everywhere. In genus 1, life becomes easier because on M¯1,1, we have

ℋr=𝒪⁡(r)=L1r.

In this case, recall the classical formula

χ⁡(M¯1,1,11−q⁢L)=1(1−q4)⁢(1−q6).

Unfortunately, computing

χ⁡(M¯1,n;11−q1⁢L⁢⋯⁢11−qn⁢L)

is too hard, so we can try to compute

χ⁡(M¯1,1;11−q1⁢L1⁢⋯⁢11−qn⁢L1)

which is known, but it is unclear how to write a good formula for it. The reason we would consider this is the operation

ℤ⟦q⟧→[]rℤ⟦q1,…,qr⟧qk→hk(q1,…,qr)≔∑ℓ1+⋯+ℓr=kq1ℓ1⋯qrℓr.

Unfortunately, You-Cheng does not know how to write

χ⁡(M¯1,1;11−q1⁢L1⁢⋯⁢11−qn⁢L1)=[1(1−q4)⁢(1−q6)]n

in a nice form. In principle we can write formulae like

[f⁡(q)]2≔q1⁢f⁢(q1)−q2⁢f⁢(q2)q1−q2,

but this does not seem to help much.

5.11 Permutation-equivariant theory of a point.

We can compute χ⁡(M¯1,1,11−q⁢L) in another way. Consider the involution on an elliptic curve, which gives a map

M¯1,1→M¯0,1+3/S3.

Then, Givental [Giv17] computes

χ⁡([M¯0,1+n−1/Sn−1],11−q⁢L)=∏i=2n−111−qi.

In particular, we obtain

1(1−q2)⁢(1−q3),

and then because the map is a μ2-gerbe (or a 2:1-cover on objects), we obtain the desired formula.

Consider ℋg,1⊂M¯g,1 to be the hyperelliptic locus. Note that the marking lies on a Weierstrass point. Note that the fixed points of the hyperelliptic involution go to 2⁢g+1 points on ℙ1, and therefore one would want to use the calculation

χ⁡(M¯0,1+2⁢g+1/S2⁢g+1,11−q⁢L)=∏i=22⁢g+111−qi

to compute the quantity χ⁡(ℋg,1,11−q⁢L). However, because of the way that the curves upstairs degenerate, we will need to consider the Hassett moduli space [Has03] where the last 2⁢g+1 markings have weight 12.

6 Quasimap wall-crossing (Yang Zhou)

The main wall-crossing theorem and master-space construction in this lecture are from [Zho22]. Earlier genus-zero and higher-genus results appear in [CK14; CK20], and the foundations of stable quasimaps are in [CKM14].

Let X be the quintic threefold. Our goal is to count genus zero curves on X, which is a problem that was solved by Givental and Lian-Liu-Yau. Via the closed immersion X⊂ℙ4, we can write

M¯0⁢(X,d)⊂M¯0⁢(ℙ4,d),

which is smooth and has a torus action by (ℂ×)5. If a map is fixed by this action, the domain must have some components which map to the fixed points and some components which form an n:1 cover of the 1-dimensional orbits. In particular, the fixed locus is indexed by a set of graphs.

In this setting, we have the quantum Lefschetz principle, which states that

[M¯0⁢(X,d)]vir=e⁡(E)∩[M¯0⁢(ℙ4,d)].

Here, the vector bundle E is defined by

E=π∗⁢f∗⁢𝒪⁢(5),

where π is the universal curve and f is the universal stable map. We will give a different perspective on the result that if

I⁡(q,z) =1+∑d>0∏k=15⁢d(5⁢H+k⁢z)∏k=1d(H+k⁢z)5⁢qd∈H∗⁢(X)⁢[z−1]⁢⟦q⟧
=I0⁢(q)⋅1+I1⁢(q)⁢Hz+I2⁢(q)⁢H2z2+I3⁢(q)⁢H3z3,

then

J⁡(Q,z)=1+∑d>0ϕα⁢⟨ϕαz⁢(z−ψ)⟩0,1X⁢Qd=II0

up to the mirror map Q=q⁢exp⁡(I1I0).

6.1 Naive counting.

We will consider “maps” ℙ1→X⊂ℙ4 from a fixed ℙ1. For simplicity, we will assume X=(∑xi5=0) is the Fermat quintic. This is given by a collection [f0,…,f4] where fi∈ℂ⁡[u,v] such that deg⁡fi=d and ∑fi5=0. To be an actual morphism, we need the fi to have no common zeroes, but this moduli is not proper, so we relax this condition. Then we consider the moduli space

QG(X,d)={[f0,…,f4]|fi∈ℂ⁡[u,v]deg⁡fi=d,∑fi5=0,(f0,…,f4)≠(0,…,0)}/ℂ×.

This lives inside the corresponding moduli space

Q⁢G⁢(ℙ4,d) ≔{[f0,…,f4]|fi∈ℂ⁡[u,v],deg⁡fi=d,(f0,…,f4)≠(0,…,0)}
≅ℙ5⁢d+5−1

of rational maps to projective space. There are two problems. First, the domain is parameterized, so we need to account for the automorphisms of ℙ1. Second, to obtain stable maps, we need to blow up the domain.

First, let ℂ× act on ℙ1 by scaling u. Consider the special fixed locus F⋆⊂Q⁢G⁢(X,d) defined by

F⋆,d={[f0,…,f4]⁢ fixed and ⁢(v=0)⁢ is not a common zero}.

Therefore, F⋆,d={[a0⁢ud,…,a4⁢ud]|[a0,…,a4]∈X}≅X. From this perspective, we can rewrite the I-function as

I⁡(q,z) =∑d>0([F⋆,d]vireℂ×⁢(Nvir))PD⁢qd
=1+∑d>0([X]eℂ×⁢(Nvir))PD⁢qd

using standard arguments in deformation theory. This lives in Hℂ×∗⁢(X)⁢⟦q⟧⁢[z−1].

6.2 Wall-crossing without rigor.

Second, consider a nodal curve C with a marking plus a tail with an action of ℂ× and suppose we have a map f:C→X. If we take the limit

limt→0[f0⁢(t−1⁢u,v),…,f4⁢(t−1⁢u,v)]=[a0⁢ud0,…,a4⁢ud0],

we see that the limit of the bubble lands in F⋆,d0, where the common zero is away from the node. Then we can replace this tail by a new marking which carries some terms of the I-function. For the quintic, this is simply I1⁢H−I0⁢ψ=[z⁢I−z]+,z=−ψ. At the end of this process, we are left with C=ℙ1 with various contributions of the I-function.

Note that if we consider ℂ× acting on ℙ4, then f:C→ℙ4 is fixed if for all t∈ℂ×, there exists φt such that

commutes. Therefore, we obtain an action of ℂ× on the domain.

We will define the moduli space Qg,nε⁢(X,d) of ε-stable quasimaps to X, which is analogous to the moduli of stable maps. We want to think of these moduli spaces as being virtually birational to each other, and each of these is a proper DM stack with perfect obstruction theory, and therefore we can define quasimap invariants

⟨γ1⁢ψ1a1⁢⋯⁢γn⁢ψnan⟩g,nε≔∫[Qg,nε⁢(X,d)]vir∏i=1nevi∗⁡(γi)⁢ψiai.

Here, ε∈ℚ>0 is a positive rational number. The space of possible ε has a wall and chamber structure, where the walls occur at 1n for positive integers n. When ε>1 we obtain Gromov-Witten theory (namely stable maps), and as we move to the left, we allow fewer rational tails but more basepoints. Eventually, in the ε→0+ limit, no rational tails are allowed. In the end, we obtain the following wall-crossing formula around the wall at 1d0:

⟨−⟩g,n,dε+−⟨−⟩g,n,dε−=∑k1k!⁢⟨−,μ,…,μ⟩g,n+k,d−k⁢d0ε+.

Here, μ=[z⁢I−z]+,qd0,z=−ψ. In the special case, where g=0, n=1, and ε=0+, we obtain

∑ϕα⁢⟨ϕαz⁢(z−ψ)⟩0,1ε=Iz<0.

Crossing all walls from the GW chamber, we obtain

I=1+∑d≥1k≥01k!⁢∑αϕα⁢⟨ϕαz⁢(z−ψ),I1⁢H−I0⁢ψ,…,I1⁢H−I0⁢ψ⟩0,1+k,d∞⁢qd,

which produces the mirror map via the dilaton and divisor equations.

6.3 Quasimaps.

Definition 6.1.

A prestable quasimap to the quintic threefold X consists of

(C,x1,…,xn,ℒ,φ0,…,φ4),

where (C,x1,…,xn) is a prestable curve, ℒ∈Pic⁡C, and φ0,…,φ4∈H0⁢(C,ℒ), such that

φ−1⁢(0)≔{x∈C|φ0⁢(x)=⋯=φ4⁢(x)=0}

is finite and away from the special points. In addition, we require that ∑φi5=0.

Importantly, we will refer to φ−1⁢(0) as the set of base points. Away from φ−1⁢(0), we have an actual morphism C∖φ−1⁢(0)→X. Geometrically, suppose we have a family over 𝔸1∖0 where in the limit as t→0, the zero loci φi−1⁢(0) will end up colliding. We can either preserve this quasimap in the central fiber, or we can blow up the central fiber some number of times to obtain an actual morphism at the cost of bubbling out a rational tail. Therefore, any moduli space of prestable quasimaps cannot be separated, so we must consider some kind of stability condition.

Definition 6.2.

A prestable quasimap (C,𝐱,ℒ,φ) is ε-stable if

  1. (1)

    For all x∈φ−1⁢(0), we have len⁡(x)≤1ε, where len⁡(x)=min⁡{ordx⁡(φi)};

  2. (2)

    The ℚ-line bundle ℒε⊗ωClog has positive degree on every irreducible component of C.

Note that for all irreducible components C′⊆C, we have deg⁡ℒ|𝒞′≥0. Therefore, the things which change are curves of genus 0 with ≤2 special points or curves of genus 1 with no marked points. Note that in the (0,0) and (1,0) cases, we have C=C′, and in the (0,2) case, stability is equivalent to deg⁡ℒ>0, so in the (0,1) case, the second condition is equivalent to

deg⁡ℒ|C′>1ε.
Example 6.3.

In the ε>1 chamber, note that the first condition implies that there are no basepoints, and the second condition implies that all unstable components have positive degree, and therefore we have recovered stable maps.

If we move into the chamber where 12<ε<1, then we must contract rational tails of degree 1. For example if we have a chain of two degree 1 rational curves ending in a tail, then we contract the outermost tail and are left with a single degree 2 rational tail with a basepoint of length 1.

If we move into the 13<ε<12 chamber, then we must contract all rational tails of degree 2 and replace them with basepoints of length 2.

Remark 6.4.

In the case of projective space, there is an actual morphism

Qgε+⁢(ℙN,d)→Qgε−⁢(ℙN,d)(Cg∪C0,ℒ,φ)↦(Cg,ℒ|Cg⁢(p),φ⁡(p)).

For a general target, this is not possible, but this idea gives intuition for the phenomenon of quasimap wall-crossing.

We will now discuss how to generalize this to more general target spaces. Let

X=V⫽θG,

where V is affine, G is reductive, and θ is a character of G. We need to require that

  1. (1)

    Vss⁢(θ)=Vs⁢(θ)≠∅;

  2. (2)

    V has at worst lci singularities and Vs⁢(θ) is smooth.

Note that we require the stable locus to have finite stabilizers. For convenience, we will also require

  1. (1)

    V⫽G is projective;

  2. (2)

    G acts freely on the stable locus.

Example 6.5.

In the case of the quintic, V is the affine cone over the quintic. The unstable locus consists of the origin, which is the unique singular point.

Example 6.6.

Another example is that we can consider ℂN⫽(ℂ×)r with generic stability condition and obtain a toric variety.

Example 6.7.

We can consider the Grassmannian

G⁡(2,4)=M2×4⫽G⁢L2,

where the unstable locus consists of matrices with rank strictly less than 2.

Remark 6.8.

The condition on the stable locus is always satisfied when G is abelian for generic stability conditions, but for non-abelian G this is not always possible.

Remark 6.9.

For a general smooth projective variety, the origin is not necessarily lci, so it is unclear how to define quasimaps in a way where we can still define a virtual cycle.

Definition 6.10.

A prestable quasimap to V⫽G is a map u:C→[V/G] such that the base locus

u−1⁢([Vun⁢(θ)/G])

is finite and away from the special points. By definition, u consists of a principal G-bundle P→C together with an equivariant map P→V, which is equivalent to a section of the associated bundle P×GV.

Example 6.11.

For the quintic, this exactly recovers a line bundle ℒ∈Pic⁡C (which is equivalent to a ℂ×-torsor) combined with a section of Tot⁡(ℒ⊕5) which satisfies the defining equation.

In order to define degrees, we can consider the line bundle ℒθ on [V/G]. Then we can define the degree of C′⊂C under u to be

deg⁡(u∗⁢ℒθ|C′).
Example 6.12.

In the G⁡(2,4) example, note that a principal GL2-bundle is equivalent to rank 2 vector bundle ℰ on C. Therefore, P×GV is equivalent to the data of ℰ⊕4, and therefore quasimaps to the Grassmannian are equivalent to stable quotients. In this case, we are looking for generically surjective

𝒪⊕4→ℰ,

and because θ=det, we see that u∗⁢ℒθ=detℰ.

Example 6.13.

Consider V=ℂN+1 and note that ℙN=V⫽ℂ×. If we consider θ1:z↦z, then we have

Vun=V⁡((xi)).

However, if we consider θ:z↦z2, then we have

Vun=V⁡((xi⁢xj)).

Here, we see that the scheme structure is sensitive to the choice of character, so we cannot simply naively define the length of a basepoint. Note that

Vun=V⁡(⟨⨁k≥1Rk⟩),Rk=H0⁢([V/G],Lθ⊗k).

In particular, we must define

len⁡(x)≔minf∈Rkk≥1⁡ordx⁡u∗⁢(f)k.
Example 6.14.

Let X=pt=ℂ⫽θℂ×. Then a prestable quasimap is simply

(C,ℒ,φ∈H0⁢(ℒ)),

where φ−1⁢(0) is finite and away from the special points. In addition, if deg⁡ℒ=1, we have precisely recovered the data of a new marked point in Csm.

Example 6.15.

Now consider X=pt=ℂn⫽(ℂ×)n. Also suppose that the degree is (1,…,1). Now we will set

θ=(a1,…,an).

Therefore, note that

⟨R1⟩=⟨(x1a1⁢⋯⁢xnan)⟩.

Because these all live in degree 1, we see that for a smooth point x∈Csm, we have

lenx=∑ordx⁡(φiai)=∑ai⁢ordx⁡φi.

If we set {pi}=φi−1⁢(0), then the condition that ε⋅len⁡(x)≤1 is equivalent to requiring that

∑x=piε⁢ai≤1.

The degree condition now states that

ε⁢∑iai+deg⁡ωC>0.

Equivalently, this states that

ωC⁢(ε⁢a1⁢p1+⋯+ε⁢an⁢pn)>0,

so we recover a weighted pointed curve with weights (ε⁢a1,…,ε⁢an).

6.4 Master space.

The proof uses virtual localization [GP99]; Hassett's weighted moduli spaces [Has03] provide one of the models for the construction.

Our method will be to perform virtual localization on a master space which interpolates the two moduli. Consider the ℂ×-action on ℙn given by

t⋅[x0:⋯:xn]=[t⁢x0,x1,…,xn].

The fixed loci consists of a ℙn−1 where x0=0 and a point [1,0,…,0]. Then we can compute

∫ℙn−1Hn−1=1

by transfering the computation to the other fixed locus. In particular, we lift to H∈Hℂ×∗⁢(ℙn)=ℚ⁡[H,z]/(H−z)⁢Hn and compute

∫ℙnHn−1 =∫ℙn−1Hn−1−z+H+∫ptzn−1zn.

Taking residues, we see that

0 =Resz=0⁡∫ℙn−1Hn−1−z+H+1
=1−∫ℙn−1Hn−1,

which recovers the desired integral. The key fact we used here is that projective space is proper.

Example 6.16 (Second toy example).

We will consider a second toy example. Recall Hassett’s moduli of weighted pointed curves

(C,x1,…,xn)

where C is nodal and the xi∈Csm can collide. The collisions are regulated by the fact that each marked point is given a weight δi∈ℚ∩(0,1] and are required to satisfy the following conditions:

  1. (1)

    For all x∈Csm, then

    ∑x=xiδi≤1;
  2. (2)

    We have the stability condition ωC⁢(δ1⁢x1+⋯+δn⁢xn)>0. For example, if we have a rational tail, then ∑xi∈C′δi>1.

Example 6.17 (Another toy example).

Our goal will be to once again compute

∫M¯0,4ψ1=1.

Our first goal will be to change the stability condition. If we set

δ+=(23,23,23,23),

we see that the stability condition does not change. However, if we set

δ−=(23,23,23,13),

the moduli space does not change, but the universal curve in fact becomes ℙ1×ℙ1 with the section x4 being the diagonal. This tells us that

∫M¯0,4δ−ψ1=0,

and we will use this to compute in the δ+ chamber. We can try to form a master space by both allowing rational tails with xi,x4 and allowing x1=x4, but if we do this, we end up with a semistable point with a rational tail where x1=x4. We want to end up with this by taking a quotient from a master space, so we will add the data of a tangent vector to the moduli. Therefore, define the δ± master space to consist of objects of the form

ξ=(C,x1,…,x4,v∈Tx4⁢C∪∞)

where C is nodal, xi are smooth points, x1,x2,x3 are disjoint,

∑xi∈C′23⁢δi>1

for all rational tails C′, if v=0, then x4 is disjoint from the other xi, and when v=∞, there are no rational tails where x4≠xi for i=1,2,3.

We now give this master space an action of ℂ× by scaling v. There are various fixed loci:

  1. (1)

    When v=0, we obtain M¯0,4δ+;

  2. (2)

    When v=∞, we obtain M¯0,4δ−;

  3. (3)

    There are fixed loci where v≠0,∞ and we have a rational tail with xi=x4.

If we consider a general point (with all four marked points disjoint), it will travel directly to itself along the ℂ×-action. However, if we start with a rational tail containing x1 and x4, then we first travel to a rational tail with general v but x1=x4, and if we smooth out the node, we obtain a single curve with x1=x4, but we allow v→∞, which is another fixed point. Now we can integrate

∫𝖬𝖺𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋ψ1=∫M¯0,4δ+ψ1−z−?+∫M¯0,4δ−ψ1z+?+Cont⁡(12|34)+Cont⁡(13|24)+Cont⁡(14|23).

Taking residues at z=0, we obtain

0 =−∫M¯0,4δ+ψ1+0+0+0+∫pt(−z)(±z)⁢(±z),

where in the final term the ±z in the denominator are node smoothing parameters, and therefore we recover the desired integral.

With all of our toy examples, we are finally ready to discuss the quasimap master space. Our first step at the 1d0 wall is to allow both degree d0 rational tails and length d0 base points. However, we can consider curves with a rational tail and a quasimap of the form

[a0⁢ud0,…,an⁢ud0],

which have infinitely many automorphisms. However, we cannot attach tangent vectors to the base points (because deformations will remove them), and there are also situations where there exists more than one degree d0 with a base point of length d0 (and then the automorphism group contains ℂ×).

Remark 6.18.

There is a key observation. Suppose that we have two rational tails of degree d0 and call the two nodes p1 and p2. Now define the space of smoothing parameters

ℂ≅Θi=Tpi⁢Ei⊗Tpi⁢Cg,

where Ei is the rational tail and Cg is the rest of the curve. We will consider the moduli

𝔐g,n,dwt→ét𝔐g,n

of weighted semistable curves labelled by degrees. Note that this morphism is highly non-separated. We will consider the open substack 𝔐g,n,dwt,ε0 where the curves have no tail of degree strictly less than d0. Then we can consider the Cartier divisor 𝒵 where there exists at least one tail of degree d0. In particular, we see that

Θi=N𝒵i|ξ

for the two branches 𝒵1 and 𝒵2 at the point of interest. We also see that Θ1⊗Θ2=𝒪⁡(𝒵)|ξ, so we can add the data of

v∈(⨂iΘi)∨∪{∞}

and the data of

w∈ℙ⁡(Θ1⊕Θ2).

The actual construction proceeds as follows. Consider 𝒵⊂𝔐=𝔐g,dwt,ε0. Define 𝔐~→⋯→𝔐 to be an iterated blowup along strata of 𝒵. Then an object of the master space (a quasimap with calibrated tails) over a scheme S is given by the data of a quasimap

inducing a morphism p:S→𝔐g,dwt,ε0, a choice of a lift

a line bundle 𝒩∈Pic⁡S, and v=(v1,v2) where v1∈H0⁢(w∗⁢𝒪⁢(−𝒵)) and v2∈H0⁢(𝒩), where (v1,v2) is nonvanishing. We also disallow basepoints of length strictly larger than d0 and require stability such that

  1. (1)

    When v=0, we obtain ε+-stability;

  2. (2)

    When v=∞, we obtain ε−-stability;

  3. (3)

    Any constant tail (degree d0 with base point of length d0) is an entangled tail. Here, we consider the last blowup such that w maps to an exceptional locus ⋂i∈I𝒵~i, and then the Ei are entangled tails for i∈I;

  4. (4)

    If there exists a degree d0 tail, then all length d0 base points are on degree d0 tails.

7 Log GLSM (Qile Chen)

Let X be a smooth projective variety (or even a DM stack). Let E be a vector bundle on X with a section s∈H0⁢(E) which defines a smooth zero section Z of the expected codimension. We will refer to X and E as ambient and s and Z as the complete intersection.

Question 7.1.

What is the relationship between the GW theory of Z and the GW theory of (X,E)?

When g=0, Givental and Lian-Liu-Yau used this relationship to compute the GW invariants of complete intersections, and when g=1, this was done by Zinger. In general, there are two approaches: (N)MSP and log GLSM. In this series of lectures, we will discuss log GLSM.11

7.1 R-maps.

We will consider the R-torus ℂω×≔ℂ×. This has a weight 1 representation, which we will call ℂω. It descends to a line bundle ℒω≔[ℂω/ℂω×] on B⁢ℂω×. The targets of R-maps will be stacks

ℙ→B⁢ℂω×

which are DM-type, separated, and (log) smooth. Now, an R-map consists of a (2-)commutative diagram

Here, the curve could be prestable, twisted, log, or even punctured.

Example 7.2.

Our first example is that of stable maps. Let 𝔓=B⁢ℂω×. Because in the diagram

the vertical arrow is the second projection, we see that this reduces to a map to X.

Example 7.3.

Consider maps

If we assume that C is unmarked, we see that the data of this map is simply a section of ωC, and therefore we recover holomorphic differentials.

Example 7.4.

Consider a morphism ℂR×→ℂω× given by z↦zrin. Then we see that

ℒR⊗rin≃ℒω|B⁢ℂR×.

Now a diagram

with C unmarked is equivalent to the data of a line bundle ℒR|C and an isomorphism ℒR⊗rin≃ωC. Alternatively, we can consider R-maps of the form

which parameterize curves with an R-spin line bundle together with a section.

Example 7.5.

Let X be a smooth projective variety. Then consider R-maps of the form

This is equivalent to a map C→X together with a section ρ∈H0⁢(E∨|C⊗ωC).

We will consider targets in the GW case. Consider the data of an ambient (X,E). Then we will set 𝔓∘≔E∨⊠ℒω. The morphism 𝔓∘→B⁢ℂω× is very nice, but it is not proper. To fix this, we will consider the log stack

𝔓=(ℙ⁡(E∨⊠ℒω⊕𝒪),∞).

Because we have a smooth divisor in a smooth stack, the map 𝔓→B⁢ℂω× is proper and log smooth. Note that we have the zero section

0𝔓⊂𝔓∘⊂𝔓⊃∞.

We will now consider targets in the r-spin case. Consider the log stack

(ℙ⁡(ℒR⊕n⊕𝒪),∞)=𝔓→B⁢ℂR×→B⁢ℂω×.

This morphism is proper and log smooth.

7.2 Log and punctured R-maps.

We will consider diagrams

where C→S is a log or a punctured (possibly twisted) curve and S is an fs log scheme. The stability condition in the GW case is that f is representable and

(ωlog)1+δ+H⊗k⊗f∗⁢𝒪⁢(∞)>0

for all 0<δ≪1 and k≫1, where H is an ample line bundle on the coarse moduli space of X. For punctured R-maps, we further require pre-stability.

Example 7.6.

Consider the case of holomorphic differentials. Then consider f∈H0⁢(ωC) such that all zeroes are concentrated in a single Weierstrass point, where C has genus 2. If we consider limλ→∞λ⋅f, then the limit consists of a genus 2 component mapping entirely to ∞ and a rational component which remembers the zero.

We will now discuss the tropicalization of log or punctured R-maps. Recall that a graph

G¯=(𝕍,ℍ,ı:ℍ→ℍ,v:ℍ→𝕍)

consists of a set 𝕍 of vertices, a set ℍ of half edges, an involution ı on the half edges, and a root map from half edges to vertices. Then we will let the set 𝕃 of legs be

𝕃={h∈ℍ|ı⁡(h)=h}.

The edges are pairs of distinct half-edges which are sent to each other by the involution:

𝔼={{h,h^}|ı⁡(h)=h^≠h}.

Now a decorated graph is a graph combined with a genus function

g:𝕍→ℕ,

an assignment

r:ℍ→ℕ,

and an ordering

m:𝕃→{0,…,n}.
Example 7.7.

For a log or punctured R-map

we will tropicalize it by taking the associated generalized cone complex of the entire diagram. Because B⁢ℂω× has no log structure, what we see is

Now suppose that S=Spec⁡(Q→ℂ) is a log point with Q an fs sharp monoid. In particular, this means that Σ⁡(S)=Qℝ∨. Because everything is (piecewise) linear, it suffices to consider an interior point t∈Σ⁡(S) and consider Σ⁢(C)t.

From each half edge, we treat it as pointing outward from the attached vertex, and in particular, this means that a linear map to ℝ≥0 corresponds to a slope. We will call these contact orders. In particular, we have c⁡(h)=−c⁡(h^) if h≠h^ are related by ı. For all v∈𝕍, we also define the degeneracy

ev:Qℝ∨→ℝ≥0t↦Σ⁢(f)t⁢(v).

In particular, ev∈Q is an integral point.

The next thing we need to introduce are punctured legs. They will be denoted by

𝕃∘={h∈ℍ|Σ⁢(f)t⁢(h)⁢ is bounded and nontrivial for all ⁢t∈Qℝ∨}.

We will define prestability at h∈𝕃∘ such that 0∈Σ⁢(f)t⁢(h)¯, which is a technically necessary assumption. Under the assumption that all punctured legs are prestable, we can define the edge length function

ℓ:𝔼∪𝕃∘→𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(Qℝ∨,ℝ≥0)x↦ℓ⁡(x):t↦ℓ⁡(x)⁢(t).

Note that ℓ⁡(E)∈Q is also an integral point for edges E. For punctured legs, this is true up to subdivision.

7.3 Log GLSM invariants.

Definition 7.8.

We will define the decorated tropical type of a log map f as

𝝉=(G,c:ℍ→ℤ,β:𝕍→H2(X)).
Definition 7.9.

A log or punctured map f is of compact type if

  1. (1)

    Im⁡Σ⁢(f)t is bounded for all t;

  2. (2)

    f⁡(ph)∈0𝔓 for all half-edges h with contact order 0.

We are now able to define the category ℛ⁡(𝔓,τ) of stable punctured R-maps fibered over the category 𝖫𝗈𝗀𝖲𝖼𝗁 of fs log schemes and marked by τ.

Theorem 7.10 ([CJR21; CJR22]).

The stack ℛ⁡(𝔓,𝛕) is represented by a proper DM stack with basic/minimal log structure.

Remark 7.11.

If 𝕍={v} is a singleton, then we will write

ℛg,c⁢(𝔓,β)≔ℛ⁡(𝔓,𝝉).

Consider the diagram

where we set ℛ≔ℛ⁡(𝔓,𝝉). Then the perfect obstruction theory is defined by

Tℛ/𝖫𝗈𝗀𝔐G→𝔼□=R⁢π∗⁢f∗⁢T𝔓/B⁢ℂω×.

Here, both tangent bundles refer to the log tangent complex. From the perfect obstruction theory, this defines the canonical virtual cycle

[ℛ⁡(𝔓,𝝉)]vir.

The main drawback of this virtual cycle is that it does not reproduce Gromov-Witten theory. However, we can consider how it differs from GW theory, but for this we need a birational modification. Let Q be a sharp monoid. It has a partial ordering by a<b if there exists a nonzero c∈Q such that a+c=b.

Definition 7.12.

We say that either f or Σ⁡(f) has uniform maximal degeneracy if there exists emax∈{ev|v∈𝕍} such that emax≥ev for all v∈𝕍.

Remark 7.13.

If f is compact type and has uniform maximal degeneracy, then Σ⁡(f) is uniformly bounded by emax.

Definition 7.14.

Define 𝒰⁡(𝔓,𝝉) to be the stack of stable punctured or log R-maps marked by 𝝉 with uniform maximal degeneracy.

Remark 7.15.

If 𝕍={v} is a singleton, then we will write

𝒰g,c⁢(𝔓,β)≔𝒰⁡(𝔓,𝝉).

If one of the contact orders is negative, then we will write

𝒰g,c⁢(∞,β)≔𝒰⁡(𝔓,𝝉).

Note that there are two types of vertices: if a vertex is mapped to 0, then either there is at least one half-edge which points upwards or all contact orders are 0, in which case all are contracted. These are called log vertices. The other type of vertex is one that does not go to 0. Either all half-edges point downwards, or there are some half-edges which point upwards. These are called ∞-vertices. Moreover, the vertices which are compact types are the ones without upwards-pointing half-edges.

If we forget the condition of having uniform maximal degeneracy, then there is a map

𝒰⁡(𝔓,𝝉)→𝐹ℛ⁡(𝔓,𝝉)

which is a subcategory over 𝖫𝗈𝗀𝖲𝖼𝗁. However, as a morphism of algebraic stacks, it is log étale, proper, and surjective. In addition, 𝒰 has a canonical perfect obstruction theory which is pulled back from ℛ. In the case when the set of vertices is a singleton, we have

F∗⁢[𝒰g,c⁢(𝔓,β)]vir =[ℛg,c⁢(𝔓,β)]vir;
F∗⁢[𝒰g,c⁢(∞,β)]vir =[ℛg,c⁢(∞,β)]vir.

In the case of a log vertex, we in fact have inclusions from the moduli of stable maps with p-fields as

If we denote the moduli of p-fields by ℛ∘, then the boundary

Δ≔𝒰∖ℛ∘

is a Cartier divisor. By the condition of having uniform maximal degeneracy, we have a section

emax∈H0⁢(M¯𝒰).

This is equivalent to the data of a morphism

𝒰→([𝔸1/𝔾m],0)

which pulls 0 back to Δ.

We will define a superpotential to be a function

Its critical locus is denoted by

Crit⁡(W)=(dW=0).

We say that W has proper critical locus if Crit⁡(W)→B⁢ℂω× is proper.

For example, suppose we are interested in GW theory. Let X be a smooth projective variety, V be a vector bundle on X, and s∈H0⁢(V). Set Z=(s=0). Then we obtain

W:𝔓∘=V∨⊠ℒω→s⊗1ωℒω.
Lemma 7.16.

W has proper critical locus if and only if Z is smooth of expected codimension.

Example 7.17.

Let X be a point, V=ℂ, and s≠0. Then dW=s≠0, so the critical locus is empty.

Using the Kiem–Li method of cosection localization [KL13], we can obtain a virtual cycle

[ℛg,c=n⁢(𝔓∘,β)]Wvir,

which is supported on the critical locus. In GW theory, this equals the GW virtual cycle,

±[M¯g,n⁢(Crit⁡(W),β)]vir,

where the sign can be explicitly calculated.

Theorem 7.18 ([CJR21; CJW21]).

Let 𝛕 be of compact type. In the compact type setting,

  1. (1)

    𝒰⁡(𝔓,𝝉) has a reduced perfect obstruction theory, which yields a reduced virtual cycle [𝒰⁡(𝔓,𝝉)]vir;

  2. (2)

    Δ has a reduced perfect obstruction theory, which yields a reduced virtual cycle [Δ]vir;

  3. (3)

    We have [𝒰g,c=n⁢(𝔓,β)]red=±[M¯g,n⁢(Crit⁡(W),β)]vir in the case of a single log vertex. Moreover, there is the formula

    [𝒰g,c=n⁢(𝔓,β)]red=[𝒰g,c=n⁢(𝔓,β)]vir−r~⁢[Δ]red,

    where r~ is the pole order of W along ∞.

7.4 Tropical decomposition and finite generation.

The tropical decomposition and its applications below are from the working draft [CJR25]. The effective invariants and their axioms are developed in [CJR22].

From now on, we will consider a simpler setup where X is a smooth projective variety and V is a line bundle on X. In this case, we will assume that Z=(s=0) is smooth of codimension 1. Moreover, we will assume that Z is a Calabi-Yau threefold. We will consider the invariants

Ng,β≔∫[M¯g,0⁢(Z,β)]vir1∈ℚ

and the generating series

Fg=∑β≥0Ng,β⁢Qβ∈Λ≔ℂ⁡⟦Q⟧.
Conjecture 7.19 (Yamaguchi-Yau, Alim-Länge [YY04; AL07]).

Suppose g=0 mirror symmetry holds for Z. Then there exists a finitely-generated ℚ-algebra R⊂Λ such that for all g≥2, Fg∈(I0⁢(q))2⁢g−2⁢R.

Our main goal is the following.

Theorem 7.20 ([CJR25]).

Let Z be a Calabi-Yau threefold hypersurface in a Fano fourfold X with no odd cohomology. Let {ϕj} be a basis of H∗⁢(X) and {ϕj} be the dual basis. Then for all g≥0, we have

Fg=(−1)1−g⁢∑τ′∈Gg′(−1)|𝕍∞||Aut⁡(τ′)|⋅∏E∈𝔼c⁡(E)
⋅∑jE|E={Elog,E∞}∈𝔼∏v∈𝕍∞g⁡(v)=1ℍv={E∞}c1eff⁢(ϕjE)⋅∏v∈𝕍∞g⁡(v)≥2Q~β⁡(v)⋅exp⁡(∫β⁡(v)K⁡(Q))
⋅(∏E∞∈ℍv′∫β⁡(v)ϕjE)⋅cg⁡(v),β⁡(v)eff⋅∏v∈𝕍logΩg⁡(v),|ℍ1⁢(v)|,|ℍ2⁢(v)|(ϕjE:Elog∈ℍ1(v)).
Example 7.21.

Let Y be a toric variety with its toric log structure. Then Σ⁡(Y) is the toric fan treated as a cone complex, and we can consider its boundary ΔY=∑ρ∈Σ⁢(Y)1Δρ.

If we consider [Δ]red, we should obtain the similar formula

[Δ]red=∑ρ∈Σ⁡(Δ)⁢(1)[Δρ]red.

The question now is what the ρ represent. In fact, they parameterize rigid tropical curves. In the tropicalization

we see that fρ is rigid if and only if the source tropical curve is a bipartite graph with one set of vertices going to emax and the other set of vertices going to 0.

Example 7.22.

Let X be a point and Z=∅. Also consider g=2,n=0. Then the possible graphs are given in Figure 5.

Theorem 7.23 (Tropical quantum Lefschetz [CJR25]).

Let X and Z be as before. For any β∈H2⁢(X), any α1,…,αn∈H∗⁢(X), and any k1,…,kn∈ℕ, we have

∫[M¯g,n⁢(Z,β)]vir∏j=1nevj∗⁡(αj)⁢ψkj= (−1)1−g+β⋅Z⋅∑τ⊢(g,n,β)(−1)|𝕍∞||Aut⁡(τ)|⋅∏E∈𝔼c⁡(E)
⋅∑{jE|E={Elog,E∞}}∏v∈𝕍∞∫[𝒰v]red∏E∞∈ℍvevE∞∗⁡ϕjE
⋅∏v∈𝕍log∫[ℛv]vir∏ElogevElog∗⁡(ϕjE)⋅∏h∈𝕃vevh∗⁡αh⋅ψhkh.
Remark 7.24.

There is also a virtual localization formula, announced in [CJR], which can be applied to either the reduced theory (with only the R-torus action) or the canonical theory (which can be applied to the full automorphisms of the ambient space).

Now consider an ∞-vertex. Set τv=(g,c,β) and set 𝒰v=𝒰g,c⁢(∞,β). Then the first computation is that

red⁡dim𝒰v =χ⁡(f∗⁢T𝔓/B⁢ℂω×)+1+trop⁢dim
=vir⁢dimM¯g,n⁢(Z,β)+∑h∈ℍ(c⁡(h)+1),

where the tropical dimension is 3⁢g−4+n. Note that all contact orders are negative, so the second term is at most zero. In particular, we have proved that

Corollary 7.25 ([CJR22]).

If vir⁢dimM¯g,n⁢(Z,β)<0, then [𝒰v]red=0.

We also have a balancing condition, which states that

(1) ∑h∈ℍc⁡(h)=deg⁡f∗⁢𝒪⁡(∞)=∫βc1⁢(V)−(2⁢g−2+n).

This can be rewritten as

0≥∑h∈ℍ(c⁡(h)+1)=∫βc1⁢(V)−(2⁢g−2).
Proposition 7.26 ([CJR22]).

We see that ∞-vertices do not exist in the following cases:

  1. (1)

    We have g=0 and V is nef;

  2. (2)

    We have g=1 and V is ample, unless β=0 and all c⁡(h)=−1.

Definition 7.27.

A marking is a unit if its contact order is −1.

Notation 7.28.

We will denote the unit sector by 𝟏 and denote τv+𝟏=(g,c+𝟏,β), 𝒰v+𝟏=𝒰g,c+𝟏⁢(∞,β), and ℛv+𝟏=ℛg,c+𝟏⁢(∞,β).

Theorem 7.29 ([CJR22, Theorems 1.16–1.17]).
  1. (1)

    There is a map F𝟏:𝒰v+𝟏→𝑠𝒞∘→𝜋𝒰v, where s is birational;

  2. (2)

8 Structure of higher-genus GW invariants of the quintic (Shuai Guo)

8.1 The problem.

We will consider the quintic threefold X=X5⊂ℙ4 and ask how many curves of genus g and degree d it contains. In genus zero, the answers begin

2875,609250,317206375,…

Because X is Calabi-Yau, the moduli space ℳ¯g,n⁢(X,β) has virtual dimension zero, and the string equation gives ⟨𝟏,γ2,…,γn⟩g,n,β=0 unless (g,n,β)=(0,3,0). We therefore define the primary invariants by

Ng,β≔⟨⟩g,0,β=∫[ℳ¯g⁢(X,β)]vir1

and we package these numbers in the generating series

Fg⁢(Q)≔∑β⁢ effectiveNg,β⁢Qβ.

The invariants Ng,β are rational numbers, while the integers we actually want are the BPS invariants ng,β. These are defined from the positive-degree part Fg+ by the multicover transformation

∑g≥0Fg+⁢(Q)⁢λ2⁢g−2=∑g≥0β>0ng,β⁢∑k≥11k⁢(2⁢sin⁡k⁢λ2)2⁢g−2⁢Qk⁢β.

Note that only the ng,β are expected to be integral, and that the numbers above are the n0,d.

We see that every column of Table 2 eventually vanishes. This is the Castelnuovo bound, which for the quintic states that ng,d=0 once g>d2+5⁢d+1010 and was proved by Liu–Ruan [LR22]. Integrality of the entries is the Gopakumar-Vafa conjecture, which was proved by Ionel–Parker [IP18].

In genus zero, Candelas-de la Ossa-Green-Parkes computed F0 using period integrals on the mirror, which we discussed in Section 3.2. In higher genus, Bershadsky-Cecotti-Ooguri-Vafa gave a recursion which produces Fg from the Fh with h<g up to finitely many unknown constants. Our goal is to explain how log GLSM determines this ambiguity.

8.2 Genus zero and the polynomial structure of the B-model.

Recall from Section 3.2 that for the quintic we consider the I-function

I⁡(q,z)=z⁢∑d≥0qH/z+d⁢∏m=15⁢d(5⁢H+m⁢z)∏m=1d(H+m⁢z)5=I0⁢z+I1⁢H+I2⁢H2z+I3⁢H3z2,

whose components are annihilated by the Picard-Fuchs operator

D4−5⁢q⁢(5⁢D+1)⁢(5⁢D+2)⁢(5⁢D+3)⁢(5⁢D+4),D=q⁢ddq.

If we write Jk=Ik/I0 and I1I0=log⁡q+τ⁡(q), so that Q=eI1/I0=q⁢eτ⁡(q)=q+O⁡(q2), then the genus zero mirror theorem states that

F0⁢(Q)=52⁢(J1⁢J2−J3).

For our purposes, it is useful to place the quintic formula in the general mirror-symmetry picture. Let 𝒳={(X,ω)} be a family of Calabi-Yau threefolds with Kähler moduli ℳ∋Q=e2⁢π⁢i⁢ω and let 𝒳∨={(X∨,J)} be a mirror family with complex moduli ℳ∨∋q. The solutions of the Picard-Fuchs equation are periods on X∨ and assemble into

I⁡(z)=z⁢I0⁢φ0+I1+I2⁢z−1+I3⁢z−2,

which lies in the span of z⁢φ0,φα,φα⁢z−1,φ0⁢z−2. Here, I1=∑αI1α⁢φα, I2=∑αI2,α⁢φα, and I3=I3,0⁢φ0, and the mirror map is again Q=eI1/I0=q⁢eτ⁡(q).

We will use three special points on the complex moduli line of the quintic: the large complex structure point q=0, the conifold point q=5−5 (where a period vanishes), and the orbifold (or Landau-Ginzburg) point q=∞. The mirror map is defined at q=0 and the expansion there produces Gromov-Witten invariants, while in higher genus we will impose boundary conditions at the other two points.

We now restate the mirror theorem in terms of three-point functions. Pick local coordinates qi on ℳ∨, let {ϕi} be the corresponding basis on the A-side, and define

Ci⁢j⁢kA⁢(Q)≔I02⁢⟨ϕi,ϕj,ϕk⟩0,3X,Ci⁢j⁢kB⁢(q)≔∫X∨∂i∂j∂kΩ∧Ω.
Theorem 8.1 (Mirror theorem [Giv98; LLY97]).

We have Ci⁢j⁢kA⁢(Q⁡(q))=Ci⁢j⁢kB⁢(q). Moreover Ci⁢j⁢kB∈Δ−1⁢ℚ⁢[q], so it is a globally defined meromorphic function on ℳ∨ with poles only along the discriminant.

In particular, after multiplying by the correct power of I0 and applying the mirror map, a genus-zero generating function becomes a rational function of q with poles only along the discriminant. Therefore, it is determined by finitely many coefficients.

Example 8.2.

For the quintic in the hyperplane basis,

C111=51−55⁢q.
Example 8.3.

For X=X3,3⊂ℙ2×ℙ2, the Yukawa couplings are

C111 =34⁢q1⁢(2+33⁢q1+33⁢q2)Δ, C222 =34⁢q2⁢(2+33⁢q1+33⁢q2)Δ,
C112 =(1−33⁢q1−33⁢q2)⁢(1+2⋅33⁢q1−33⁢q2)Δ,
C122 =(1−33⁢q1−33⁢q2)⁢(1−33⁢q1+2⋅33⁢q2)Δ,

where

Δ=1−3⋅33⁢(q1+q2)+3⋅36⁢(q12−7⁢q1⁢q2+q22)−39⁢(q1+q2)3.

In higher genus, we expect normalized potentials fg,iA satisfying

fg,iA⁢(Q⁡(q))=fg,iB⁢(q)∈Δ−(2⁢g−2+n)⁢ℚ⁢[q],

where the right hand side is computed by a sum over graphs.

8.3 The BCOV Feynman rule.

The B-model Feynman rule and holomorphic anomaly equation originate in [BCOV94]. For the quintic, Chang–Guo–Li prove polynomiality in [CGL21] and the Feynman rule in [CGL26].

We will now discuss the BCOV recursion as a Feynman rule. It comes from a finite-dimensional model for the quantization of a symplectic transformation as in Section 3.6. Let ℋ=ℋ−⊕ℋ+⊂ℋ∞ be symplectic with d+1=dimℋ+=dimℋ− and set

R=(ABCD)∈End⁡ℋ,𝒬⁡(𝐱,𝐩)=(𝐩,D−1⁢𝐱)−12⁢(𝐩,D−1⁢C⁢𝐩).

Given a total potential F⁡(ℏ,𝐱), we formally define the transformed potential by the Gaussian integral

f⁡(ℏ,𝐱)≔(R̂⁢F)⁢(ℏ,𝐱)=ln⁡∫eℏ−1⁢(𝒬⁡(𝐱,𝐩′)−𝐱′⁢𝐩′)+F⁡(ℏ,𝐱′)⁢d𝐱′⁢d𝐩′.

Expanding by stationary phase gives a sum over graphs. Here, D−1⁢C supplies the propagator on each edge and F supplies the vertices.

For a Calabi-Yau threefold the propagators are written Sφ⁢φ, Sφ, and S according to the number of indices, and the vertices are the normalized A-model correlators

Pg,nA⁢(Q)=I02−2⁢g⁢⟨ϕ1,…,ϕn⟩g,nX.

Note that these have nothing to do with the operator Sτ⁢(z) solving the quantum differential equation, which will appear later.

Example 8.4.

For the quintic in genus two with no markings, the Feynman rule reads

f2B= P2+12⁢Sφ⁢φ⁢P1,12+12⁢Sφ⁢φ⁢P1,2+(Sφ⁢φ)2⁢P1,1+18⁢(Sφ⁢φ)2⁢P0,4
+18⁢(Sφ⁢φ)3+112⁢(Sφ⁢φ)3+χ24⁢Sφ⁢P1,1+12⁢χ24⁢Sφ⁢Sφ⁢φ
+12⁢χ24⁢(χ24−1)⁢S,

where χ=χ⁡(X5)=−200. This is a cubic polynomial in the propagators.

We can interpret this as a sum over stable graphs, as in Section 3.4. A vertex v contributes the lower-genus correlator Pgv,val⁡(v); an internal edge contracts two of the insertions against a propagator; the legs record the remaining insertions. Each graph is weighted by 1|Aut⁡Γ|. As usual

g⁡(Γ)=h1⁢(Γ)+∑vgv,2⁢gv−2+val⁡(v)>0,

and fgB is the sum of the contributions of all stable graphs of genus g.

8.4 The holomorphic anomaly equation.

We will now rewrite the recursion as a differential equation. The B-model amplitudes ℱg⁢(z,z¯) are not holomorphic, and for g≥2 their failure to be holomorphic is given by

∂i¯ℱg=12⁢C¯i¯j⁢k⁢(Dj⁢Dk⁢ℱg−1+∑r=1g−1Dj⁢ℱr⁢Dk⁢ℱg−r).

Here, Ci⁢j⁢k is the Yukawa coupling, C¯i¯j⁢k is obtained from C¯i¯⁢j¯⁢k¯ by raising two indices with the Weil-Petersson metric, and Dj is the covariant derivative on the appropriate power of the Hodge line bundle. The two terms on the right are the two boundary strata of ℳ¯g, namely a non-separating and a separating node. The 12 forgets the ordering of the two branches.

If we choose local ∂¯-primitives

∂i¯Sj⁢k=C¯i¯j⁢k,∂i¯Sj=Gi⁢ℓ¯⁢Sℓ⁢j,∂i¯S=Gi⁢ℓ¯⁢Sℓ,

so that, modulo a holomorphic term, the anomaly equation becomes the polynomial PDE

∂ℱg∂Sj⁢k=12⁢(Dj⁢Dk⁢ℱg−1+∑r=1g−1Dj⁢ℱr⁢Dk⁢ℱg−r).

These propagators are only defined up to holomorphic tensors, and this freedom is the source of the holomorphic ambiguity.

Remark 8.5.

In the one-parameter normalized variables we will use for the quintic, this reads

−∂0Pg=12⁢Pg−1,2+12⁢∑r=1g−1Pr,1⁢Pg−r,1,−∂1Pg=0.

To see why the graph sum satisfies this equation, note that in an unmarked potential the non-holomorphic generators occur only in the edge factors. A derivative in a propagator direction therefore picks out a single edge and cuts it. The two half-edges become markings on the resulting lower-genus vertices, and the covariant derivatives correspond to those markings by the divisor equation. We obtain Pg−1,2 by cutting a loop and Pg1,1⁢Pg2,1 by cutting a separating edge.

Remark 8.6.

For clarity, the implication only goes one way. The BCOV graph rule implies the anomaly equation, but the anomaly equation by itself does not determine the graph rule. To recover the same solution, we also need the propagator convention, the lower-genus vertex data, and the boundary conditions.

If all lower-genus vertices are known, then the right hand side is known, so we can integrate with respect to the non-holomorphic generators to obtain

Pg=Pgparticular+fg⁢(Y),

where finite generation gives the holomorphic ambiguity

fg⁢(Y)=Pg|A=B1=B2=B3=0=∑i=03⁢g−3ai,g⁢Yi,Y=(1−55⁢q)−1.

We see that the anomaly equation leaves 3⁢g−2 unknown coefficients in each genus.

Remark 8.7.

For the quintic, the degree-zero data together with orbifold regularity remove ⌈3⁢g−35⌉+1 of these freedoms and the conifold gap supplies 2⁢g−2 further conditions, so that

3⁢g−2−(⌈3⁢g−35⌉+1)−(2⁢g−2)=⌊2⁢g−25⌋

parameters remain and are genuinely new effective invariants. This is exactly the number of ∞-vertex unknowns predicted by Equation 1, namely the number of β with β≤2⁢g−25.

We therefore obtain the following conjectural algorithm proposed by physicists: the BCOV Feynman rule, orbifold regularity at the Landau-Ginzburg point (a form of the LG/CY correspondence, which for the quintic is work in progress of Guo-Ruan-Janda), and the conifold gap condition. To these we may add the Gopakumar-Vafa integrality and the Castelnuovo bound.

8.5 Four theories.

Recall from Section 7 that the log GLSM carries two virtual cycles. The reduced cycle recovers quintic Gromov-Witten theory, while the canonical equivariant cycle admits a root of unity specialization which is semisimple and therefore computable by Givental-Teleman. The bipartite graph sum

Ωg,nGW=∑Γ⁢ bipartite1|Aut⁡Γ|⁢(∏v∈V∞⁢(Γ)cgv,βveff)⁢ContΓcan

expresses the former in terms of the latter, at the cost of introducing the effective invariants cg,βeff at the ∞-vertices. Replacing these by formal parameters 𝐂={cg,β} gives the extended 𝐂-family, whose vertex data is supplied by the meromorphic and rubber log GLSM theories.

We will consider the following four theories.

  • •

    The t-twisted geometric theory sets λi=0 and keeps the auxiliary weight t. It has both stable-map and stable-quotient versions, and the quotient version gives the genus two localization formula below.

  • •

    The formal quintic, or formal λ-twisted theory, sets t=0 and λi=ζ5i⁢λ. It is a semisimple CohFT, so it has a universal and computable R-matrix.

  • •

    The extended 𝐂-family interpolates between these, and is where bipartite graphs with both formal and meromorphic vertices live.

  • •

    Quintic Gromov-Witten theory is obtained by setting 𝐂=𝐂eff and then letting λ→0, and is the theory we want to compute.

Warning 8.8.

In higher genus the t0 coefficient of the t-twisted stable quotient theory is not the λ0 coefficient of the formal λ-twisted theory.

8.6 The formal quintic.

The formal quintic and its holomorphic anomaly equations are studied in [LP19]; the comparison with the extended theory is developed in [GJR18].

Let E=𝒪ℙ4⁢(5) and let π:𝒞→ℳ¯g,n⁢(ℙ4,d) be the universal curve. The t-twisted cycle is

e⁡(R⁢π∗⁢f∗⁢E⊗[1])∩[ℳ¯g,n⁢(ℙ4,d)]vir,

where [1] has equivariant first Chern class t. Starting instead from the fully (ℂ×)5-equivariant cycle, the formal quintic is the root of unity specialization

[ℳ¯g,n⁢(ℙ4,d)]vir,λ≔(e⁡(R⁢π∗⁢f∗⁢E⊗[1])∩[ℳ¯g,n⁢(ℙ4,d)](ℂ×)5vir)|t=0,λi=ζ5i⁢λ,

where ζ5=e2⁢π⁢i/5. The relation H5=λ5 makes the quantum product generically semisimple while retaining λ as a parameter.

The state space, unit, and pairing are given by

ℋλ=ℚ⁡(λ)⁢[H]/(H5−λ5),𝟏=1,(γ1,γ2)λ=∫ℙ4,(ℂ×)5e⁡(𝒪⁡(5))⁢γ1⁢γ2|λi=ζ5i⁢λ,

and the CohFT classes are

Ωg,nλ⁢(γ1,…,γn)=∑d≥0qd⁢ρ∗⁢(∏i=1nevi∗⁡(γi)∩[ℳ¯g,n⁢(ℙ4,d)]vir,λ),

where ρ forgets the map and stabilizes the domain. If we shift by τ⁡(q)⁢H with τ⁡(q)=I1λ⁢(q)/I0λ⁢(q), then the shifted theory Ωλ,τ is semisimple. After extending scalars to ℚ⁡(ζ5,λ), the idempotent basis satisfies

ωg,nλ⁢(eα1,…,eαn)=∑αΔαg−1⁢∏iδα,αi.

Then Theorem 3.24 gives

Ωg,nλ,τ=∑Γ∈Gg,n1|Aut⁡Γ|⁢ι∗⁢ContΓ

with the decorations of Section 3.4. A leg carrying γ gets R−1⁢(ψ¯)⁢γ, an edge gets

VR⁢(z1,z2)=∑αeα⊗eα−∑αR−1⁢(z1)⁢eα⊗R−1⁢(z2)⁢eαz1+z2,

and a vertex gets the topological field theory ω, with the missing unit-preserving part inserted at forgotten markings via T⁡(z)=z⁢(𝟏−R−1⁢(z)⁢𝟏).

Remark 8.9.

We see that the edge factor has no pole. Setting z2=−z1 and using the symplectic condition in the form R−1⁢(z)=R∗⁢(−z), the numerator vanishes. Therefore, it is divisible by z1+z2, and VR is a power series in the two cotangent line variables. The coefficient of z1p⁢z2q is the class placed at a node with ψ¯1p⁢ψ¯2q, and contracting it against the two adjacent topological field theory tensors glues the branches.

8.7 How to compute the R-matrix.

To compute the R-matrix, we begin with the formal equivariant I-function

Iλ⁢(q,z)=z⁢∑d≥0qd⁢∏m=15⁢d(5⁢H+m⁢z)∏m=1d((H+m⁢z)5−λ5)=z⁢I0+I1λ⁢H+z−1⁢I2λ⁢H2+⋯.

The coefficients through H are independent of λ, so I1λ=I1−I0⁢log⁡q and the mirror shift τ⁡(q)=I1λ⁢(q)/I0⁢(q) is free of logarithms. Set

D=q⁢ddq,Y=(1−55⁢q)−1,L=Y1/5

and introduce the bases

ϕk=I1,1⁢⋯⁢Ik,k⁢Hk,ϕ¯k=I0⁢L−k−1⁢ϕk,

where the diagonal Birkhoff factors are defined recursively by

Ip,0=Ip,Ip,r=Ip−1,r−1Ir−1,r−1+D⁡(Ip,r−1Ir−1,r−1),1≤r≤p,

so that in particular I1,1=1+D⁢τ. The idempotents and canonical coordinates are given by

eα=15⁢∑i=04hα−i⁢ϕiLi,uα=hα⁢∫0q(L⁡(s)−1)⁢dss,hα=ζ5α⁢λ.

We will use the quantum differential equation to determine the q-dependence of the R-matrix. The fundamental solution satisfies

zDSτ(z)+Sτ(z)H=MτSτ(z),Mτ=τ˙⋆,τ˙≔(1+Dτ)H=I1,1H,

and in the normalized canonical direction α the stationary phase asymptotics give

(Sτ)i⁢α¯⁢(z)⁢Cα⁢(z)−1=euα/z⁢Ri⁢α¯⁢(z),

so that

(z⁢D+hα⁢L)⁢Ri⁢α¯=∑j(Mτ)ij⁢Rj⁢α¯.

Here, Cα⁢(z) is the q=0 quantum Riemann-Roch (equivalently, Gamma function) factor, and together with the symplectic condition it fixes the constants that the differential equation cannot see. As at the end of Section 3.7, the differential equation gives a recursion and an oscillating integral gives the initial conditions.

Writing R⁡(z)=Id+R1⁢z+R2⁢z2+⋯, we can use the equation above to determine each Rk+1 from the preceding ones. There are two features which make the quintic tractable. First, the root of unity basis has five sectors, and a mod 5 charge rule permits only one residue pattern in each row. Then most matrix entries vanish before any computation starts. Second, every coefficient lies in the finitely generated ring

ℛ=ℚ⁡[A,B1,B2,B3,Y],A=D⁢I1,1I1,1,Bk=Dk⁢I0I0,

so the stable graph sum reduces to a finite algebraic computation.

Remark 8.10.

In particular, a fixed genus only needs finitely much of R for dimensional reasons. On ℳ¯g,n only classes of total degree at most 3⁢g−3+n contribute and everything else integrates to zero, so for an unmarked potential we need only R0,…,R3⁢g−3. Genus 4 stops at z9 and genus 5 at z12.

8.8 Genus two.

The genus-two mirror formula discussed here is due to Guo–Janda–Ruan [GJR17].

We will now carry out both routes in genus two. The geometric route uses the t-twisted stable quotient theory, applies virtual localization to get five contributions, and then applies stable quotient wall crossing to land on quintic Gromov-Witten theory. The formal route uses the semisimple λ-twisted theory and the R-matrix to compute a stable graph sum. This gives only the formal leading part. Then the effective and meromorphic rest graphs must still be added.

Notation 8.11.

Write

⟨α1,…,αn⟩g,nt,SQ≔∑d≥0qd⁢∫[ℳ¯g,n⁢(ℙ4,d)]vire⁡(R⁢π∗⁢ℒ⊗5⊗[−1])⁢∏ievi∗⁡(αi),

where ℒ is the universal stable quotient line bundle and c1ℂ×⁢([−1])=−t (a sign convention we return to below). This is the stable quotient sign convention, and is not the same as the [1] appearing in the stable map cycle above.

The four non-constant graphs are drawn in Figure 6, and their contributions are

ContΓ2 =⟨⟩2,0t,SQ,
ContΓ1 =−⟨−52⁢H3+524⁢H4⁢t−1(t−5⁢H)⁢(t−5⁢H−ψ)⟩1,1t,SQ,
