ContΓa0=⟨53⁢(H3⊗H4+H4⊗H3)⁢t−1+6524⁢H4⊗H4⁢t−2(t−5⁢H1)⁢(t−5⁢H1−ψ1)⁢(t−5⁢H2)⁢(t−5⁢H2−ψ2)⟩0,2t,SQ.

Note that these correlators live on ℙ4, so H4 is present and nonzero.

There is a fifth contribution from the degree zero graph, which is the constant

−2⁢c2,0=−5144,c2,0=−12⁢N2,0=5288,

and adding the five contributions, we obtain the localization identity

F2SQ⁢(q)=ContΓ2+ContΓ1+12⁢ContΓa0+12⁢ContΓb0−2⁢c2,0,

where the two factors of 12 are the automorphisms of Γa0 and Γb0.

Set Q=q⁢eτ⁡(q) and L=(1−55⁢q)−1/5, where τ⁡(q)=I1⁢(q)/I0⁢(q)−log⁡q is the ordinary mirror shift. We now apply stable quotient wall crossing to obtain the exact identity

F2GW⁢(Q)=I0⁢(q)2⁢F2SQ⁢(q).

Introducing Du=L−1⁢q⁢ddq and the generators

𝒳k=Duk⁢log⁡I0L,𝒴k=Duk⁢log⁡I0⁢I1,1L2,I1,1=1+q⁢dτdq,Du⁢L=15⁢(L5−1),

the individual twisted graph contributions involve extra generators. The important point for us is that these cancel in the above linear combination and leave precisely the finite generation variables. Writing X=𝒳1 and Y1=𝒴1, we obtain

F2GW⁢(Q)=I02L2⁢( 709⁢𝒳3+57518⁢X⁢𝒳2+55772⁢X3+56⁢Y1⁢𝒳2
−62972⁢Y1⁢X2−2324⁢Y12⁢X−124⁢Y13
+12536⁢𝒳2⁢L4−524⁢X2⁢L4−359⁢Y1⁢X⁢L4−524⁢Y12⁢L4
−1441300⁢X⁢L3−41300⁢Y1⁢L3+314597200⁢X⁢L8+21417200⁢Y1⁢L8
+2962112000⁢L12−11636936000⁢L7+547750⁢L2).

If we expand at large radius, then we obtain

F2GW⁢(Q)=−5144+57548⁢Q+51252⁢Q2+79303756⁢Q3+O⁡(Q4),

and these coefficients are the Gromov-Witten invariants N2,d, not the BPS integers of Table 2.

We now turn to the formal route. The Givental-Teleman formula for Ω2,0λ is a sum over the seven stable graphs of genus two with no legs, which are drawn in Figure 7. Only R−1⁢(z) through z3 is needed, and the translations expand the seven topologies into 17 decorated strata.

Remark 8.12.

These are dual graphs of stable curves and are not the graphs of Figure 5, which are the rigid tropical types obtained by applying the tropical decomposition formula to the reduced theory of the log GLSM. The two lists of topologies happen to coincide here, but a vertex means something different in each. Here it is a component of the domain curve carrying a topological field theory tensor. There it is a level of a bipartite tropical curve carrying either a log or an ∞-vertex moduli problem.

For the formal route, we define the normalized potential intrinsically by

P2λ≔YI02⁢F2λ,Y=L5.

The complete graph sum lies in ℚ⁡[L,𝒳1,𝒳2,𝒳3,𝒴1] and equals

P2λ= −1128⁢L12−23960⁢L8⁢𝒳1−9640⁢L8⁢𝒴1+10916000⁢L7
−380⁢L4⁢𝒳12−19320⁢L4⁢𝒳1⁢𝒴1−380⁢L4⁢𝒴12−164⁢L4⁢𝒳2
+191920⁢L3⁢𝒳1−4748000⁢L2
−671152⁢𝒳13−1011152⁢𝒳12⁢𝒴1−548⁢𝒳1⁢𝒴12−124⁢𝒴13
−25288⁢𝒳1⁢𝒳2−148⁢𝒳2⁢𝒴1−191152⁢𝒳3.

For clarity, this is the exact formal λ-twisted answer and is not F2GW. Note also that Y=L5 is the discriminant generator while 𝒴1 is a logarithmic derivative generator.

8.9 Finite generation and the extended family.

Recall the finitely generated ring ℛ=ℚ⁡[A,B1,B2,B3,Y] from above, which we will grade by

deg⁡A=deg⁡B1=1,deg⁡B2=2,deg⁡B3=3,deg⁡Y=0.

For ϕk=I1,1⁢⋯⁢Ik,k⁢Hk as before, set

Ω~g,nλ≔5g−1⁢(YI02)g−1⁢Ωg,nλ,τ.
Theorem 8.13 (Graded finite generation [GJR18]).

We have

Ω~g,nλ⁢(ϕa1,…,ϕan)∈⨁k≥0λ5⁢k⁢H2⁢(3⁢g−3+∑iai−5⁢k)⁢(ℳ¯g,n,ℚ)⊗ℛ3⁢g−3+∑iai.

Consequently, after assembling the bipartite rest graphs, the non-equivariant component of the extended family satisfies

Pg,n𝐂=51−g⁢∫ℳ¯g,nΩ~g,n𝐂⁢(ϕ1⊗n)=(YI02)g−1⁢∫ℳ¯g,nΩg,n𝐂⁢(ϕ1⊗n)∈ℛ3⁢g−3+n.

In particular, at each fixed (g,n) only finitely many graded monomials can appear, and only R-matrix orders up to 3⁢g−3+n can contribute.

We organize the extended theory using the bipartite graph sum

Ωg,n𝐂,λ=∑Γ⁢ bipartite1|Aut⁡Γ|⁢∏v∈V∞⁢(Γ)Cgv,μv∞⁢(𝐂;a→v)⁢∏v∈V0⁢(Γ)Cgv,δ→vλ⁢(a→v)⁢∏e∈E⁡(Γ)Ve,

where C∞ is an effective or meromorphic vertex factor, Cλ is a formal zero-vertex correlator, the μv and δ→v record incident degrees, and Ve is the edge factor. The limit λ→0 is taken only after the complete graph sum. Setting 𝐂=0 leaves the formal λ-twisted leading sector. Setting 𝐂=𝐂eff and λ→0 recovers quintic Gromov-Witten theory. Differentiating a universal edge cuts it and produces the holomorphic anomaly equation, while leaving the effective vertices untouched.

To derive the holomorphic anomaly equation, write Pg𝐂≔Pg,0𝐂 and introduce

𝒰=B1,𝒱=A+2⁢B1,𝒱2=D⁢𝒰+𝒰2−𝒰⁢𝒱,𝒱3=(D+𝒱)⁢𝒱2,

together with the two non-holomorphic directions

∂1=∂𝒰,∂0=∂𝒱−𝒰⁢∂𝒱2−𝒰2⁢∂𝒱3.
Theorem 8.14 (Holomorphic anomaly equation for the extended family [GJR18]).

We have

−∂0Pg𝐂=12⁢Pg−1,2𝐂+12⁢∑g1+g2=gg1,g2≥1Pg1,1𝐂⁢Pg2,1𝐂,−∂1Pg𝐂=0.

We prove this by the cutting argument of Section 8.4, which works because the derivative of the R-matrix propagator is simply

5⁢ℬ∂0=ϕ¯1⊗ϕ¯1,5⁢ℬ∂1=ϕ¯0⊗ϕ¯2+ϕ¯2⊗ϕ¯0.

Derivatives of R−1 and of every edge remain inside the same graded ring, so cutting a differentiated edge closes up on lower-genus correlators in ℛ. If we set 𝐂=0, then we recover the same equations for the formal λ-twisted theory.

8.10 Boundary conditions.

We will use two sources of conditions on the holomorphic ambiguity.

First, we use regularity at the orbifold or Landau-Ginzburg point q=∞, equivalently L→0. For either the formal or an assembled extended potential Fg⋆, set

𝒫gorb,⋆≔(LI0)2⁢g−2⁢Fg⋆=Φg⋆⁢(𝒳1,𝒳2,𝒳3,𝒴1,L−1,L5).

Theorem 8.13 bounds the possible Laurent powers of L, and the formal LG/CY identification says that after analytic continuation and identification of the normalized CY and LG bases, the same formal R-matrix polynomial describes both phases. Therefore

limL→0Φg⋆⁢(𝒳1,𝒳2,𝒳3,𝒴1,L−1,L5)⁢ exists,

and for fg⁢(Y)=∑i=03⁢g−3ai,g⁢Yi with Y=L5 the quintic bound is

ai,g=0for ⁢i≤⌈3⁢(g−1)5⌉.

Note that this is a statement about the assembled normalized graph contribution, and not about individual bare meromorphic or rubber vertex correlators.

Second, we study the conifold. Set

q=5−5⁢(1+tc)−1,Tc=I1co⁢(tc)I0co⁢(tc),

where I0co,I1co form a local conifold period pair normalized so that the vanishing flat coordinate satisfies Tc=0 at the conifold. Given a rational expression f in the finite generation data, we obtain its conifold value fco by substituting the Laurent expansions of all generators as series in Tc. Theorem 8.13 gives the pole bound

Fg𝐂,co=O⁡(Tc−(2⁢g−2)),

but what we need is the stronger gap condition

Fgco=cgTc2⁢g−2+O⁡(1),

namely that every intermediate negative power Tc−(2⁢g−3),…,Tc−1 vanishes. This is 2⁢g−2 conditions and is not implied by finite generation.

Conjecture 8.15 (Formal conifold gap).

The formal λ-twisted potential has the universal leading term

Fgλ,co=(−1)g−1⁢B2⁢g2⁢g⁢(2⁢g−2)⁢Tc2⁢g−2+O⁡(1),

where B2⁢g is a Bernoulli number.

Example 8.16.

In genus two the computed expansion begins

F2λ,co=1240⁢Tc2+316000−71693600000⁢Tc+2295145000000⁢Tc2+O⁡(Tc3).

This is the genus two gap, not merely the pole order bound.

We must also consider the formal correlators with rational descendant insertions which occur in the rest graphs, namely

Cg,δ→λ⁢(a→)≔⟨H3−a1−5⁢H⁢(−5⁢Hδ1−ψ1),…,H3−an−5⁢H⁢(−5⁢Hδn−ψn)⟩g,nλ

with δi≥1 and ai∈{0,1,2,3,4}.

Conjecture 8.17 (Regularity with special insertions).

We have (Cg,δ→λ⁢(a→))co=O⁡(1).

For fixed a→ and δ→, individual terms in the ψ-expansion may have poles. Note that the assertion concerns the complete rational descendant insertion, whose negative powers cancel before the rest graph sum over a→ is taken. It is a statement about these specific formal correlators rather than about every unassembled meromorphic correlator.

We can use Conjectures 8.15 and 8.17 to transfer the gap to quintic Gromov-Witten theory. A rest graph contribution has the shape

∑a→∏v∈V∞⁢(Γ)I02⁢gv−2+ℓ⁡(μv)⁢Cgv,μv∞⁢(a→v)⁢∏v∈V0⁢(Γ)Cgv,δ→vλ⁢(a→v),

and the C∞ factors are finite polynomials in q, so they are conifold regular. Then the formal leading gap together with regularity of the special correlators implies the gap for the extended family, and therefore for the quintic.

Remark 8.18.

Conjectures 8.15 and 8.17 are open in general, but have been verified for the quintic through g≤5 by Guo-Janda-Ruan. The pole bound for the extended family is a theorem, and the gap follows from the two conjectures and is proved for g≤5 by explicit computation. At the time of these lectures, the all-genus gap for quintic Gromov-Witten theory was therefore conditional on them and unconditional for g≤5.13

Putting all of this together, we begin with the Picard-Fuchs data and compute the Givental R-matrix and the operator Sτ⁢(z). We then obtain the formal stable graphs and meromorphic rest graphs, use the holomorphic anomaly equation and finite generation, and finally impose the orbifold and conifold boundary conditions to determine FgGW.

9 Structure of higher-genus GW theory of local ℙ1 (Shuai Guo)

This lecture is based on joint work with Jingyi Xu and Qingsheng Zhang.

9.1 The geometry of Xp.

We will consider the total space

Xp≔Tot⁡(𝒪ℙ1⁢(p−1)⊕𝒪ℙ1⁢(−p−1)),

which is a non-compact toric Calabi-Yau threefold. For p=0 this is the resolved conifold.

Let N≃ℤ3 be a lattice of rank 3 and let M≔Hom⁡(N,ℤ) be the dual lattice, which we identify with the characters of 𝕋≃(ℂ×)3. The one-dimensional cones of the fan of Xp are generated by

b1=(1−p,−1,1),b2=(0,1,1),b3=(1,0,1),b4=(0,0,1),

and Xp contains 𝕋 as an open dense subset. Using the dual vector e3∨∈M we obtain the Calabi-Yau subtorus

𝕋′≔ker(χe3∨:𝕋→ℂ×)≃(ℂ×)2,

whose action preserves the Calabi-Yau form. The toric graph consists of two triangles, which correspond to the two fixed points of the torus action. The weights of the 𝕋′-action at the first fixed point are

(0,1),(1,0),(−1,−1),

and at the second fixed point they are

(0,−1),(1,1−p),(−1,p).

We can therefore express the invariants in terms of equivariant cohomology by localizing at these two fixed points. Here, H𝕋′∗⁢(pt)=ℂ⁡[λ1,λ2].

Unfortunately, for p≥2 the toric graph of Xp is not convex. Then Xp is not semiprojective. This is the reason the case at hand is not covered by the existing literature, as we will explain in Section 9.5.

9.2 The conjecture of CGMPS.

In 2007, Caporaso, Griguolo, Mariño, Pasquetti, and Seminara studied the Gromov-Witten theory of Xp. Writing

FˇXp⁢(w,ℏ)≔∑g≥0FˇgXp⁢(w)⁢ℏ2⁢g−2

for the total free energy, they computed the genus-one part exactly and proposed the ansatz

(2) FˇgXp=𝒫~g⁢(w,p)(w−wc)5⁢g−5,𝒫~g⁢(w,p)=∑i=15⁢g−5ag,i⁢(p)⁢(w−1)i

for g≥2. Here, the variable w is related to the Kähler parameter q by w=1−q and wc=1−1p2. Our convention will differ by FgXp=(−1)g−1⁢FˇgXp for g≥2.

Analyzing the asymptotics of the genus-zero invariants, CGMPS defined the scaled string coupling by

z5/2=ℏ−2⁢p84⁢wc5⁢(w−wc)5

and introduced the double-scaling limit Fds⁢(z), which is obtained from FˇXp⁢(w,ℏ) by letting w→wc and ℏ→0 with z fixed. Combining their genus-zero and genus-one results with the ansatz gives

Fds⁢(z)=−415⁢z5/2−148⁢log⁡z+∑g≥2bg⁢z−5⁢(g−1)/2,

where bg=(p84⁢wc5)g−1⁢𝒫~g⁢(wc,p).

Conjecture 9.1 (CGMPS [Cap+07]).

The double-scaling limit Fds⁢(z) coincides with the free energy F(3,2)⁢(z) of the (3,2) minimal model.

The free energy of the (3,2) minimal model has the form

F(3,2)⁢(z)=−415⁢z5/2−148⁢log⁡z+∑g≥2ag⁢z−5⁢(g−1)/2,ag=41−g(3⁢g−3)!⁢⟨τ23⁢g−3⟩g,

where

⟨τ23⁢g−3⟩g≔∫ℳ¯g,3⁢g−3ψ12⁢⋯⁢ψ3⁢g−32,

so we see that Conjecture 9.1 is equivalent to the statement that bg=ag for all g≥2.

9.3 The main results.

The global mirror symmetry picture of Section 8 applies here as well. Our goal is to describe the behavior of FgXp at the three boundary points of the one-dimensional B-model moduli space. The limit q→0 is the large complex structure limit and gives the Gromov-Witten expansion in the A-model variable Q. At q→1, we will use the framed R-matrix to prove that Fg remains regular. The interesting point is q→1p2, which is a higher-order critical point. Unlike an ordinary conifold singularity, whose genus-g leading pole has order 2⁢g−2, this degeneration has pole order at most 5⁢g−5. Its leading coefficient is governed by the (3,2) minimal model.

Theorem 9.2.

For any integer p≥2 and any g≥2, the Gromov-Witten potential of Xp is computed by the Eynard-Orantin topological recursion of a spectral curve 𝒞, namely

FgXp⁢(Q)=(−1)g−1⁢ℱgXp⁢(q).

In particular, this gives a non-semiprojective toric Calabi-Yau example of the remodeling conjecture.

Theorem 9.3.

For g≥2, the potential FgXp is the expansion of a rational function

FgXp=(−1)g−1⁢𝒫g⁢(Δ,p2)Δ5⁢g−5,Δ≔1−p2⁢q1−q=p2⁢(w−wc)w,

where 𝒫g∈1(p2−1)2⁢g−2⁢ℚ⁢[p2]⁢[Δ]≤5⁢g−5.

In particular, this proves the structural ansatz Equation 2.

To identify the double-scaling limit, it remains to determine the constant term of 𝒫g at Δ=0.

Theorem 9.4.

The constant term of 𝒫g is

𝒫g⁢(0,p2)=p6⁢g−6(p2−1)2⁢g−2⁢1(3⁢g−3)!⁢⟨τ23⁢g−3⟩g.

Because 𝒫~g⁢(wc,p)=𝒫g⁢(0,p2)⁢(1p2−1p4)5⁢g−5, Theorem 9.4 gives

bg=41−g(3⁢g−3)!⁢⟨τ23⁢g−3⟩g=ag,

which proves Conjecture 9.1.

9.4 Gromov-Witten theory of Xp.

For the equivariant theory of local curves and its localization formulas, see [BP08].

Because Xp is noncompact, the moduli space ℳ¯g,0⁢(Xp,d) is not proper and the degree of the virtual class is not defined a priori. To define the invariants, we will introduce a torus action and pass to a twisted theory on ℙ1, where we can apply virtual localization.

We choose a framing f∈ℤ and let 𝕋f≔ker⁡(λ2−f⁢λ1). The two localized weight rows, each of which includes one zero weight, are

[0f1−f−1],[−f01−f⁢p+f−1+f⁢p].

If f≠0, then rescaling the character gives an equivalent symmetric weight vector

[1−1−𝔣𝔣],𝔣=1−p+2f,

and we denote the adjusted torus by 𝕋𝔣. If H𝕋𝔣∗⁢(pt)=ℂ⁡[λ], this normalization is

λ1=−2𝔣⁢λ,λ2=−2⁢λ.

Let π:ℳ¯g,1⁢(ℙ1,d)→ℳ¯g,0⁢(ℙ1,d) be the forgetful map and let ev be the evaluation at the marking. Then we define

Ng,dXp≔∫[ℳ¯g,0⁢(ℙ1,d)]𝕋𝔣vire𝕋𝔣−1⁢(R∙⁢π∗⁢ev∗⁡(𝒪⁡(p−1)⊕𝒪⁡(−p−1))),

where e𝕋𝔣 is the equivariant Euler class. For p=0 this specializes to the usual resolved conifold formula.

We obtain a CohFT Ωλ,𝔣 with state space the equivariant cohomology ring

H𝕋𝔣∗⁢(ℙ1)=ℂ⁡[H,λ](H+λ)⁢(H−λ)

and pairing

(a,b)≔∫ℙ1a∪b∪e𝕋𝔣−1⁢(𝒪⁡(p−1)⊕𝒪⁡(−p−1)).

In the flat basis {𝟏,H} the Gram matrix is given by

1((p−𝔣)2−1)⁢((p+𝔣)2−1)⁢(2⁢𝔣⁢p⁢λ−3(1−𝔣2−p2)⁢λ−2(1−𝔣2−p2)⁢λ−22⁢𝔣⁢p⁢λ−1).

We define the correlators by

Ωg,nλ,𝔣⁢(α1,…,αn)≔∑d≥0st∗⁡(∏i=1nevi∗⁡αi∩[ℳ¯g,n⁢(ℙ1,d)]vir,λ,𝔣)⁢e−d⁢t,

where st is the forgetful map to ℳ¯g,n. The twisted virtual class is given by

[ℳ¯g,n⁢(ℙ1,d)]vir,λ,𝔣≔e𝕋𝔣−1⁢(R∙⁢π∗⁢ev∗⁡(𝒪⁡(p−1)⊕𝒪⁡(−p−1)))∩[ℳ¯g,n⁢(ℙ1,d)]𝕋𝔣vir.

Set Q=(−1)p+1⁢e−t. Then the genus-g potential is given by

FgXp⁢(t)=∫ℳ¯gΩg,0λ,𝔣.
Remark 9.5.

The degree-positive invariants Ng,d≥1Xp are independent of 𝔣 by the topological vertex [LLLZ09], and their λ-independence also follows from Theorem 9.8. We will use the 𝔣-independence in the proof of Theorem 9.3.

In genus zero, we have

N0,dXp=(−1)(p+1)⁢d−1d3⁢(p2⁢d−1d−1),d≥1,

which allows us to compute the Yukawa coupling exactly:

Y=−∂t3F0Xp⁢(t)=1−𝔣2−p2((p−𝔣)2−1)⁢((p+𝔣)2−1)+qp2⁢q−1.

Here, q and Q are related by the mirror map Q=q⁢(1−q)p2−1. Evaluating the quantum product using (v1⋆v2,v3)=Ω0,3λ,𝔣⁢(v1,v2,v3), we obtain

H⋆H=−(𝔣2−1)⁢q+1p2⁢q−1⁢λ2⁢𝟏−2⁢𝔣⁢p⁢qp2⁢q−1⁢λ⁢H,

or in matrix form

H⋆=(0−(𝔣2−1)⁢q+1p2⁢q−1⁢λ21−2⁢𝔣⁢p⁢qp2⁢q−1⁢λ).

The eigenvalues Lα of this matrix are generically distinct. Then Ωλ,𝔣 is semisimple. We write {eα} for the idempotent basis, Δα−1=(eα,eα) for the lengths, and e¯α≔Δα1/2⁢eα for the normalized canonical basis.

Because the theory is semisimple, Theorem 3.24 gives

Ωλ,𝔣=R.TR.(⨁β=01ΩβKW),

where ΩβKW is a one-dimensional trivial CohFT and TR⁢(z)=z⁢(𝟏~−R−1⁢(z)⁢𝟏) with 𝟏~≔∑βe¯β. We determine the R-matrix from the quantum differential equation

z⁢dSτ⁡(z)=dτ⋆τSτ⁢(z).

Equivariant localization and quantum Riemann-Roch relate the fundamental solution to the R-matrix by

(Sτ∗⁢(z)⁢𝟏,e¯α)|q=0⁢Cα⁢(z)=(𝟏,R⁡(z)⁢e¯α)⁢euα⁢(q)/z,

where the initial condition Cα⁢(z) is an exponential involving Bernoulli numbers. Writing Ri⁢α¯⁢(z)≔(R∗⁢(z)⁢Hi,e¯α), we obtain from the quantum differential equation the second-order equation

((z⁢D+Lα)2+2⁢𝔣⁢p⁢qp2⁢q−1⁢λ⁢(z⁢D+Lα)+(𝔣2−1)⁢q+1p2⁢q−1⁢λ2)⁢R0⁢α¯=0,

where D=−∂t. We can then compute the R-matrix order by order in z.

9.5 Topological recursion and the remodeling conjecture.

We now pass to the B-model side. Our goal is to identify the reconstruction supplied by topological recursion with the Givental-Teleman reconstruction above. The Eynard–Orantin topological recursion [EO07] takes as input a spectral curve (Σ,x,y,B), where Σ is a Riemann surface; x is locally defined with meromorphic differential dx having finitely many simple zeros; y is holomorphic near those zeros, with dy≠0 there; and B is a fundamental bidifferential on Σ×Σ. Near a zero zβ of dx, let z¯≠z be the local conjugate point with x⁡(z¯)=x⁡(z) and define the recursion kernel

Kβ⁢(z0,z)≔∫z¯zB⁡(z0,z′)2⁢(y⁡(z)−y⁡(z¯))⁢d⁢x⁢(z).

If we set ω0,0=ω1,0=0, ω0,1⁢(z)=y⁡(z)⁢dx⁡(z), and ω0,2⁢(z1,z2)=B⁡(z1,z2), then the multi-differentials are defined recursively for 2⁢g−2+n+1>0 by

ωg,n+1⁢(z0,z[n])= ∑βResz=zβ⁡Kβ⁢(z0,z)
⋅(ωg−1,n+2⁢(z,z¯,z[n])
+∑′g1+g2=gI⊔J=[n]′⁢ωg1,|I|+1⁢(z,zI)⁢ωg2,|J|+1⁢(z¯,zJ)),

where the primed sum excludes ω0,1. For g≥2 the free energy is given by

ℱg=ωg,0≔12−2⁢g⁢∑βResz=zβ⁡ωg,1⁢(z)⁢∫z′=zβzω0,1⁢(z′).

The remodeling conjecture [BKMP09] of Bouchard, Klemm, Mariño, and Pasquetti asserts that the all-genus open and closed Gromov-Witten invariants of a toric Calabi-Yau threefold X coincide with the invariants ωg,n produced by topological recursion on its mirror curve. It was proved for ℂ3, the resolved conifold, and local curves by Eynard-Orantin, Zhou, and Chen-Li-Liu. Then Fang–Liu–Zong [FLZ20] proved it for all semiprojective toric Calabi-Yau threefolds. Unfortunately, Xp is not semiprojective for p≥2, so it falls outside the scope of that proof.

To compare the two sides we use the reconstruction of Dunin-Barkowski, Orantin, Shadrin, and Spitz [DOSS14], which identifies the stable topological recursion correlators with the Givental reconstruction of a semisimple CohFT. Around each critical point zβ, define the local Airy coordinate ηβ⁢(z) by

x⁡(z)=x⁡(zβ)+12⁢(ηβ⁢(z))2

and the globally defined meromorphic reference form

dζβ¯⁡(z)≔−Resz′=zβ⁡B⁡(z′,z)ηβ⁢(z′).

The state space V of the associated CohFT is spanned by the basis {e¯β} corresponding to the critical points, and the pairing is diagonal with η⁡(e¯β,e¯γ)=δβ,γ. The curve R-matrix Rˇ is defined by the asymptotic Laplace transform

u2⁢π⁢u⁢∫ℒγe−x⁡(z)/u⁢dζβ¯⁡(z)≍e−xγ/u⁢η⁢(e¯γ,Rˇ∗⁢(−u)⁢e¯β),

and the analogous transform of dy defines T⁡(u), and if the resulting CohFT has a flat unit, then T⁡(u)=u⁢(𝟏~−Rˇ−1⁢(u)⁢𝟏). Then Rˇ is symplectic, the curve CohFT is Ωˇ=Rˇ.T.(⨁βΩβKW), and writing dζkβ¯≔(−d∘1d⁢x)k⁢dζβ¯, the correspondence reads

ωg,n⁢(z1,…,zn)= ∑k1,…,kn≥0β1,…,βn∈[N](∫ℳ¯g,nΩˇg,n⁢(e¯β1⁢ψ1k1,…,e¯βn⁢ψnkn))
⋅∏i=1ndζkiβi⁡(zi).

For Xp, we will consider the spectral curve

𝒞𝔣=(ℙ1,x𝔣⁢(z),y⁡(z),B⁡(z1,z2)=dz1⁢dz2(z1−z2)2),x𝔣⁢(z)=x⁡(z)+2⁢𝔣⁢λ2⁢y⁢(z),

where

x⁡(z) =t0+λ⁢log⁡q+λ⁡(p−1)⁢log⁡z+λ⁡(−p−1)⁢log⁡q−z1−z,
y⁡(z) =p+12⁢λ⁢log⁡(1−q)+12⁢λ⁢log⁡z−12⁢λ⁢log⁡(1−z)−12⁢λ⁢log⁡(q−z).

Solving dx𝔣=0, we obtain the critical points

zα=1−𝖫α1+𝔣+p⁢𝖫α,𝖫α=λ−1⁢Lα,q=𝖫α2−1(p⁢𝖫α+1)2−1,

and the inner products are given by η⁡(eα,eβ)=δα,β⁢y′⁢(zα)2x𝔣′′⁢(zα). Then the resulting lengths satisfy Δˇα=Δα. Therefore, the Frobenius structure of the spectral curve is the quantum product of Xp.

We have now matched the Frobenius structures, so it remains to match the two R-matrices. Integration by parts on the Lefschetz thimbles gives

u⁢∂t0(e−xγ/u⁢Rˇ∗⁢(−u)𝟏γ¯) =−e−xγ/u⁢Rˇ∗⁢(−u)Hγ¯,
u⁢∂t0(e−xγ/u⁢Rˇ∗⁢(−u)Hγ¯) =−λ⁢b⁢(q)⁢e−xγ/u⁢Rˇ∗⁢(−u)Hγ¯−λ2⁢c⁢(q)⁢e−xγ/u⁢Rˇ∗⁢(−u)𝟏γ¯,

where

c⁡(q)=−(𝔣2−1)⁢q+1p2⁢q−1,b⁡(q)=−2⁢𝔣⁢p⁢qp2⁢q−1

are exactly the entries of the quantum product computed above, so these agree with the quantum differential equation for the Gromov-Witten R-matrix. To match the initial conditions, we take the limit q→0 of the Laplace transforms along the thimbles, which produces Beta functions and therefore products of Gamma functions. Then Stirling’s expansion matches the Bernoulli-number initial condition Cα⁢(z).

Proposition 9.6.

The two R-matrices coincide, namely R⁡(z)=Rˇ⁢(u)|u=−z.

We have now shown that the canonical lengths and the R-matrices agree. After the substitution u=−z, the genus-g stable graph sums differ by the overall parity (−1)3⁢g−3=(−1)g−1, which proves Theorem 9.2.

9.6 Rationality.

Because the higher-genus potential is independent of 𝔣, we may, for simplicity, set 𝔣=0. This simplifies both the canonical basis and the quantum differential equation, and the latter becomes

((z⁢D+Lα)2−1−q1−p2⁢q⁢λ2)⁢R0⁢α¯=0,Lα=(−1)α⁢λ⁢L,L=(1−q1−p2⁢q)1/2,

and we denote the entries of the R-matrix by (Rk)iα. Set

Δ≔1L2=1−p2⁢q1−q,ℛ≔ℚ⁡[p2,Δ],ℛ≤d≔{P∈ℛ|degΔ⁡P≤d}.

We now use induction on the coefficients of the quantum differential equation to obtain a polynomial structure.

Proposition 9.7.

For k∈ℤ≥0 and i=0,1, we have

(Rk)iα∈1(p2−1)k⁢λk−i⁢Δ(3⁢k+i)/2⁢ℛ≤2⁢k.

Analyzing the degree contributions of the stable graph sum in the Givental-Teleman reconstruction, and tracking the powers of λ, Δ, and p2−1, we obtain the following.

Theorem 9.8.

Writing [⋅]d for the codimension-d component, we have

[Ωg,nλ⁢(Ha1,…,Han)]d∈ λ3⁢g−3−d+∑iai(p2−1)d−(g−1)⁢Δ12⁢(g−1+3⁢d+∑iai)⁢ℛ≤2⁢d
⊗H2⁢d⁢(ℳ¯g,n,ℚ).

Taking n=0 and d=3⁢g−3=dimℳ¯g in Theorem 9.8 gives

FgXp∈1(p2−1)2⁢g−2⁢Δ5⁢g−5⁢ℛ≤6⁢g−6,

so Theorem 9.3 will follow if the degree of the numerator in Δ is bounded by 5⁢g−5. We can see this bound at q=1. Because Δ has a simple pole there, regularity of FgXp forces the numerator to cancel the highest powers of Δ. We have therefore reduced rationality to regularity at q=1. This regularity follows from the 𝔣-independence of FgXp together with the existence of the limit q→1 of the R-matrix for 𝔣≠0.

9.7 The limit Δ=0.

To determine the remaining constant term, we now study the limit Δ=0, which is precisely the double-scaling limit. We rescale the canonical lengths by

δα≔Δ1/2⁢Δα=(−1)α+1⁢2⁢(p2−1)⁢λ3

and define the modified R-matrix entries by isolating the leading terms at Δ=0 in Proposition 9.7, namely

(R¯k)iα≔[(−1)k⁢(Rk)iα⁢Δ(3⁢k+i)/2]|Δ=0,i=0,1.

Then the graph sum for FgXp becomes a formula for 𝒫g⁢(0,p2) after replacing Δα by δα and (Rk)iα by (R¯k)iα.

Lemma 9.9.

Solving the leading-order quantum differential equation at Δ=0 gives the closed forms

(R¯k)0α =p2⁢k(p2−1)k⁢λk⁢(−1)k⁢α⁢∏n=1k(6⁢n−7)⁢(6⁢n+1)48⁢n,
(R¯k)1α =p2⁢k(p2−1)k⁢λk−1⁢(−1)(k−1)⁢α⁢1−6⁢k1+6⁢k⁢∏n=1k(6⁢n−7)⁢(6⁢n+1)48⁢n.

After factoring out the p-dependent terms in Lemma 9.9, we obtain purely rational coefficients. We now construct the topological field theory Ωtop on V=span⁡{ϕ0,ϕ1} with unit ϕ0, where

(ϕ0,ϕ0)=(ϕ1,ϕ1)=0,(ϕ0,ϕ1)=−1,ϕ1⋆ϕ1=ϕ0.

Applying reconstruction by R⁡(z) together with its flat-unit translation, we obtain a constant Cg with

𝒫g⁢(0,p2)=p6⁢g−6(p2−1)2⁢g−2⁢Cg,

and it remains to identify the reconstructed CohFT.

The (2,3) minimal model has spectral curve

x⁡(z)=13⁢(z3−3⁢ε2⁢z)+τ0,y⁡(z)=12⁢(z2−2),

with flat coordinate τ1=ε4/2. If we set τ0=0 and ε=1 and identify ϕ0=∂τ0 and ϕ1=∂τ1, then the R-matrix obtained from Xp at Δ=0 coincides with the R-matrix of this curve. Therefore, Cg is exactly the free energy of the (2,3) minimal model.

Finally, we apply the symplectic swap (x,y)↦(y,−x), under which the curve becomes

x⁡(z)=12⁢(z2−2),y⁡(z)=−13⁢(z3−3⁢z).

The swapped curve has one-dimensional state space, trivial R-matrix, and translation T⁡(u)=u2⁢e¯, so that

Cg=1(3⁢g−3)!⁢⟨τ23⁢g−3⟩g,

which is Theorem 9.4. Note that this swap is the correspondence between the (2,3) and the (3,2) minimal models, which is why the intersection numbers appearing here are those of Conjecture 9.1.
